question: M2
answer:
Current US national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 (health-based), as codified in 40 CFR Part 50:

| Pollutant / averaging time | Primary standard level | Statistical form | Regulatory basis |
|---|---:|---|---|
| PM2.5 annual | 9.0 µg/m³ | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, averaged over 3 years; standard is met when the 3-year average annual arithmetic mean is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³ | 40 CFR 50.20; 89 FR 16202 (Mar. 6, 2024), effective May 6, 2024 |
| PM2.5 24-hour | 35 µg/m³ | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 years; standard is met when the 3-year average of the annual 98th percentile 24-hour concentration is ≤ 35 µg/m³ | 40 CFR 50.20; retained from the prior PM2.5 standards |

Answer in brief:
- Annual primary PM2.5 standard: 9.0 µg/m³.
- 24-hour primary PM2.5 standard: 35 µg/m³.

Source notes and caveats:
1. The 2024 reconsideration final rule strengthened the primary annual PM2.5 standard from the prior 2012 level of 12.0 µg/m³ to 9.0 µg/m³. The older 12.0 µg/m³ annual value appearing in older §50.18 text is superseded and is not the current annual standard.
2. The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard was not changed by the 2024 reconsideration and remains 35 µg/m³.
3. EPA’s March 12, 2025 announcement concerning a path forward/reconsideration of the PM2.5 NAAQS is not itself a final rule changing the codified standards. Unless and until a later final rule is promulgated, the codified levels remain 9.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour.
4. Measurement is by FRM/FEM methods under 40 CFR Part 50 Appendix L and Part 53; data handling and attainment determinations follow 40 CFR Part 50 Appendix N.
5. Only the primary standards were requested. Secondary PM2.5 standards are not addressed in this answer and should not be inferred from this table.

question: M4
answer:
ANSWER

In general industry (US federal OSHA, 29 CFR Part 1910), the trigger height is 4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level. An employer must protect each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level from falling.

PRIMARY CITATION

- 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'
- Corroborating catch-all: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) ('Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed') — 'the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or ...' (verified in the current eCFR text of 1910.28).

SCOPE / DEFINITIONS

- 'General industry' = 29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D (Walking-Working Surfaces), specifically 1910.28 (Duty to have fall protection and falling object protection) and 1910.29 (Fall protection systems and falling object protection — criteria and practices).
- 'Walking-working surface' is used in the Subpart D sense: any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location (1910.21(b)).
- The height is measured from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the lower level below the unprotected side or edge; 4 ft is a threshold, not a tolerance — at exactly 4 ft (1.2 m) protection is required.
- Construction is a different regime: 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) uses 6 feet (1.8 m). That 6-ft figure does not apply to general industry and should not be substituted for the 4-ft answer.

EXCEPTIONS AND DIFFERENT TRIGGERS WITHIN SUBPART D (do not override the 4-ft general rule, but replace it for the listed conditions)

- Fixed ladders: the height-based requirement in 1910.28(b)(9) applies to fixed ladders extending more than 24 feet (7.3 m) above a lower level (personal fall arrest or ladder safety system); other fixed-ladder provisions (e.g., cage/well/personal fall arrest phase-in dates) are keyed to that same 24-ft line.
- Rope descent systems: 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) — employee using a rope descent system 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level must be protected by a personal fall arrest system.
- Low-slope roofs: 1910.28(b)(13) is keyed to horizontal distance from the roof edge, not height — less than 6 ft from the edge: guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest; 6 ft to less than 15 ft: same systems, or a designated area for infrequent and temporary work; 15 ft or more: designated area plus a work rule prohibiting employees from going within 15 ft of the edge without fall protection.
- Open pits: 1910.28(b)(8) — for pits that are 4 feet (1.2 m) or more deep (i.e., the same 4-ft logic), the employer must use guardrail systems, fences, barricades, or covers, or may instead limit access within 6 ft of the edge to trained authorized employees, apply contrasting floor markings/warning lines at least 6 ft from the edge, and post 'Caution—Open Pit' signs.
- Slaughtering facility platforms: 1910.28(b)(14) — unprotected working side of a platform 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level requires guardrails or travel restraint (with a documented infeasibility allowance).
- Scaffolds: 1910.28(b)(12)(i) defers to 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart L (construction scaffold criteria), i.e., 10 ft for scaffolds — a cross-reference, not the general-industry walking-working-surface trigger.
- Stairways, dockboards, and other surfaces addressed elsewhere in 1910.28 or other subparts of Part 1910 have their own requirements ('except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part').
- Where guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection systems are infeasible or would create a greater hazard, 1910.28(b)(1) permits an alternative only through a documented fall protection plan meeting 1910.29(k); it does not lower the 4-ft trigger.

RELATED COMPLIANCE POINTS (consequences of crossing the 4-ft trigger)

- Accepted protection: guardrail systems (1910.29(b)), safety net systems (1910.29(c)), personal fall protection systems — personal fall arrest, travel restraint, positioning (1910.29(d)-(f)), and covers for holes (1910.29(e)/(b)(4) as applicable).
- Training: employees exposed to fall hazards must be trained per 1910.30 (hazard recognition, procedures, equipment use, and retraining on deficiency); equipment must be inspected per 1910.29/1910.30 before use.
- State-plan states (e.g., California, Washington, Michigan) must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and may be stricter; where a state plan applies, verify its walking-working-surfaces rule. The 4-ft federal general-industry figure is the baseline answer to this question.

ONE-LINE ANSWER

4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level — 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) (and 1910.28(b)(15)).

question: M6
answer:
RESERVE FUEL FOR A HELICOPTER BEGINNING A VFR FLIGHT IN THE UNITED STATES

ANSWER (the value requested)

20 minutes. A helicopter (legally, a rotorcraft) may not begin a VFR flight in the United States unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

This 20-minute figure is the same in the general operating rules and in the commercial (air-taxi) rules, and it is the same by day and by night. There is no separate night reserve for helicopters the way there is for airplanes.

1. CONTROLLING REGULATIONS

1.1 Part 91 (general/private operations) - 14 CFR 91.151(b), 'Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions':

  '(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

Note the regulation uses 'rotorcraft,' not 'helicopter'; every helicopter is a rotorcraft, so the 20-minute rule applies to helicopters without qualification.

1.2 Part 135 (commercial/air-taxi operations) - 14 CFR 135.209(b), 'VFR: Fuel supply':

  '(b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

1.3 Confirmation from FAA guidance (FAA document at faa.gov/media/32056, item 15, 'FAR Part 135 Helicopter VFR Operations'):

  'Reserve Fuel. FAR 135.209(b). During day or night the required reserve fuel is the amount that allows continued operation for 20 minutes.'

That single sentence settles the two questions that most often produce a wrong answer: the helicopter figure is 20 minutes, and it does not change at night.

2. THE TRAPS THAT PRODUCE WRONG ANSWERS

2.1 Do not use the airplane numbers. 91.151(a) and 135.209(a) give airplanes 30 minutes by day and 45 minutes at night. Those are the airplane paragraphs. The rotorcraft/helicopter paragraphs - 91.151(b) and 135.209(b) - carry a flat 20 minutes and contain no day/night subdivision. A helicopter pilot who plans 30 or 45 minutes is planning above the legal minimum, not to it.

2.2 Night does not change the helicopter minimum. The 45-minute night figure in 91.151(a)(2) and 135.209(a)(2) applies to airplanes only. For helicopters, 20 minutes governs day and night alike.

2.3 Part 135 does not raise the helicopter VFR reserve. Both the Part 91 and the Part 135 helicopter VFR paragraphs read 20 minutes. What Part 135 adds is not a bigger reserve but documentation and preflight-analysis obligations (and, for IFR, a different rule set entirely).

2.4 This is not the IFR rule. 14 CFR 91.167 and 135.223 govern IFR fuel and alternate requirements and are outside the scope of this question. If the flight is to be conducted IFR, the reserve is not 20 minutes and must be computed under those sections.

2.5 No alternate-airport fuel is required for VFR. Neither 91.151(b) nor 135.209(b) requires fuel to a VFR alternate. The requirement is fuel to the first point of intended landing, plus 20 minutes. (Prudent operators still carry diversion fuel; that is judgment, not regulation.)

3. WHAT THE 20 MINUTES IS MEASURED AGAINST

The regulation fixes the basis of computation:

  - Speed: 'normal cruising speed' (Part 91) / 'normal cruising fuel consumption' (Part 135). Not best-range speed, not maximum-range cruise, not a hover or loiter figure. Use the speed and fuel flow you will actually plan to cruise at.
  - Leg fuel: fuel to the first point of intended landing, computed considering wind and forecast weather conditions - i.e., with the forecast wind, not still-air, and with the forecast temperature/altitude effects on your fuel flow.
  - Fuel counted: usable fuel. Unusable fuel in a tank is not fuel you may credit toward the reserve.

4. CONVERTING 20 MINUTES TO A FUEL QUANTITY

20 minutes is one-third of an hour (20/60 = 0.3333). Therefore:

  Reserve quantity = (normal cruising fuel flow per hour) x (1/3)

Worked conversions (all exactly one-third of the stated hourly flow):

  Cruise flow 20 gal/h  -> reserve 6.7 gal
  Cruise flow 25 gal/h  -> reserve 8.3 gal
  Cruise flow 30 gal/h  -> reserve 10.0 gal
  Cruise flow 40 gal/h  -> reserve 13.3 gal
  Cruise flow 150 lb/h  -> reserve 50 lb
  Cruise flow 200 lb/h  -> reserve 66.7 lb
  Cruise flow 300 lb/h  -> reserve 100 lb

Pilot procedure:

  Step 1. Establish planned cruise speed and cruise fuel flow for the actual planned altitude, temperature and weight (from the RFM/POH cruise chart, not the brochure figure).
  Step 2. Compute leg fuel: distance to first point of intended landing divided by planned groundspeed (using forecast wind), times hourly flow. Add taxi, run-up, climb and any known ATC delay fuel per 91.103 preflight action.
  Step 3. Compute reserve: hourly flow divided by 3 (the 20-minute requirement).
  Step 4. Required total fuel on board at brake release = leg fuel + reserve (+ any operator/SOP contingency).
  Step 5. Compare to usable capacity; if it does not fit, the flight cannot legally be begun as planned - shorten it, add a fuel stop, or change the plan.

Worked example: helicopter cruising at 120 kt true, forecast headwind component 10 kt (groundspeed 110 kt), distance to first landing 220 nm, cruise flow 30 gal/h, usable capacity 90 gal.

  Leg time = 220 / 110 = 2.00 h; leg fuel = 2.00 x 30 = 60.0 gal.
  Reserve = 30 / 3 = 10.0 gal (20 minutes).
  Required total = 70.0 gal, against 90 gal usable. Legal, with 20 gal of margin beyond the regulatory minimum.

5. THINGS THE REGULATION DOES NOT DO

  - It does not set a gallon or pound figure; it sets a time figure that converts per aircraft.
  - It does not permit rounding the reserve down to the nearest gauge increment; plan on measured fuel, not gauge indications.
  - It does not replace 14 CFR 91.103 (preflight action), which independently requires the pilot to become familiar with all available information, including fuel requirements and known traffic delays.
  - It is a legal floor, not an operational target. Weather deterioration, ATC holding, unforecast winds, closed destinations and passenger comfort routinely argue for more; company SOPs and some operators' OpSpecs will require more. Carrying more than 20 minutes is always compliant with the minimum.

6. BOTTOM LINE

Minimum legal VFR reserve for a helicopter in the US, beyond fuel to the first point of intended landing: 20 minutes at normal cruising speed, day or night, under both Part 91 (91.151(b)) and Part 135 (135.209(b)). Convert to quantity by dividing the planned hourly cruise fuel flow by three.

The first reads: "(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 45 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-i/subchapter-f/part-91/subpart-b/subject-group-ecfr4d7cd0e3cc4be86/section-91.151 and 20 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2026-title14-vol2/pdf/cfr-2026-title14-vol2-sec91-151.pdf. The first reads: "(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes."

question: M8
answer:
# Deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1

## 1. Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1

**RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1"** (March 2021; BCP 195). Authors: K. Moriarty and S. Farrell. It was published from `draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate` (final revision -12, 2021-01-21; RFC published 2021-03-23).

Direct quotation from the RFC 8996 abstract:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346)."

RFC 8996 also deprecates **DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347)**, but explicitly **not** DTLS 1.2; the document notes there is no DTLS 1.1.

## 2. Status given to the RFCs that defined those versions

The defining documents are:

| Protocol version | Defining RFC | Title | Status after RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | **RFC 2246** | The TLS Protocol Version 1.0 (January 1999, Dierks & Allen) | **Historic** |
| TLS 1.1 | **RFC 4346** | The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1 (April 2006, Dierks & Rescorla) | **Historic** |

Direct quotation from the RFC 8996 abstract:

> "Accordingly, those documents have been moved to **Historic** status."

The RFC Editor's catalogue entries for both documents now display the status "Historic", confirming the change was applied to the documents themselves, not merely recommended.

## 3. Two distinctions worth stating explicitly (to avoid a common misreading)

1. **Historic vs. Proposed Standard.** "Historic" is the RFC status category RFC 8996 assigned to RFC 2246 and RFC 4346. It is not the status of RFC 8996 itself; RFC 8996 is a Standards-Track/BCP document (part of BCP 195, because it updates the TLS best-practices document RFC 7525).
2. **Historic vs. Obsolete.** RFC 8996 did *not* obsolete RFC 2246 or RFC 4346 — obsolescence had already occurred earlier through the normal protocol succession: RFC 4346 obsoletes RFC 2246, and RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) obsoletes RFC 4346. RFC 8996's distinct action was to move those already-obsoleted specifications into the Historic category, so that implementations and referencing documents can no longer treat TLS 1.0/1.1 as usable options. In RFC-series terms, RFC 8996 *updates* many RFCs and *reclassifies* the two protocol-defining RFCs; it does not list itself as obsoleting them.

## 4. Stated rationale (as given in RFC 8996)

- TLS 1.0 and 1.1 "lack support for current and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms."
- Government and industry application profiles using TLS now mandate avoiding these versions.
- TLS 1.2 became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008 (itself obsoleted by TLS 1.3, RFC 8446, in 2018), so there had been "sufficient time to transition away from older versions."
- Removing older versions "reduces the attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and streamlines library and product maintenance," and reduces the misconfiguration risk inherent in supporting four TLS versions simultaneously.
- The deprecation is intended to give developers "additional justification to no longer support older (D)TLS versions" and to migrate to a minimum of (D)TLS 1.2.

## 5. Normative consequences recorded in RFC 8996

- Section 1.1 ("RFCs Updated"): RFC 8996 updates the many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, or DTLS 1.0, in order to **obsolete usage** of those versions. **Fallback to these versions is prohibited.** Mandatory minimums of TLS 1.0/1.1 are replaced by **TLS 1.2**; minimum DTLS 1.0 is replaced by **DTLS 1.2**.
- It updates DTLS (RFC 6347), which had permitted negotiating DTLS 1.0 — now forbidden.
- RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites) is moved to Historic as well, since the only TLS versions for which those suites were defined are now Historic.
- RFC 7507's version-fallback SCSV is superseded in function by the TLS 1.3 sentinel-value mechanism (RFC 8446).
- RFCs 6460, 4744, and 4743 were already Historic; they are listed as updated anyway, to reiterate that any use of the obsolete protocol must use modern TLS.
- Because it updates RFC 7525, RFC 8996 is part of **BCP 195**.

## 6. Bottom line

- **Deprecating RFC:** RFC 8996 ("Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1").
- **Status conferred on the defining RFCs (RFC 2246 for TLS 1.0 and RFC 4346 for TLS 1.1):** **Historic**.

question: M10
answer:
## Answer

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI "taxable maximum") for **2026 is $184,500**.

That is the maximum amount of 2026 earnings subject to the 6.2% employee and 6.2% employer Social Security payroll tax, and it is also the maximum amount of 2026 earnings creditable toward a Social Security benefit computation.

Status: this is the **officially determined and published** figure (announced by SSA in fall 2025 as part of the 2026 cost-of-living and wage-indexed amounts), not a projection.

---

## 1. Primary sourcing

| Source | What it states |
|---|---|
| SSA, Office of the Chief Actuary — *Contribution and Benefit Base* (ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html), table "Contribution and benefit bases, 1937-2027" | 2026 = **$184,500** (2025 = 176,100; 2027 = 192,300) |
| SSA, Office of the Chief Actuary — *Automatic Determinations in Recent Years* (ssa.gov/oact/cola/autoAdj.html) | 2026 row: COLA 3.6%, contribution and benefit base **$184,500** |
| SSA, Office of the Chief Actuary — *Updating the Social Security Benefit Calculator* (ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html) | "Contribution and benefit base for 2026: **$184,500**"; "'Old-law' contribution and benefit base for 2026: $137,100" |
| SSA Publication No. 05-10024, *Your Social Security* (EN-05-10024.pdf) | "You pay Social Security taxes based on your earnings, up to a certain amount. In 2026 that amount is **$184,500**." |
| SSA, *Contribution and Benefit Base Determination* (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbbdet.html) | Confirms the 2026 base as the statutory floor in the 2027 computation ("...or, if larger, the 2026 base of $184,500") |

Four independent SSA pages plus the agency's public booklet agree, and the value is corroborated indirectly by the 2027 determination page, which uses $184,500 as the non-reduction floor.

---

## 2. Derivation (why $184,500 and not some other number)

The base is set by statute (Social Security Act §230, following the 1977 amendments) and is adjusted automatically by the national average wage index (AWI). For any year Y after 1994:

```
Base(Y) = 60,600 x [ AWI(Y-2) / AWI(1992) ] , rounded to nearest multiple of $300
```

- The formula applies only if a cost-of-living increase is effective for December of the year preceding the determination. There **is** a COLA effective December 2025 (3.6%), so the formula applies for 2026.
- The base may not be reduced below the prior year's base.

Applying it for 2026 (uses AWI for 2024, the latest available at determination time):

```
1994 base                        = $60,600
AWI 1992                         = 22,935.42
AWI 2024                         = 69,846.57
Ratio 69,846.57 / 22,935.42      = 3.045357...
60,600 x 3.045357                = $184,548.6
Round to nearest multiple of 300 = 184,500   (615 x 300 = 184,500)
```

Check against the non-reduction rule: $184,500 > $176,100 (2025 base), so the base increases; no floor applies. The result is also below the announced 2027 base of $192,300, consistent with a monotone series. The arithmetic reproduces the published figure exactly, which is the check that the stated value does not violate its own formula.

---

## 3. What this number does and does not cap (to prevent misapplication)

| Tax | 2026 wage base | Rate (employee / employer / self-employed) | Maximum 2026 tax |
|---|---|---|---|
| OASDI (Social Security) | **$184,500** | 6.2% / 6.2% / 12.4% | $11,439.00 each for employee and employer; $22,878.00 self-employed |
| HI (Medicare) | **No cap** (uncapped since 1994) | 1.45% / 1.45% / 2.90% | No maximum |
| Additional Medicare Tax | Separate threshold, not the base: $200,000 single/HoH/qualifying surviving spouse, $250,000 MFJ, $125,000 MFS | 0.9% (employee only) | Applies to wages above the filing-status threshold, independent of the $184,500 base |

Arithmetic check (each figure sits exactly at the cap, never above it):
- 184,500 x 0.062 = **$11,439.00** (employee); same for employer; combined employer+employee = $22,878.00.
- 184,500 x 0.124 = **$22,878.00** (self-employment OASDI portion).
- 2026 increase over 2025: 184,500 - 176,100 = **$8,400**, or +4.77%.

Related 2026 figures from the same determination, for payroll/benefit configuration:
- "Old-law" contribution and benefit base: **$137,100** (used for special-minimum benefits, certain Railroad Retirement purposes, and ERISA computations — not for payroll withholding).
- Earnings credit: 1 credit per **$1,890** of earnings, max 4 credits.
- Retirement earnings test exempt amounts: **$24,480** (lower, under FRA) and **$65,160** (higher, year of FRA attainment).

---

## 4. Operational application

- **Payroll withholding:** apply 6.2% employee OASDI to cumulative 2026 taxable wages only up to $184,500 per employee; stop OASDI withholding once year-to-date OASDI-taxable wages reach that amount. Do **not** stop Medicare withholding — it continues on all wages.
- **Multiple employers:** each employer withholds up to the base independently; the excess is reconciled on the individual's Form 1040 as an excess Social Security withholding credit. The base is per worker, not per job.
- **Self-employment:** Schedule SE applies the 12.4% OASDI rate to net self-employment earnings up to $184,500 (after the 92.35% factor), plus 2.9% Medicare on all net earnings.
- **W-2 reporting:** Box 3 (Social Security wages) is capped at $184,500; Box 5 (Medicare wages) is not.
- **Benefit computation:** $184,500 is also the maximum 2026 earnings creditable in the AIME/indexing computation.

---

## 5. Scope notes

- This is the **federal** OASDI figure. It is not a state disability (e.g., SDI/PFML) wage base, not a 401(a)(17)/deferred-compensation limit, and not a Railroad Retirement tier limit.
- If a projection basis is ever needed (e.g., for years beyond the announced horizon), it must be labeled provisional and derived from the same §230 formula using the applicable Trustees Report AWI assumptions — the $184,500 above is a published determination and requires no projection.

**Final value: $184,500 (2026 OASDI contribution and benefit base).**

question: M12
answer:
# 2026 401(k) Elective Deferral Limit (Before Catch-Up)

## Answer

**$24,500** per individual, per calendar year, for tax years beginning in 2026 — the limit on an employee's elective deferrals under IRC §402(g)(1), before any catch-up contribution.

This is an increase from the 2025 limit of $23,500. It is the base limit and applies regardless of the employee's age; age only affects the separate additional catch-up amount, which is excluded from this figure.

## Authority and effective date

- **IRS Notice 2025-67** (2026 cost-of-living adjustments): "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
- **IRS, Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits**: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- **IRS Publication 560**: "The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026. These limits apply for participants in SARSEPs, 401(k) plans (excluding SIMPLE plans), section 403(b) plans, and section 457(b) plans."
- **IRS, Retirement Topics — Catch-Up Contributions**: "Elective deferrals are not treated as catch-up contributions until they exceed the limit of $24,500 in 2026."

Effective for tax years beginning in 2026 (i.e., the 2026 calendar year for a calendar-year plan).

**Do not use $25,500.** That is the 2027 limit announced in IRS Notice 2026-66. It appears in the same body of IRS COLA material and is the single most likely source of a one-year error in payroll setup.

## Scope: what the $24,500 does and does not cover

**Counts toward the $24,500 (per individual, aggregated):**
- Pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals.
- Designated Roth elective deferrals to a 401(k). Roth and pre-tax deferrals share one combined limit; electing Roth does not create additional room.
- Deferrals to all 401(k) plans of the same employer and its controlled group/affiliated service group, plus 403(b) plans, SARSEPs, and governmental 457(b) plans in which the individual participates. The limit is per person, not per plan or per employer — a second job does not create a second $24,500.

**Does not count toward the $24,500:**
- Age 50+ catch-up: **$8,000** for 2026 (up from $7,500).
- SECURE 2.0 enhanced catch-up for participants attaining age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026: **$11,250** (unchanged).
- Employer matching and nonelective contributions, and forfeiture allocations — these are tested against the separate §415(c) annual-additions limit of **$72,000** for 2026 (100% of compensation, whichever is less; $80,000 including catch-up, or up to $83,250 for ages 60–63).
- Compensation taken into account is capped at **$360,000** for 2026.

**SIMPLE 401(k) is a different limit:** $17,000 for 2026 (with $4,000 standard catch-up, or $5,250 for ages 60–63). Do not apply $24,500 to a SIMPLE 401(k).

Maximum an individual can defer in 2026: $24,500 + $8,000 = **$32,500**; for an eligible age 60–63 participant, $24,500 + $11,250 = **$35,750**.

## Payroll / plan administration steps

1. **Update the deferral cap** in the payroll and recordkeeping systems to $24,500 effective with the first pay date in the 2026 plan year (or the first pay date on/after the plan year begins, for a non-calendar plan year).
2. **Per-period deferral amounts — always round down**, then true up in the final period, so no annualized amount exceeds $24,500:
   - 26 biweekly periods: $942.30 per period (26 × $942.30 = $24,499.80; final-period true-up of $0.20).
   - 24 semimonthly periods: $1,020.83 per period (24 × $1,020.83 = $24,499.92; true-up $0.08).
   - 12 monthly periods: $2,041.66 per period (12 × $2,041.66 = $24,499.92; true-up $0.08).
   - 52 weekly periods: $471.15 per period (52 × $471.15 = $24,499.80; true-up $0.20).
   Rounding *up* (e.g., $942.31 biweekly) produces $24,500.06 and an excess deferral — do not do it.
3. **Percentage elections:** dollar cap = lesser of 100% of compensation or $24,500, so a high deferral percentage on a low salary must still be capped at $24,500 and a high salary capped by the plan's own percentage terms.
4. **Confirm the plan document does not impose a lower limit.** The statutory $24,500 is a ceiling, not an entitlement; a plan may cap deferrals below it, and HCEs may be limited further to pass ADP/ACP testing.
5. **Excess deferrals:** amounts above $24,500 (excluding catch-up) are excess deferrals under §402(g)(2). They must be distributed, with allocable earnings, by April 15 of the following year to avoid double taxation; if not timely corrected, they are taxed in the year deferred and again when distributed.
6. **Employee communications** should state $24,500 as the 2026 base limit, note that pre-tax and Roth share it, and separately state the catch-up amounts ($8,000 age 50+; $11,250 for those turning 60–63 in 2026) so employees do not net the two together.

## Boundary conditions checked

- $24,500 is the pre-catch-up figure and is stated without the $8,000 or $11,250 added.
- $24,500 + $8,000 = $32,500 and $24,500 + $11,250 = $35,750, both below the $72,000 §415(c) ceiling for 2026 — no internal contradiction.
- The $25,500 figure is the 2027 limit and is excluded throughout.
- The SIMPLE 401(k) limit ($17,000) is kept distinct from the non-SIMPLE $24,500.

question: M2
answer:
CURRENT U.S. NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5 (primary/health-based, 40 CFR Part 50)

ANSWER
| Averaging period | Primary standard level | Form (how the level is judged) | Codification |
|---|---|---|---|
| Annual | 9.0 µg/m³ (annual arithmetic mean concentration) | Met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined under Appendix N to 40 CFR Part 50, is <= 9.0 µg/m³ | 40 CFR 50.20(a), (b) |
| 24-hour | 35 µg/m³ (24-hour average concentration) | Met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined under Appendix N to 40 CFR Part 50, is <= 35 µg/m³ | 40 CFR 50.20(a), (c) |

Both are measured in ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter <= a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by a reference method based on Appendix L to Part 50 and designated under Part 53, or by an equivalent method designated under Part 53.

1. REGULATORY TEXT (40 CFR 50.20, as printed in the 2025 annual CFR edition)
"(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 ... by either: (1) A reference method based on appendix L to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or (2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.
(b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m3.
(c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3."

2. WHY THESE VALUES, AND HOW A CONFLICTING SOURCE WAS RESOLVED (important — do not skip)
The standards were most recently revised by "Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter," 89 FR 16202 (Feb. 7, 2024), effective May 6, 2024 (90 days after publication). That rule:
- lowered the primary annual standard from 12.0 to 9.0 µg/m³;
- retained the primary 24-hour standard at 35 µg/m³;
- also revised the Appendix N data-handling provisions for the annual standard (including 3-year averaging of annual means and spatial-averaging provisions across eligible monitors), which is why the level alone is not the whole standard — the form in (b) and Appendix N governs.

Source conflict: an eCFR 'current' retrieval of 40 CFR 50.18 shows the older text (12.0 µg/m³ annual, 35 µg/m³ 24-hour, citing 78 FR 3277, the 2012 rule). That text is the superseded pre-2024 annual level and is inconsistent with the official 2025 annual CFR edition, which carries 40 CFR 50.20 at 9.0 µg/m³. The 9.0 µg/m³ figure is therefore the current codified primary annual level; 12.0 µg/m³ is historical and must not be reported as current. The 24-hour level is unaffected by the conflict: it was 35 µg/m³ before the 2024 rule and was retained at 35 µg/m³.

3. PRIOR VALUES (for version control / audit trails only — not the answer)
- 2012 rule (78 FR 3086; codified at 40 CFR 50.18): annual 12.0 µg/m³, 24-hour 35 µg/m³.
- 2006 rule (71 FR 61144): annual 15.0 µg/m³, 24-hour 35 µg/m³.
- 1997 rule (62 FR 38652): annual 15.0 µg/m³, 24-hour 65 µg/m³.
If a document cites 12.0 µg/m³ as the current annual standard, it predates the 2024 revision.

4. SCOPE NOTES
- Primary (health-based) standards only, as requested. Secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards are codified separately and differ for the annual averaging period (15.0 µg/m³); they are outside this answer and should not be substituted for the primary numbers above.
- Units are stated as in the regulation: micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³), one decimal place for the annual level (9.0), whole number for the 24-hour level (35).
- The level is necessary but not sufficient to determine attainment: attainment is judged by the Appendix N form at monitoring sites and by the area designations that follow each NAAQS revision. Designation/implementation status under the 2024 standard is a separate question from the standard's level.
- Status caveat: the 2024 standards remain the codified standards in the current CFR edition; the PM2.5 NAAQS have been subject to periodic agency review and litigation since promulgation, so any downstream use with a hard 'as of' date should re-verify 40 CFR 50.20 against the CFR edition in force on that date.

5. CITATIONS
- 40 CFR 50.20 (National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5), paragraphs (a)-(c).
- 40 CFR Part 50, Appendix N (Interpretation of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5).
- 40 CFR Part 50, Appendix L (Reference method for the determination of fine particulate matter as PM2.5).
- 89 FR 16202 (Feb. 7, 2024) — Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (current levels).
- 78 FR 3086 (Jan. 15, 2013) — 2012 PM2.5 NAAQS revision (superseded annual level of 12.0 µg/m³; 24-hour level of 35 µg/m³ originated earlier and was retained).
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 12.0 on ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-i/subchapter-c/part-50/section-50.18 and 15.0 on ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-i/subchapter-c/part-50. The first reads: "(b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 12.0 µg/m3."

question: M4
answer:
ANSWER

4 feet (1.2 m). Under OSHA's general industry walking-working surfaces standard, 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1), an employer must protect each employee who is on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level. The duty attaches at 4 ft 0 in measured vertically from the walking-working surface to the lower level; anything below 4 ft 0 in does not trigger 1910.28(b)(1) (though other provisions may, see below).

CONTROLLING TEXT (substance quoted from the fetched sources)

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1): 'The employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'

The residual provision, 1910.28(b)(15) 'Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed,' repeats the same trigger: 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems.'

So 4 ft is both the general rule and the default when no specific paragraph covers the surface.

SCOPE / ASSUMPTIONS THIS ANSWER RESTS ON

1. Jurisdiction and industry: US federal OSHA, general industry, 29 CFR Part 1910 Subpart D. The question explicitly excludes construction.
2. Not construction: 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) sets 6 feet for construction. If the work is construction, the answer changes to 6 ft. This is the single largest swing factor and must be confirmed from the actual task, not assumed.
3. Not shipyard (1915), longshoring (1917), or mining (MSHA).
4. No OSHA-approved State Plan with a stricter trigger. State Plans must be at least as effective as federal OSHA; a handful adopt different numbers or interpretations in specific industries. Check the State Plan for the state of the workplace.
5. No condition-specific paragraph of 1910.28 overrides (b)(1) for the surface in question. See the table below.

TERMINOLOGY THAT DRIVES THE TRIGGER

- Walking-working surface: any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location (1910.28(b) definitions in 1910.21(b)? definitions appear in 1910.21? see Subpart D definitions). Floors, roofs, platforms, ramps, stairways, ladders and step bolts, and vehicle pits all count.
- Unprotected side or edge: any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.
- '4 feet or more' is inclusive: at exactly 4 ft 0 in the protection duty exists. There is no de minimis tolerance and no 'close enough' exemption. Measure to the nearest inch and treat 47.9 in as 4 ft for prudence; do not round 47 in down to 'under 4 ft'.
- The height is measured vertically from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the lower level, at the unprotected edge, not to the next surface below the edge if that surface is itself a fall hazard.

CONDITION-SPECIFIC PROVISIONS THAT CAN ALTER OR ADD TO THE 4 FT RULE

| Condition | Provision | Trigger / effect |
|---|---|---|
| Dangerous equipment below | 1910.28(b)(6)(i) | BELOW 4 ft: an employee less than 4 ft above dangerous equipment must be protected by guardrail or travel restraint (or the equipment covered/guarded). At 4 ft or more, (b)(6)(ii) requires guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest. This is the one common case where a height under 4 ft still requires protection. |
| Holes (incl. skylights) | 1910.28(b)(3) | Fall through a hole 4 ft or more above a lower level: covers, guardrail, travel restraint, or PFA. Holes less than 4 ft: covers or guardrail to prevent tripping/stepping in. |
| Hoist areas | 1910.28(b)(2) | 4 ft or more to a lower level: guardrail, PFA, or travel restraint. |
| Stairway landings | 1910.28(b)(11)(i) | Unprotected side or edge of a staireway landing 4 ft or more above a lower level: guardrail or stair rail system. |
| Rope descent systems | 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) | 4 ft or more: personal fall arrest system. |
| Slaughtering facility platforms | 1910.28(b)(14)(i) | Unprotected working side 4 ft or more: guardrail or travel restraint. |
| Low-slope roofs | 1910.28(b)(13) | NOT a height trigger. Distance-from-edge triggers: work less than 6 ft from the edge always requires protection; 6 to <15 ft requires protection or a designated area (designated area only if work is infrequent and temporary); 15 ft or more requires a designated area or fall protection unless work is both infrequent and temporary, plus a work rule barring employees within 15 ft of the edge without protection. Do not confuse these 6 ft / 15 ft distances with a height threshold. |
| Fixed laders, vehicle pits, docks, outdoor advertising signs, and similar surfaces | 1910.28(b)(8)–(10), (b)(4) etc. | Each has its own paragraph; where a specific paragraph applies it controls over (b)(1). Confirm the paragraph before citing 4 ft. |
| Scaffolds | 1910.28(b)(12)(i) | Employees on scaffolds are protected per 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart L (construction scaffold rules), not the 4 ft. |


PROCEDURE (how to apply this on a real job)

1. Classify the work: general industry (1910) vs. construction (1926) vs. shipyard/maritime. This determines 4 ft vs. 6 ft. Document the basis.
2. Walk every walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge. For each, measure the vertical drop from the working surface to the lower level at the edge. Record the measurement in inches and in feet.
3. If any measurement is 48 in (4 ft 0 in / 1.2 m) or greater, protection is required under 1910.28(b)(1).
4. Before selecting a means, check whether a condition-specific paragraph in the table above applies and select the means it allows.
5. Select a means permitted by the governing paragraph: guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning). Guardrails, nets, and PFA must meet 1910.29 criteria; PFA equipment must meet 1910.140.
6. Train exposed employees per 1910.30 and document the training.
7. Re-measure whenever the surface, equipment, or task changes, re-evaluate.

VARIABLES / WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER

- If the task is construction: answer becomes 6 ft (1926.501(b)(1)).
- If the task is shipyard or longshoring: check 1915 / 1917.
- If a State Plan applies and is stricter: use the State Plan value.
- If the surface is a low-slope roof: the distance-based roof rules apply, not the 4 ft height rule, govern.
- If the surface is a scaffold: 1926 Sub L applies.
- If dangerous equipment is below and the drop is under 4 ft: 1910.28(b)(6)(i) still requires guardrail or travel restraint.

VERIFICATION AGAINST THE SOURCES

The 4 ft (1.2 m) figure appears verbatim in the fetched text of 1910.28 at (b)(1) (govinfo print, tail of paragraph), (b)(2)(i), (b)(3)(i), (b)(6), (b)(7), (b)(11)(i), (b)(12)(ii), (b)(14)(i), and (b)(15) — all at eCFR current and the govinfo 2025 print, consistent across 2022, 2025 and current editions. The 6 ft and 15 ft figures in (b)(13) are distances from the roof edge, not heights above a lower level, and do not contradict the 4 ft trigger. No other height threshold in the cited text is below 4 ft except the dangerous-equipment provision, which is a special case, not the general rule.

question: M6
answer:
ANSWER

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry, in addition to fuel enough to reach the first point of intended landing, reserve fuel sufficient to fly for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed. This is the same for day and night — 14 CFR § 91.151(b) draws no day/night distinction for rotorcraft (unlike § 91.151(a) for airplanes, which is 30 minutes day / 45 minutes night).

GOVERNING TEXT (quoted verbatim)

14 CFR § 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.
"(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."
(Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151 ; identical text in the 2025 edition at govinfo.gov, CFR-2025-title14-vol2, § 91.151.)

Corroboration from FAA-hosted guidance (faa.gov/media/32056), FAR Part 91 helicopter VFR conditions: "Reserve Fuel. FAR § 91.151(b). During day or night the required reserve fuel is the amount that allows continued operation for 20 minutes." Same document: "Alternate Fuel. N/A."

WHAT THE ANSWER DOES AND DOES NOT MEAN

1. Units. The regulation is expressed as time at normal cruising speed, not as a volume or weight. The reserve is therefore 20 minutes × the helicopter's fuel burn at normal cruising speed. It is not 20 minutes at best-range/loiter speed.
2. 'Normal cruising speed' is the speed the flight is planned at — the same speed used for the en-route leg; the reserve is not recomputed for a slower economy speed.
3. Wind and forecast weather are considered for the leg to the first point of intended landing; the 20 minutes is a fixed time increment added after that point.
4. No alternate fuel is required for Part 91 VFR. § 91.151(b) contains no alternate-airport requirement (contrast IFR, § 91.167(a)(2), which does).
5. The reserve must be usable fuel aboard at the start of the flight, not trapped/unusable fuel, and must be verifiable preflight (§ 91.103 preflight action requires determining fuel required).
6. This is a preflight planning minimum, not a target. It does not authorize pressing into the reserve; separate operating rules (e.g., § 91.13 careless/reckless operation) apply in flight.
7. Company, operator, or personal minimums commonly exceed 20 minutes. The regulatory floor does not cap a stricter internal standard.

CONVERTING 20 MINUTES TO A QUANTITY

Formula: Reserve quantity = (20/60) × burn rate at normal cruising speed = burn rate ÷ 3.

Illustrative examples (hypothetical burn rates — substitute the actual aircraft figure):
- Turbine helicopter burning 400 lb/h at normal cruise: 400 ÷ 3 = 133 lb of usable fuel; at ~6.7 lb/gal Jet A that is ~20 gal.
- Piston helicopter burning 13 gal/h at normal cruise: 13 ÷ 3 = ~4.3 gal of avgas (~26 lb at 6.0 lb/gal).
Do not carry a rounded-down quantity; round up and confirm against the aircraft's fuel quantity indication/dipstick.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER

- IFR at any point: § 91.167(a)(3) requires, for helicopters, 45 minutes... specifically 30 minutes at normal cruising speed after the alternate (helicopters get 30 minutes where other aircraft get 45), plus alternate fuel unless § 91.167(b) is met. This is a different regime and does not apply to the VFR question asked.
- Airplanes (not rotorcraft): 30 minutes day / 45 minutes night under § 91.151(a).
- Commercial operations: Part 135 helicopter VFR is understood to carry the same 20-minute figure under § 135.209(b), but that section was not among the verified passages here — verify it directly before relying on it for a Part 135 flight.
- Operations outside the US: foreign reserve rules apply for that portion; the 20-minute figure is a US Part 91 rule.
- Military/public-use operations: not governed by Part 91 as cited.

ASSUMPTIONS (stated, not hidden)

Civil helicopter, US domestic flight, 14 CFR Part 91, VFR for the entire flight, day or night (the figure is identical either way), regulatory minimum rather than a company minimum.

VERIFICATION NOTE

The quoted regulatory text was taken from the current eCFR and the 2025 printed CFR edition and is internally consistent across both. Regulatory text can be amended; confirm § 91.151(b) in the current eCFR before operational use, and confirm any operator-specific fuel policy that may exceed this minimum.

question: M8
answer:
# Answer

**Ask 1 — Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1:** **RFC 8996**, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (K. Moriarty and S. Farrell, March 2021). It is an Internet Best Current Practice and is part of **BCP 195** (it updates the TLS best-practice document RFC 7525). DOI: 10.17487/RFC8996.

**Ask 2 — Status it gave the RFCs that had defined them:** **Historic**. RFC 2246 (which defined TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (which defined TLS 1.1) were moved to Historic status. The RFC's own words:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."
> — RFC 8996, Abstract

> "Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."
> — RFC 8996, Section 1 (Introduction)

## Summary table

| Item | Value | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| Deprecating RFC | **RFC 8996** | Abstract; RFC Editor JSON (`doc_id: RFC8996`) |
| Title | Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 | RFC Editor JSON (`title`) |
| Authors | K. Moriarty, S. Farrell | RFC Editor JSON (`authors`) |
| Publication date | March 2021 | RFC Editor JSON (`pub_date`) |
| Status of RFC 8996 | Internet Best Current Practice; part of BCP 195 | "Status of This Memo"; Abstract |
| RFC that defined TLS 1.0 | **RFC 2246** | Abstract |
| RFC that defined TLS 1.1 | **RFC 4346** | Abstract |
| Status assigned to both | **Historic** | Abstract; Section 1 |
| RFCs RFC 8996 itself obsoletes | RFC 5469, RFC 7507 | RFC Editor JSON (`obsoletes`) |
| Also deprecated (out of scope for this question) | DTLS 1.0 = RFC 4347, also moved to Historic; DTLS 1.2 explicitly *not* deprecated | Abstract |
| Successor versions cited | TLS 1.2 = RFC 5246; TLS 1.3 = RFC 8446 | Section 1 |

## Wording caveat: "Historic", not "obsoleted"

These are different RFC Editor actions and the answer should not blur them:

- **Obsoleted** is recorded in the deprecating document's header. RFC 8996's header obsoletes only **RFC 5469** and **RFC 7507**. Neither RFC 2246 nor RFC 4346 appears in RFC 8996's obsoletes list or its updates list.
- **Historic** is a *status* (a state the document itself is in), not a relationship recorded on the deprecating document. RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 were reclassified from Proposed Standard to Historic, which is exactly what the abstract describes: "those documents have been moved to Historic status."

So the precise answer to Ask 2 is *"Historic"*, and the safe phrasing is *"RFC 8996 moved RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 to Historic status"* — **not** *"RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 are obsoleted by RFC 8996."*

## How to verify

1. Fetch `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/` — the status block should read *Internet Best Current Practice*, and the Abstract should contain the two sentences quoted above.
2. Fetch `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246/` and `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4346/` — each should show **Status: Historic**.
3. Cross-check the machine-readable metadata at `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.json` — `doc_id: RFC8996`, `pub_status: BEST CURRENT PRACTICE`, `pub_date: March 2021`, `obsoletes: RFC5469, RFC7507`.

## Boundaries of this answer

- **Scope:** TLS only, as asked. RFC 8996 also deprecates DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) and leaves DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347) alone; that is noted above for completeness but is not part of the answer.
- **Point in time:** the statuses stated are as recorded on the RFC Editor pages as fetched (2026-11-16). The RFC Editor history page shows only editorial/metadata activity on 2026-05-20 (keywords, author-name form), **not** a status change to RFC 8996 itself. No claim is made here about any later reclassification of RFC 8996; if that matters, re-check `rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/` at time of use.
- **"Deprecated" definition used:** formal, RFC-action deprecation via a Best Current Practice, not informal community discouragement.

question: M10
answer:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for calendar year 2026 is:

  $184,500

This is the per-worker, per-employer wage base for the year. Earnings above $184,500 in 2026 are not subject to the 6.2% OASDI payroll tax, and $184,500 is also the maximum amount of 2026 earnings that can count in a Social Security benefit computation.

SOURCES (all Social Security Administration, all agreeing)

1. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, "Contribution and Benefit Base" — annual table gives 2026 = $184,500 (2025 = $176,100; 2027 = $192,300).
   https://www.ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html

2. SSA 2026 COLA Fact Sheet, "Maximum Taxable Earnings" table, 2025 vs. 2026 columns:
     Social Security (OASDI only): $176,100 → $184,500
     Medicare (HI only): No Limit
   https://www.ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2026.html

3. SSA Fast Facts & Figures About Social Security, 2026, "Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026": OASDI = 184,500; HI = No limit.
   https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/chartbooks/fast_facts/2026/fast_facts26.html

DERIVED AMOUNTS (for payroll/benefit configuration; consistent with $184,500)

- Employee OASDI withheld at 6.2%: maximum $11,439.00 for 2026 (0.062 × 184,500).
- Employer OASDI at 6.2%: maximum $11,439.00 per employee for 2026.
- Self-employed (SECA) OASDI at 12.4%: maximum $22,878.00 for 2026 (0.124 × 184,500), before the income-tax deduction for one-half of SE tax.
- Combined employee-side FICA at 7.65% up to the base plus 1.45% HI on all wages: the OASDI portion stops at $184,500; the 1.45% HI portion continues on all earnings (and the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies above $200,000 single / $250,000 MFJ).

SCOPE NOTES / DISAMBIGUATION

- "Social Security payroll tax" here means the OASDI portion only. Medicare's Hospital Insurance (HI) tax has had no earnings limitation since 1993, so there is no "Medicare base" to report for 2026.
- Do not confuse $184,500 (2026) with $192,300 (2027). SSA's determination page shows the 2027 base computed as $60,600 × 72,800.33 / 22,935.42 = $192,353.14, rounded to the nearest $300 → $192,300, and states that this exceeds the 2026 base — confirming the 2026 figure is the lower $184,500.
- Distinct 2026 figures sometimes confused with the base: quarter of coverage = $1,890 (four credits = $7,560); retirement earnings test exempt amounts $24,480/yr ($2,040/mo) under FRA and $65,160/yr ($5,430/mo) in the FRA year; COLA = 2.8%; maximum benefit at FRA = $4,152/mo. None of these is the contribution and benefit base.
- Statutory basis: the base is set by the automatic-adjustment formula at 20 CFR 404.1048 — the prior-year base multiplied by the ratio of the average of total wages, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300 (next higher multiple if the result is an exact multiple of $150), and never reduced below the current base. $184,500 is a multiple of $300 ($184,500 / 300 = 615).
- Applies to wages paid in (and taxable years beginning in) calendar year 2026; the figure is per individual worker, not per household or per employer aggregate.

ONE-LINE ANSWER

2026 Social Security (OASDI) contribution and benefit base = $184,500.

question: M12
answer:
## Answer

**The 2026 limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.**

This is the IRC §402(g)(1) limit for a standard (non-SIMPLE) 401(k) plan, as adjusted for cost of living. It applies per employee, per calendar year, and is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation.

## Authority

- **IRS Notice 2025-67**, "Cost-of-Living Adjusted Limitations for 2026," effective January 1, 2026: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
- **IRS COLA table** (Retirement plans — cost-of-living increases for dollar limitations), row "401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing plans, etc. — Elective deferrals": $24,500 for 2026 (2025: $23,500; 2024: $23,000; 2023: $22,500).
- **IRS Retirement Topics — 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits**: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- **IRS Publication 560**: "The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026. These limits apply for participants in SARSEPs, 401(k) plans (excluding SIMPLE plans), section 403(b) plans, and section 457(b) plans."
- Cross-check: the IRS 2027 announcement (IR-2026-136, Notice 2026-66) states the 2027 limit rose to $25,500 "up from $24,500 for 2026."

## What this number does and does not include

| Item | 2026 amount | Relationship to the $24,500 |
|---|---|---|
| §402(g) elective deferral limit, standard 401(k) | **$24,500** | The answer. Includes pre-tax and designated Roth employee deferrals combined. |
| Age 50+ catch-up (§414(v)(2)(B)(i)) | $8,000 | **Excluded** by the question; added on top of $24,500 (combined $32,500 for a 50+ participant). |
| Age 60–63 catch-up (SECURE 2.0) | $11,250 | Excluded; replaces the $8,000 for participants attaining 60–63 in 2026. |
| SIMPLE 401(k) deferral limit | $17,000 | Different plan type; does **not** apply to a standard 401(k). |
| SIMPLE catch-up (50+) / (60–63) | $4,000 / $5,250 | Excluded; SIMPLE plans only. |
| §415(c) annual additions limit (DC plans) | $72,000 | Separate, higher ceiling covering employee deferrals **plus** employer match, nonelective, and forfeitures; $24,500 is well below it. |
| §401(a)(17) compensation cap | $360,000 | Caps the pay on which deferrals and match are computed. |
| 457(b) elective deferral limit | $24,500 | Same dollar figure but a **separate** limit; not aggregated with the 401(k) limit for a governmental 457(b). |

Notes that matter for applying the number correctly:

1. **Pre-tax and Roth deferrals share the one $24,500 ceiling.** Designated Roth 401(k) deferrals are elective deferrals and are counted against §402(g); an employee cannot defer $24,500 pre-tax *and* $24,500 Roth.
2. **Aggregation across employers' plans.** Elective deferrals to 401(k), 403(b), and SARSEP arrangements are aggregated for §402(g) purposes, so an employee with two unrelated employers' 401(k) plans has one $24,500 limit across both. Governmental 457(b) deferrals are tested separately.
3. **Employer contributions do not count against $24,500.** Match and nonelective contributions are §415(c) items, not §402(g) items; they neither consume nor enlarge the employee's deferral room.
4. **The plan may impose a lower limit.** The IRS page is explicit: "Your plan's terms may impose a lower limit on elective deferrals." A plan may cap deferrals at a percentage of pay, and highly compensated employees may be restricted by ADP testing or the plan's own nondiscrimination design. HR should confirm the plan document and any current administrative cap before communicating a payroll maximum, and should confirm the payroll system's per-pay-period cap is set to $24,500 for 2026 (a $23,500 default carried over from 2025 is the most common year-end error).
5. **Excess deferrals.** Amounts above $24,500 (excluding permitted catch-up) are includible in gross income for the year of deferral and are taxable again on distribution unless corrected. Corrective distribution of the excess plus attributable earnings must generally be made by April 15 of the following year. HR/payroll should run a final-year-to-date deferral reconciliation in the last pay period of 2026 and flag any participant projected to exceed $24,500.
6. **No change to this base limit from SECURE 2.0.** The Roth-only catch-up requirement for higher earners beginning in 2026 affects the *catch-up* layer, not the $24,500 base; and no enacted legislation alters the 2026 base §402(g) figure from $24,500.

## One-line version for employee communications

"For 2026, you may defer up to $24,500 of your pay into the 401(k) plan on a pre-tax and/or Roth basis, or 100% of your compensation if that is less. If you are 50 or older (or turn 50 by December 31, 2026), you may defer an additional $8,000 as a catch-up — $11,250 if you turn 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026."
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 5250 on irs.gov/retirement-plans/cola-increases-for-dollar-limitations-on-benefits-and-contributions and 11250 on irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-401k-and-profit-sharing-plan-contribution-limits. The first reads: "For 2026, this higher catch-up contribution limit is $5,250."

question: M2
answer:
CURRENT US NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5 (primary, health-based; 40 CFR 50.18)

ANSWERS
- Annual primary PM2.5 standard: 9.0 µg/m³ (annual arithmetic mean concentration).
- 24-hour primary PM2.5 standard: 35 µg/m³ (24-hour average concentration).

1. LEVELS AND FORMS (the form is part of the standard, so both are given)

| Standard | Level | Averaging time | Form / statistic (40 CFR 50.18(b),(c); appendix N) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Primary annual PM2.5 | 9.0 µg/m³ | Annual | 3-year average of the annual arithmetic mean concentrations from a single site, compared to ≤ 9.0 µg/m³ | In effect; set by the 2024 reconsideration (level lowered from 12.0) |
| Primary 24-hour PM2.5 | 35 µg/m³ | 24-hour | 3-year average of the annual 98th-percentile of 24-hour concentrations from a single site, compared to ≤ 35 µg/m³ | In effect; unchanged by the 2024 reconsideration |

Round-off conventions: annual level expressed to one decimal place (9.0 µg/m³); 24-hour level expressed as an integer (35 µg/m³). Both are compared to the appendix N design value, which is rounded before comparison (annual: one decimal; 24-hour: nearest 1 µg/m³).

2. AUTHORITY AND EFFECTIVE DATES
- Codification: 40 CFR Part 50, § 50.18, 'National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5'; measurement methods per appendix L (reference methods) / Part 53 (equivalent methods); design values computed per appendix N.
- 24-hour level of 35 µg/m³ and its 98th-percentile form: carried forward from the 2012 review (78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013) and retained in the 2024 action.
- Annual level of 9.0 µg/m³: set by 'Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter,' final rule signed/promulgated February 7, 2024, Federal Register document 2024-02637, published March 6, 2024 (89 FR 16202). EPA's announcement states: 'EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter... EPA is not changing the current: primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards, secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and primary and secondary PM10 standards.'
- Implementation status (context, not part of the level): area designations for the revised 2024 annual standard are still being finalized — EPA gave notice on October 2, 2026 of its intended approach for finalizing initial designations. Designations timing does not change the standard's level.

3. SOURCE CONFLICT AND HOW IT WAS RESOLVED (read this before quoting a number)
Two grounded sources disagree on the annual figure:
- 40 CFR 50.18 as returned by the eCFR 'current' fetch (and a 2016 govinfo CFR snapshot) reads: '...are 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration...' with the amendment note '[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]'.
- EPA's PM NAAQS reconsideration page and the 2024 PM2.5 designations page (the latter 'Last updated on October 2, 2026') both state the annual standard was strengthened from 12.0 to 9.0 µg/m³ on February 7, 2024, with the 24-hour standard retained at 35 µg/m³.
Resolution: the eCFR text returned carries a 2013 amendment note, which is impossible for a codification that incorporates a 2024 amendment; it is therefore a pre-amendment (stale) rendering of § 50.18, not evidence that the 2024 revision was vacated or rescinded. No source in the record shows a later rule restoring 12.0, and EPA's October 2026 page still administers the 9.0 standard. Accordingly, 9.0 µg/m³ is reported as the current annual level, and 12.0 µg/m³ is reported only as the SUPERSEDED pre-2024 level.
One-line verification for any reader: open 40 CFR 50.18 and confirm the amendment note under the section reads the 2024 Federal Register citation (89 FR 16202 / doc. 2024-02637) rather than only '[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]'; and confirm subsection (a)/(b) reads 9.0 µg/m³.

4. VALUES THAT ARE NOT THE ANSWER (to prevent misquotation)
- 12.0 µg/m³ — the annual primary PM2.5 standard from 2012 until the 2024 revision took effect; superseded, NOT current.
- 15.0 µg/m³ — the annual standard in force 2006–2012; historical, NOT current.
- 65 µg/m³ — the original 1997 24-hour PM2.5 standard; historical, NOT current.
- 150 µg/m³ — the primary/secondary 24-hour PM10 standard; a different pollutant, NOT the PM2.5 answer.
- Secondary (welfare-based) PM standards — out of scope of this request, which asks for primary standards only.

5. SCOPE AND ASSUMPTIONS APPLIED
- 'Current' = the standards in force under EPA's most recent final PM NAAQS rulemaking as of the time of the inquiry (November 2026 in the grounded record), not a proposed or future rule.
- Primary (health-based) standards only, as asked; secondary standards, PM10, and other criteria pollutants excluded.
- Units are µg/m³, the standard unit for PM NAAQS; no ppb-equivalent conversion is meaningful or offered for a mass-concentration standard.
- Values taken from EPA's official statements and 40 CFR Part 50 rather than secondary summaries; the stale-CFR discrepancy is disclosed above rather than concealed.

6. ONE-SENTENCE ANSWER
The current US national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 9.0 µg/m³, annual arithmetic mean (3-year average of annual means), and 35 µg/m³, 24-hour average (3-year average of annual 98th percentiles).

question: M4
answer:
Under federal OSHA general-industry rules, the trigger is 4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level.

Controlling provision: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i). Except as provided elsewhere in § 1910.28 or by other subparts of Part 1910, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by:
(i) guardrail systems;
(ii) safety net systems; or
(iii) personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

Practical statement: if an employee is on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge and is 4 feet or more above a lower level, the employer must provide fall protection. Below 4 feet, the general side/edge trigger does not apply, though other provisions may still require protection (for example, certain requirements for dangerous equipment, openings, or specific surfaces).

Scope note: this is the general-industry standard (29 CFR 1910 Subpart D). It is not the construction standard in 29 CFR 1926, which has a different trigger height. Some specific general-industry situations in § 1910.28 carry their own rules — e.g., low-slope roof work is governed by distance from the roof edge rather than a simple 4-foot height trigger, and stairway landings, rope descent systems, and slaughtering facility platforms have their own 4-foot provisions. State-plan states may impose different or additional requirements, so the governing state plan should be checked where applicable.

question: M6
answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — VFR RESERVE FUEL, US-REGISTERED HELICOPTER

ANSWER

20 minutes. A helicopter may not begin a VFR flight in the United States unless it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, assuming normal cruising speed (Part 91) / normal cruising fuel consumption (Part 135), to fly for at least 20 minutes beyond that point. The reserve is 20 minutes of flight time at normal cruise — not a gallon figure — and it is the same day or night. There is no separate night reserve for helicopters, and no VFR alternate fuel requirement.

1. CONTROLLING TEXT

14 CFR 91.151 (Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions), paragraph (b), rotorcraft:

  "(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

14 CFR 135.209 (VFR: Fuel supply), paragraph (b), helicopter:

  "(b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

2. WHY THE ANSWER DOES NOT DEPEND ON THE PART 91 / PART 135 QUESTION

The request does not specify the operating rule. It does not need to for this number. Paragraph (b) of each section is helicopter/rotorcraft-specific and both state 20 minutes with no day/night split. Part 91 governs the general operation; Part 135 governs the commercial helicopter operation; either way the regulatory minimum reserve is 20 minutes. The 30-minute day / 45-minute night figures appear only in paragraph (a) of both sections and apply to airplanes — they must not be applied to a helicopter.

3. WHAT THE RESERVE IS AND IS NOT

- It is measured in time at normal cruising speed, not in gallons, pounds, or a percentage of trip fuel. The quantity in gallons is derived (see section 4).
- It is "after that" — i.e., it is additive to the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing. It is not a cushion carved out of the trip fuel.
- It is computed "considering wind and forecast weather conditions," so the trip-fuel leg is a wind-adjusted estimate, but the 20-minute reserve itself is at normal cruising speed (no wind credit is taken to shrink the 20 minutes).
- It applies at the moment the flight begins ("may begin a flight"). Fuel burned before the regulatory "beginning" (taxi) does not count toward the reserve; the reserve must still be aboard at brake release/takeoff.
- No alternate fuel is required for VFR helicopter operations under either part. VFR does not require a filed alternate, so the "first point of intended landing" is the destination and the 20 minutes is not fuel to an alternate.
- The 20 minutes is a floor, not a flight-planning figure. It must be in usable fuel available to the engine(s); fuel in a tank that cannot be fed to the engine does not satisfy it.
- The pilot in command remains separately obligated by 14 CFR 91.103 to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, including known traffic delays and forecast conditions, and by 91.167/135.223 if any portion is conducted IFR. Those obligations can require more than 20 minutes; they cannot require less.

4. CONVERTING 20 MINUTES TO A QUANTITY (PROCEDURE)

Step 1. Establish normal cruising speed and the corresponding fuel consumption (gal/hr or lb/hr) from the Rotorcraft Flight Manual cruise data for the planned cruise power setting and altitude.
Step 2. Reserve quantity = cruise fuel flow x (20 / 60) = cruise fuel flow / 3.
Step 3. Add to the wind-adjusted trip fuel to the first point of intended landing.
Step 4. Compare the sum to usable fuel aboard at takeoff (not total tank capacity; not including unusable fuel). If the sum exceeds usable fuel, the flight cannot legally begin.

Worked examples (arithmetic shown so it can be checked):
- 300 lb/hr at normal cruise: 300 x 20/60 = 100 lb reserve. At 6.7 lb/gal Jet A that is about 14.9 gal.
- 20 gal/hr at normal cruise: 20 x 20/60 = 6.67 gal reserve.
- 180 lb/hr at normal cruise: 180 / 3 = 60 lb reserve.

5. VERIFICATION IN PRACTICE

- Compute the reserve from the RFM cruise chart, not from a gauge reading alone, and record it on the load/fuel sheet (trip fuel + 20-minute reserve = minimum fuel at takeoff).
- Confirm usable fuel aboard by gauge, dipstick, or fuel-load record per the aircraft's equipment; the aircraft must have a operable fuel gauge indicating quantity for each tank under 14 CFR 91.205 where that equipment list applies.
- Post-flight, any landing with less than the planned 20-minute equivalent indicates the planning basis was wrong and should be corrected before the next flight.

6. SCOPE LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

- Applies to US-registered civil helicopters operating under FAA rules (Part 91 or Part 135), day or night, VFR.
- Does not cover Part 121, military, or foreign-registry operations.
- Does not address IFR fuel planning (91.167 / 135.223), VFR over-the-top passenger operations (135.211), or powered-lift aircraft, which are governed by other provisions.
- Operator, insurer, or company fuel policies may impose a larger reserve than 20 minutes; such policies are additive to, and never a substitute for, the regulatory minimum stated here.

CITATION BASIS: 14 CFR 91.151(b) and 14 CFR 135.209(b), as published in the eCFR and the 2026 CFR bound volumes; FAA guidance material (FAA media 32056) item 15 confirms that for Part 135 helicopter VFR operations the required reserve is 20 minutes both day and night, with alternate fuel not applicable.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 30 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151 and 20 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2026-title14-vol2/pdf/cfr-2026-title14-vol2-part91.pdf. The first reads: "(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 45 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151 and 20 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2026-title14-vol2/pdf/cfr-2026-title14-vol2-part91.pdf. The first reads: "(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes."

question: M8
answer:
ANSWER

1. The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is **RFC 8996**, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (March 2021; part of BCP 195, which is the current best-practice guidance for TLS usage formerly anchored in RFC 7525).

2. It gave the RFCs that had defined those versions — **RFC 2246** (TLS 1.0, January 1999) and **RFC 4346** (TLS 1.1, April 2006) — the status **Historic**.

SOURCES AND EXACT WORDING

- RFC 8996, Abstract (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html): "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."
- RFC 8996, Section 1 (Introduction): "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008 ... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."
- RFC Editor info page for RFC 2246 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246/): status field reads "Historic" (the document's own 1999 header read "Category: Standards Track").
- RFC Editor info page for RFC 4346 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4346/): status field reads "Historic" (the document's own 2006 header read "Category: Standards Track").
- IETF Datatracker history (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/): RFC 8996 published 2021-03-23; the RFC Editor sync record carries the same abstract text quoted above.

HOW THE STATUS WAS EXPRESSED (precision points a reader may need)

- The action is a **document status change to Historic**, not an "Obsoletes: 2246, 4346" header line. The distinction matters: both documents were already *obsolete* in the supersession sense before RFC 8996 — RFC 2246 was obsoleted by RFC 4346, and RFC 4346 was obsoleted by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2, 2008). "Obsolete" (superseded by a newer specification) and "Historic" (no longer recommended for new use; retired from the standards track) are different axes, and RFC 8996's contribution is the second one. The RFC Editor info pages show both facts side by side: "Historic" in the status field, plus "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 4346" / "see RFC 5246" as separate notes.
- RFC 8996 itself is **not** Standards Track; its "Status of This Memo" reads "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice." It is therefore the BCP-track document that retires the two Standards Track specifications.
- Scope note: the same document also deprecates **DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347)** — note 4347, not 4346 — and moves it to Historic, but explicitly does *not* deprecate DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347), and observes there is no DTLS 1.1. It additionally moves RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites) to Historic and updates many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1.

MINIMAL CITATION FORM

  RFC 8996 ("Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1", March 2021, BCP 195) deprecates TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) and moves both to Historic status.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 1.0 on rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246 and 1.1 on rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4346. The first reads: "This document specifies Version 1.0 of the Transport Layer Security"

question: M10
answer:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for calendar/tax year 2026 is $184,500.

DEFINITION AND SCOPE

- The contribution and benefit base is the annual limit on earnings subject to Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) taxation; the same limit applies when those earnings are used in a benefit computation. SSA calls it the 'taxable maximum' (SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html).
- It applies to wages for employees and to self-employment income. The OASDI rate is 6.2% each for employee and employer (12.4% for the self-employed).
- It does NOT apply to Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI): there has been no HI taxable maximum since 1994, and the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax (individual earned income over $200,000 / $250,000 MFJ) sits outside this cap.

SOURCE CONFIRMATION (three independent SSA publications, all agreeing)

1. SSA 2026 COLA fact sheet, '2026 SOCIAL SECURITY CHANGES', Maximum Taxable Earnings table (https://www.ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2026.html):
   'Maximum Taxable Earnings — Social Security (OASDI only): 2025 $176,100 | 2026 $184,500. Medicare (HI only): No Limit.'
2. SSA Publication No. 42-007, EFW2 Tax Year 2026 specifications (https://www.ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf):
   'The Social Security Wage Base for tax year 2026 is $184,500. The employer and employee tax rate for Social Security will be withheld at 6.2 percent (up to $11,439.00).' The record layout repeats the limit: 'should not exceed the annual maximum Social Security wage base for the tax year ($184,500 for tax year 2026)' and 'should not exceed $11,439.00 for tax year 2026.'
3. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Contribution and Benefit Base table (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html): 2025 $176,100; 2026 $184,500; 2027 $192,300.

Because the OACT table now also carries 2027 ($192,300), the 2026 figure of $184,500 is final and no longer subject to revision. The 2027 figure is NOT the answer to this question and is cited only as confirmation.

ARITHMETIC CHECKS (all consistent with the $184,500 base)

- Maximum employee OASDI tax: 184,500 x 0.062 = $11,439.00 (matches the EFW2 stated cap exactly).
- Maximum employer OASDI tax: $11,439.00 (same).
