question: M4
answer:
# Fall-Protection Trigger Height — General Industry (US, Federal OSHA)

## 1. Answer

**4 feet (1.2 m).** In general industry, a US employer must protect each employee who is on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge **4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level** from falling. Because the standard reads "4 feet or more," the duty attaches *at* exactly 4 feet, not above it.

Authority: **29 CFR 1910.28(b)** — Subpart D, Walking-Working Surfaces (general industry). The general rule for unprotected sides and edges is 1910.28(b)(1)(i); the catch-all provision confirming the same 4-ft trigger for surfaces not otherwise addressed is 1910.28(b)(15).

## 2. Controlling text (quoted from 29 CFR 1910.28, 2025 edition)

**1910.28(b)(15) — Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed:**

> "Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by:
> (i) Guardrail systems;
> (ii) Safety net systems; or
> (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

**1910.28(b)(1)(i) — Unprotected sides and edges (general rule):** the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is **4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level** is protected by (A) guardrail systems, (B) safety net systems, or (C) personal fall protection systems such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

Note on sourcing: the verbatim excerpt set available for this answer quotes (b)(15) and the special categories below directly; (b)(1)(i) is stated here as the general provision and is numerically consistent with every quoted 4-ft threshold in the section ((b)(6), (b)(7), (b)(11), (b)(12)(ii), (b)(14), (b)(15)). A compliance writer should paste (b)(1)(i) verbatim from eCFR before publishing if the exact words of the general rule are needed.

## 3. What the employer must provide once 4 ft is reached

At or above 4 feet, one or more of the following must protect the employee:

1. **Guardrail system** (1910.29(b): top rail 42 in ± 3 in, midrail, toeboard where required, 200-lb load criteria).
2. **Safety net system** (1910.29(c)).
3. **Personal fall protection system** — personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning system (1910.29(d)–(f), 1910.140).

Where the employer can demonstrate that using these systems is infeasible or would create a greater hazard, 1910.28(b)(1)(ii) requires a **written fall protection plan** meeting 1910.29(k) instead — this is a documented, site-specific alternative, not an exemption from the 4-ft trigger.

Employees exposed to the hazard must be trained under 1910.30.

## 4. Scope qualifiers — where the 4-ft trigger is not the operative test

The 4-ft rule is the default for ordinary walking-working surfaces. The following categories inside 1910.28(b) are "otherwise addressed" and must be checked separately; each of the ones listed below still uses 4 ft, except low-slope roofs:

| Category | Citation | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| Unprotected sides and edges (default) | 1910.28(b)(1)(i) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level |
| Surfaces not otherwise addressed | 1910.28(b)(15) | 4 ft (1.2 m) |
| Dangerous equipment | 1910.28(b)(6) | Below 4 ft: guardrail or travel restraint (unless covered/guarded). At 4 ft or more: guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or PFAS |
| Openings (inside bottom edge < 39 in, outside bottom edge ≥ 4 ft above lower level) | 1910.28(b)(7) | 4 ft (1.2 m) |
| Runways and similar walkways | 1910.28(b)(5) | 4 ft (1.2 m); narrow runways may use PFAS/travel restraint |
| Stairway landings (unprotected side or edge) | 1910.28(b)(11)(i) | 4 ft (1.2 m) — guardrail or stair rail system |
| Rope descent systems | 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) | 4 ft (1.2 m) — PFAS required |
| Slaughtering facility platforms | 1910.28(b)(14) | 4 ft (1.2 m) — guardrail or travel restraint; documented infeasibility exception |
| Low-slope roofs | 1910.28(b)(13) | **Distance from edge, not height:** < 6 ft from edge — guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or PFAS; 6 to < 15 ft — same, or a designated area if work is infrequent and temporary; ≥ 15 ft — protection or designated area, and no fall protection required if work is both infrequent and temporary, plus a work rule barring employees within 15 ft of the edge without protection |
| Scaffolds | 1910.28(b)(12)(i) | Governed by 29 CFR 1926 Subpart L, not by the 4-ft figure |

Other separately addressed surfaces in 1910.28(b) (dockboards, hoist areas, holes, ladders, mobile ladder stands, repair/service/assembly pits) carry their own text and should be read directly; do not assume the 4-ft default applies to them without checking.

## 5. Not construction — do not use 6 feet

- **General industry (this answer):** 29 CFR 1910.28 → **4 ft (1.2 m)**.
- **Construction:** 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) → **6 ft (1.8 m)** for unprotected sides and edges; 1926 Subpart M also uses 10 ft for scaffolds and 15 ft for certain steel-erection work. These figures do **not** apply to general industry employers.
- Other OSHA parts have their own rules: shipyard employment (29 CFR 1915), longshoring (1918), and agriculture (1928). Confirm the part that covers the operation before applying 4 ft.

## 6. Definitions and measurement

- **Walking-working surface** (1910.21(b)): any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
- **Unprotected sides and edges** (1910.21(b)): any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.
- **Lower level:** 1910.28 does not define the term separately. Measure vertically from the walking-working surface the employee is on down to the surface to which the employee could fall; the trigger is the fall distance the employee is actually exposed to, not the height of the building or the elevation of the floor slab.
- **Height measurement:** vertical distance from the walking-working surface to the lower level, taken at the unprotected edge. If the exposure reaches 4 ft anywhere along that edge, protection is required for the exposed employee.

## 7. State-plan states

Twenty-plus states and territories operate OSHA-approved State Plans. They must be **at least as effective** as federal OSHA and may be **more stringent** (lower trigger heights, stricter means of protection). Example: Oregon OSHA Division 2, Subdivision D mirrors the federal 4-ft trigger in 1910.28(b)(12)–(15). For a multi-state employer, verify the specific state plan's text; a state plan may not be *less* protective than 4 ft for this hazard, but it may require more.

## 8. One-line compliance statement for use in a policy or audit

> "Employees on walking-working surfaces with unprotected sides or edges 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level are protected by a guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system, per 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) and (b)(15); exposures below 4 feet are evaluated under the applicable paragraph of 1910.28(b) (e.g., dangerous equipment, openings) and under the General Duty Clause, 29 U.S.C. 654(a)(1), where a recognized hazard remains."

## 9. Traceability

- 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15), (b)(6), (b)(7), (b)(11), (b)(12), (b)(13), (b)(14) — quoted from the 2025 edition of 29 CFR Chapter XVII, Part 1910, Subpart D (govinfo PDF/XML and eCFR, fetched 2026-11-16).
- Definitions — 29 CFR 1910.21(b) / Subpart D definitions page (eCFR; Oregon OSHA Division 2 mirror).
- Construction contrast — 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) (6 ft), stated from the standard, not from the fetched excerpts.

question: M6
answer:
RESERVE FUEL FOR A HELICOPTER BEGINNING A VFR FLIGHT IN THE UNITED STATES

1. DIRECT ANSWER

A helicopter must carry, beyond the fuel needed to fly to the first point of intended landing, enough fuel to fly for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed. This is the same for day and night VFR. The governing rule is 14 CFR 91.151(b) for Part 91 operations; 14 CFR 135.209(b) imposes the identical 20-minute rotorcraft reserve for Part 135 (commercial helicopter) VFR operations.

Answer in the form requested: 20 minutes.

2. GOVERNING TEXT (verbatim)

14 CFR 91.151 — Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions:

"(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

14 CFR 135.209 — VFR: Fuel supply:

"(a) No person may begin a flight operation in an airplane under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
(b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

3. APPLICABILITY — WHY THE ANSWER IS 20 MINUTES UNDER EITHER PART

- Part 91: 91.151(b) is written for "rotorcraft" and applies to any person beginning a VFR flight in the United States under the general operating rules. No day/night split.
- Part 135: 135.209(b) is written for "helicopter" and applies to VFR flight operations conducted for compensation or hire under Part 135. No day/night split.
- Because both parts specify 20 minutes for rotorcraft, the answer does not change if the flight turns out to be a for-hire operation. The 30-minute day / 45-minute night figures are airplane-only and must not be applied to a helicopter.
- Part 121: VFR helicopter operations under Part 121 are effectively nonexistent in US civil operations. If one were contemplated, the Part 121 fuel rules (121.639 VFR domestic, 121.641/121.643/121.645/121.647) would have to be checked separately; they are outside the scope of this answer and are not a realistic case for the question asked. The 20-minute figure above is the operative legal minimum for every practical US helicopter VFR operation.

4. WHAT THE 20 MINUTES IS MEASURED AGAINST — COMPLIANCE DETAIL

To be compliant, at the moment the flight begins (i.e., at takeoff), the fuel on board must satisfy all of the following simultaneously:

(a) Trip fuel: enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing, computed considering wind and forecast weather conditions along the planned route, at normal cruising speed.
(b) Reserve: an additional 20 minutes of flight at normal cruising speed, computed on the same wind/forecast basis.
(c) Usable fuel only: the reserve must be usable fuel. Unusable fuel specified in the rotorcraft flight manual (e.g., the unusable portion in each tank, or fuel that cannot be delivered in the expected attitude) does not count toward either the trip fuel or the 20-minute reserve.
(d) No alternate fuel is required for VFR. Under VFR there is no regulatory requirement to carry fuel to a destination alternate (that requirement, 14 CFR 91.167, is an IFR rule). The only regulatory add-on beyond trip fuel for a VFR helicopter is the 20-minute reserve.
(e) Taxi, hover, run-up, and air-traffic delays are not separately mandated by the rule, but they consume fuel and must be accounted for inside the pilot's own planning; they are not permitted to erode the 20-minute reserve.
(f) "Normal cruising speed" means the speed/burn the aircraft is actually expected to be operated at in cruise for that flight — not best-range or maximum-endurance speed. The reserve must be computed at that normal cruise burn.

Formula: Minimum fuel at takeoff = (trip fuel to first point of intended landing, wind-adjusted, at normal cruise) + (normal cruise fuel flow x 20/60).

5. CONVERTING THE 20 MINUTES TO A QUANTITY (if gallons or pounds are wanted)

Reserve quantity = normal cruise fuel flow / 3 (because 20 minutes = one-third of an hour).

- Gallons (avgas or Jet A): reserve gal = (cruise burn in gal/hr) / 3.
- Pounds: reserve lb = reserve gal x 6.0 lb/gal for 100LL avgas, or x 6.7 lb/gal for Jet A/Jet A-1.
- Kilograms: reserve kg = (cruise burn in kg/hr) / 3.

Illustrative worked examples (numbers are illustrative of typical cruise burns only; the operator must use the actual aircraft's flight-manual/POH cruise fuel flow):
- Piston light helicopter burning 15.0 gal/hr at normal cruise: reserve = 15.0 / 3 = 5.0 US gal (about 30 lb of 100LL).
- Piston light helicopter burning 8.4 gal/hr at normal cruise: reserve = 8.4 / 3 = 2.8 US gal (about 17 lb of 100LL).
- Turbine helicopter burning 400 lb/hr at normal cruise: reserve = 400 / 3 = 133 lb (about 20 US gal of Jet A at 6.7 lb/gal).

These quantities are the reserve only; trip fuel to the first point of intended landing is added on top.

6. COMMON ERRORS THIS ANSWER GUARDS AGAINST

- Applying the airplane 30-minute day / 45-minute night reserve to a helicopter. Wrong: rotorcraft get 20 minutes, day and night, under both 91.151(b) and 135.209(b).
- Assuming a helicopter needs a larger night reserve than a day reserve. Wrong: the rotorcraft paragraph contains no day/night distinction.
- Treating the 20 minutes as including the flight to the destination. Wrong: it is "after that" — in addition to fuel to the first point of intended landing.
- Computing the reserve at max-endurance or best-range speed to shrink it. Wrong: the rule specifies normal cruising speed / normal cruising fuel consumption.
- Counting unusable fuel toward the reserve. Wrong: the fuel must be usable.
- Assuming a VFR alternate fuel requirement exists. It does not; there is no VFR destination-alternate fuel rule for helicopters.
- Assuming a Part 135 helicopter gets a different (larger) VFR reserve. It does not under 135.209(b); however, Part 135 operators may have additional fuel requirements imposed through operations specifications and their FAA-approved fuel policy, which must be checked separately.

7. LEGAL MINIMUM VS. PRUDENT PRACTICE

The 20 minutes is a legal floor, not a target. Standard helicopter safety practice, and the guidance in FAA/industry helicopter training material, is to plan a substantially larger reserve — commonly 30 minutes or more, and more still for night, over-water, mountainous, or degraded-weather (IIMC-risk) flights — plus a personal-minimum buffer. Operator fuel policy, insurance conditions, and Part 135 operations specifications may also require more than 20 minutes. None of these change the regulatory answer: 20 minutes.

8. SOURCES CONSULTED

- 14 CFR 91.151 (eCFR, current) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151
- 14 CFR 91.151 (2026 GPO CFR XML, Title 14 vol. 2) — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title14-vol2/xml/CFR-2026-title14-vol2-sec91-151.xml
- 14 CFR 135.209 (2026 GPO CFR PDF, Title 14 vol. 3) — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title14-vol3/pdf/CFR-2026-title14-vol3-sec135-209.pdf
- Related Part 135 helicopter VFR sections reviewed in the same volume (135.203, 135.205, 135.207) for context on helicopter VFR operating limitations.

## Answer (short form)

- **Deprecating RFC:** **RFC 8996**, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (K. Moriarty, S. Farrell; March 2021; DOI 10.17487/RFC8996).
- **Status given to the defining RFCs:** RFC 8996 moved both **RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0)** and **RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1)** to **Historic** status. It did *not* list them as Obsoleted.

## 1. The deprecating document

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| RFC number | RFC 8996 |
| Title | Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 |
| Authors | K. Moriarty, S. Farrell |
| Publication date | March 2021 (Datatracker records the RFC at 2021-03-23) |
| Stream / category | IETF; **Best Current Practice** (part of BCP 195) |
| Source WG | Transport Layer Security (TLS) |
| Internet-Draft | draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12 |
| DOI | 10.17487/RFC8996 |
| Obsoletes | RFC 5469, RFC 7507 |
| Updates | A long list of RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1, including RFC 6347 and RFC 7525 |

RFC 8996 is a **BCP, not a Standards Track document** — consistent with the usual practice that retiring a protocol version is handled as a status/BCP action rather than as new protocol specification.

## 2. The status it assigned to the defining RFCs

RFC 8996 states the status change explicitly, in both the abstract and Section 1 (Introduction):

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to **Historic status**." — RFC 8996, Abstract

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. … Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to **Historic status**." — RFC 8996, Section 1

So, per defining RFC:

| Defining RFC | Protocol version | Status assigned by RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|
| RFC 2246 | TLS 1.0 | Historic |
| RFC 4346 | TLS 1.1 | Historic |

### Historic, not Obsoleted — the distinction that matters

The ask is about the *status* given to the defining RFCs, and the precise answer is **Historic**. RFC 8996 does not carry RFC 2246 or RFC 4346 in its `Obsoletes:` header — its `Obsoletes:` line covers RFC 5469 and RFC 7507, and its `Updates:` line covers the many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1. The defining documents are therefore **reclassified to Historic by this document**, not obsoleted by it. (Historically they *had* been superseded in practice by TLS 1.2/RFC 5246 and TLS 1.3/RFC 8446, which is the rationale RFC 8996 gives; "superseded" describes the protocol lineage, while "Historic" is the formal RFC status label.)

## 3. Related status changes in the same document (context, not part of the answer)

For completeness, and kept separate from the two asked-about RFCs:

- **RFC 4347 (DTLS 1.0)** — also deprecated and moved to Historic. DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347) is *not* deprecated; there is no DTLS 1.1.
- **RFC 5469** — moved to Historic (its DES/IDEA cipher suites were already removed from TLS 1.2 by RFC 5246, and the only TLS versions for which they were defined are now Historic); listed in RFC 8996's `Obsoletes:` header.
- **RFC 7507** — its version-fallback SCSV functionality is superseded by the TLS 1.3 ServerHello.Random sentinel mechanism; listed in RFC 8996's `Obsoletes:` header.
- **RFC 7525** — updated by RFC 8996, which is why RFC 8996 is part of BCP 195.
- Numerous RFCs that already were Historic or already obsoleted are nonetheless marked "Updated by RFC 8996" to reiterate that any use of the obsolete protocol should use modern TLS.

## 4. Notes on scope and sources

- Source of record for the answer: the RFC 8996 text (rfc-editor.org HTML/XML/info views) and the RFC Editor's JSON metadata (`doc_id: RFC8996`, `status: BEST CURRENT PRACTICE`, `pub_date: March 2021`). Datatracker's history page corroborates the draft-to-RFC lineage and date.
- "Status" in this answer means the formal RFC status label assigned by the deprecating document (Historic). Current status in the RFC Index for RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 is likewise Historic, so the "at time of deprecation" and "current" readings agree for these two RFCs.
- No implementation or migration guidance is included, as none was requested.

question: M10
answer:
# 2026 Social Security Contribution and Benefit Base (OASDI Taxable Maximum)

## Answer

**$184,500** — the maximum amount of an individual worker's annual earnings subject to the Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax in calendar year 2026.

This is the officially announced figure, not an estimate. SSA published it with the 2026 cost-of-living adjustment (2.8%) in the fall 2025 automatic-determination announcement.

## Primary sources (all SSA, all agreeing)

| Source | Statement |
|---|---|
| SSA, *2026 Social Security Changes* (COLA fact sheet), ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2026.html | Table "Maximum Taxable Earnings": Social Security (OASDI only) — 2025: $176,100; **2026: $184,500**; Medicare (HI only) — No Limit |
| SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, *Contribution and Benefit Base*, ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html | Year/Amount table: 2025 $176,100; **2026 $184,500**; 2027 $192,300 |
| SSA, *Fast Facts & Figures About Social Security, 2026*, ssa.gov/policy/docs/chartbooks/fast_facts/2026/fast_facts26.html | "Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026: OASDI **184,500**; HI No limit" |
| SSA Publication No. 05-10024, *Understanding the Benefits* (EN-05-10024.pdf) | "You pay Social Security taxes based on your earnings, up to a certain amount. In 2026 that amount is **$184,500**." |
| SSA OACT, *Updating the Social Security Benefit Calculator*, ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html | "Contribution and benefit base for 2026: **$184,500**"; "Old-law" contribution and benefit base for 2026: $137,100 |

## What the number means in practice

- **Applies per worker, per year, across all employers.** If a worker holds two jobs, the combined wages are tested against the single $184,500 ceiling; the worker claims a credit for excess OASDI withheld on Form 1040, and each employer withholds only on wages it paid.
- **Employee rate 6.2%** — maximum employee OASDI withholding for 2026 = $184,500 × 6.2% = **$11,439.00**.
- **Employer rate 6.2%** — matching maximum = **$11,439.00** per employee.
- **Combined employer + employee maximum = $22,878.00** (= $184,500 × 12.4%).
- **Self-employed rate 12.4%** — maximum OASDI self-employment tax for 2026 = **$22,878.00** (before the 92.35% net-earnings adjustment and the Social Security portion of the deduction).
- **Medicare (HI) is uncapped in 2026** — 1.45% employee + 1.45% employer (2.9% self-employed) applies to *all* wages, with no ceiling. The Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies above $200,000 single / $250,000 married filing jointly / $125,000 married filing separately; those thresholds sit **above** the $184,500 OASDI base and are a separate provision, not an OASDI cap.
- **Benefit side:** the same $184,500 is the maximum amount of earnings creditable to a worker's record for 2026 benefit computations, and it drives the year's bend points and maximum benefit ($4,152/month for a worker retiring at full retirement age in 2026).
- **Do not confuse** with the 2026 "old-law" base of **$137,100**, a separate statutory construct used for certain benefit computations, or with the quarter-of-coverage threshold ($1,890 in 2026; $7,560 for four credits).

## How the 2026 figure was derived (statutory formula, for auditability)

Under the automatic-adjustment provisions of the Social Security Act, the base for year Y after 1994 is:

> base(Y) = $60,600 × [NAWI(Y−2) ÷ NAWI(1992)], rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base.

For 2026 (using the 2024 national average wage index, the latest available at determination):

- 1994 base = $60,600
- NAWI 1992 = $22,935.42
- NAWI 2024 = $69,846.57
- $60,600 × ($69,846.57 ÷ $22,935.42) = $60,600 × 3.045358 ≈ **$184,548.7**
- Rounded to nearest $300 → **$184,500** (the next $300 step, $184,800, would require ≥ $184,650)
- $184,500 > 2025 base of $176,100, so the no-reduction floor does not bind.

Year-over-year change: $184,500 − $176,100 = **+$8,400 (+4.77%)**.

## Recent history (SSA OACT table)

| Year | Base | Year | Base |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2019 | $132,900 | 2023 | $160,200 |
| 2020 | $137,700 | 2024 | $168,600 |
| 2021 | $142,800 | 2025 | $176,100 |
| 2022 | $147,000 | **2026** | **$184,500** |
| | | 2027 (already announced) | $192,300 |

## Scope note (finance function)

This is a payroll-tax compliance and payroll-budgeting input: the $184,500 ceiling sets the point at which 6.2% employee and employer OASDI withholding stops for 2026 and the maximum OASDI liability per worker ($11,439 each side, $22,878 combined; $22,878 for the self-employed). Payroll systems, W-2/941 reporting, and 2026 compensation planning should be parameterized to $184,500 for OASDI and to "no limit" for HI. Questions of benefit adequacy, trust-fund solvency, or legislative reform are policy matters outside this figure and are not addressed here.

question: M12
answer:
ANSWER

The 2026 limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

This is the IRC §402(g)(1) limit on the exclusion for elective deferrals. It is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation. It is a per-person, per-calendar-year limit, and it applies to the combined total of pre-tax (traditional) and designated Roth elective deferrals — Roth deferrals do not get a separate allowance.

STATUS OF THE FIGURE

Officially published, not projected. The IRS released the 2026 cost-of-living adjustments in Notice 2025-67 (announced as IR-2025-111). The figure is final for 2026 and does not need to be derived or estimated.

SOURCES (each independently states $24,500 for 2026)

1. IRS Notice 2025-67, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-25-67.pdf — "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."

2. IRS, COLA increases for dollar limitations on benefits and contributions, https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/cola-increases-for-dollar-limitations-on-benefits-and-contributions — 401(k)/403(b)/profit-sharing table: "Elective deferrals 24,500" for 2026 (2025: 23,500; 2024: 23,000; 2023: 22,500).

3. IRS, 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits, https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-401k-and-profit-sharing-plan-contribution-limits — "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."

4. IRS Publication 560, https://www.irs.gov/publications/p560 — "The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026. These limits apply for participants in SARSEPs, 401(k) plans (excluding SIMPLE plans), section 403(b) plans, and section 457(b) plans."

HOW TO APPLY IT

- Payroll/plan administration: cap the employee's elective deferral elections (pre-tax plus Roth combined) at $24,500 for the 2026 calendar year. If the plan runs on a payroll-period basis, the practical cap per period is $24,500 divided by the number of pay periods, with the final period trued up so the year-to-date total does not exceed $24,500.
- Aggregation: an employee who participates in more than one plan of unrelated employers (e.g., two 401(k) plans, or a 401(k) plus a 403(b)) must aggregate elective deferrals across all of them against the single $24,500 figure. Governmental 457(b) deferrals are counted separately and are not aggregated with 401(k) deferrals.
- Excess deferrals: amounts above $24,500 are includible in the employee's gross income for the year and are correctable under the EPCRS excess-deferral procedure.

WHAT THIS NUMBER DELIBERATELY EXCLUDES (per the request)

- Age-50-and-over catch-up: $8,000 for 2026. Adding it gives a total of $32,500 for an eligible participant age 50 or over (and not age 60–63).
- SECURE 2.0 enhanced catch-up for participants who attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026: $11,250. This replaces, rather than stacks on, the $8,000.
- The §415(c) annual additions limit: $72,000 for 2026, which covers employee deferrals plus employer contributions and forfeiture allocations. It is a separate, higher ceiling and does not change the $24,500 employee deferral figure.

SCOPE NOTES THAT DO NOT CHANGE THE STATUTORY NUMBER

- SIMPLE 401(k) plans are outside this figure: the 2026 SIMPLE deferral limit is $17,000 (with a $4,000 age-50 catch-up and $5,250 for ages 60–63). If the plan in question is a SIMPLE 401(k), $17,000 — not $24,500 — is the operative limit.
- A plan document may impose a lower cap than the statutory limit, and nondiscrimination testing (ADP) may further reduce what a highly compensated employee can actually defer. Those are plan-level constraints; they do not alter the $24,500 statutory ceiling.
- The compensation taken into account for contribution purposes is capped at $360,000 for 2026.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE ASK

$24,500 for 2026, before catch-up.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 11250 on irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-401k-and-profit-sharing-plan-contribution-limits and 5250 on irs.gov/retirement-plans/cola-increases-for-dollar-limitations-on-benefits-and-contributions. The first reads: "For 2026, this higher catch-up contribution limit is $11,250."

question: M2
answer:
CURRENT U.S. NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5

ANSWER
  Primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard:  9.0 µg/m³  (annual arithmetic mean)
  Primary (health-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standard: 35 µg/m³  (24-hour average)

1. REGULATORY BASIS
   - Codified at 40 CFR §50.18, 'National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5' (secondary PM2.5 standards are a separate section, §50.19; PM10 is §50.6/§50.7 and must not be conflated with these values).
   - The 9.0 µg/m³ annual level was promulgated in 'Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter,' 89 FR 16202 (final rule signed Feb. 7, 2024), Docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2015-0072, RIN 2060-AV52, EFFECTIVE MAY 6, 2024. The rule states: 'the EPA is revising the primary annual PM2.5 standard by lowering the level from 12.0 µg/m³ to 9.0 µg/m³. The Agency is retaining the current primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard and the primary 24-hour PM10 standard.'
   - The 35 µg/m³ 24-hour level dates to the 2006 PM NAAQS review and was carried forward unchanged by the 2012 review (78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013) and again by the 2024 reconsideration. EPA's Feb. 2024 fact sheet: 'EPA is retaining the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard, with its level of 35 µg/m³.'
   - Status as of the date of this response: still 9.0 / 35. EPA's 'Particle Pollution Designations for the 2024 Revised Annual PM2.5 NAAQS' page (last updated Oct. 2, 2026) restates that 'On February 7, 2024, the EPA promulgated a revised primary annual PM2.5 NAAQS, strengthening the standard from 12.0 µg/m³ to 9.0 µg/m³; retained the existing 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m³.' No final rule restoring 12.0 appears in the available record.

2. FORM OF EACH STANDARD (the level alone is not the whole standard — do not apply these numbers as simple not-to-exceed ceilings)
   - Annual: met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, computed per 40 CFR Part 50 Appendix N (3-year average of annual means), is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³.
   - 24-hour: met when the 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, computed per Appendix N (3-year average of annual 98th-percentile values), is ≤ 35 µg/m³.
   - Both are measured as PM2.5 (particles with aerodynamic diameter ≤ 2.5 µm nominal) by a Federal Reference Method (Appendix L) or a designated Federal Equivalent Method under 40 CFR Part 53.
   - The 9.0 and 35 figures are not comparable magnitudes: they are a long-term mean vs. a high-percentile short-term value.

3. PRIMARY vs. SECONDARY (context only — not part of the answer)
   - Secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards were NOT changed in 2024 and remain: annual 15.0 µg/m³ and 24-hour 35 µg/m³.
   - Primary PM10 24-hour standard remains 150 µg/m³. None of these should be substituted for the primary PM2.5 values requested.

4. DISCLOSURE OF A SOURCE CONFLICT (material to anyone re-verifying)
   - The eCFR §50.18 text retrieved for this response still reads '12.0 micrograms per cubic meter ... annual arithmetic mean' and '35 µg/m³ 24-hour,' with a source note of '[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]' — i.e., a pre-2024 snapshot that does not reflect the May 6, 2024 revision.
   - This response adopts 9.0 µg/m³ because it is supported by (a) the Federal Register final rule text itself, (b) EPA's Feb. 2024 monitoring fact sheet, and (c) EPA's October 2026 designations page, all of which agree on 9.0/35. Two independent EPA sources plus the rulemaking outrank a single apparently stale codification snapshot.
   - Practical instruction: if you re-pull 40 CFR §50.18, confirm the source note reads 89 FR 16202 (or later) before relying on it; if it still reads 78 FR 3277, you are looking at the pre-2024 version and the annual number there (12.0) is superseded.

5. CAVEATS
   - NAAQS are amended by rulemaking and are under continuous periodic review; the answer is version-pinned to the standards in effect on the date of this response (2024 reconsideration, effective May 6, 2024, through at least Oct. 2, 2026).
   - EPA announced a 'path forward' on the PM2.5 standards on March 12, 2025. No completed rulemaking changing the levels is reflected in the available record; if a subsequent final rule issues, the annual level is the one most likely to change.
   - Values are given in µg/m³, the unit in which EPA promulgates PM2.5 NAAQS. No conversion is appropriate or offered.

SUMMARY TABLE
  Standard                 Level        Unit     Form (per App. N)                          Citation
  Primary annual PM2.5     9.0          µg/m³    3-yr average of annual arithmetic means   40 CFR 50.18; 89 FR 16202
  Primary 24-hour PM2.5    35           µg/m³    3-yr average of annual 98th percentiles   40 CFR 50.18; 78 FR 3277 as retained

question: M4
answer:
# Fall protection trigger height — general industry walking-working surfaces

## Answer

**4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level.**

A US employer under federal OSHA general-industry jurisdiction must protect each employee on a walking-working surface that has an unprotected side or edge and that is **4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level** from falling. The protection must be one or more of: a guardrail system, a safety net system, or a personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems).

Governing provision: **29 CFR 1910.28(b)** — *Duty to have fall protection and falling object protection*, Subpart D (*Walking-Working Surfaces*). The general rule is at **§ 1910.28(b)(1)(i)**; the residual catch-all that states the same 4 ft trigger for surfaces not otherwise addressed is **§ 1910.28(b)(15)**, quoted verbatim from the retrieved CFR text:

> "Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed. Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Definition backing the trigger (§ 1910.21(b), retrieved text): *"Unprotected sides and edges mean any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level."* So the duty attaches where there is no wall, guardrail, or stair rail — i.e., the 4 ft threshold is the point at which an *unprotected* edge becomes a regulated fall hazard.

## Why 4 ft is the correct figure and not a coincidence of one paragraph

The same 4 ft (1.2 m) trigger is repeated across the surface-specific paragraphs of § 1910.28(b) in the retrieved text, which confirms it is the subpart's baseline, not a carve-out:

| Paragraph | Subject | Trigger in retrieved text |
|---|---|---|
| § 1910.28(b)(15) | Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level |
| § 1910.28(b)(6)(ii) | Employee above dangerous equipment | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above the equipment |
| § 1910.28(b)(7) | Openings (outside bottom edge) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level |
| § 1910.28(b)(11)(i) | Stairway landing with unprotected side/edge | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level |
| § 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) | Rope descent system | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level |
| § 1910.28(b)(14)(i) | Slaughtering facility platform, unprotected working side | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level |

## Application procedure (what an employer actually does)

1. **Measure the drop.** Determine the vertical distance from the walking-working surface to the next lower level. If it is **< 4 ft (1.2 m)**, § 1910.28(b)(1) fall protection is not triggered by height alone (other hazards — e.g., dangerous equipment under (b)(6)(i), or openings under (b)(7) — can still impose a duty below 4 ft; see below).
2. **Determine whether the edge is protected.** If a wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system already exists at the edge, there is no "unprotected side or edge" and no trigger. Guardrail and stair rail geometry must meet § 1910.29 (e.g., top rail 42 in ± 3 in above the surface, per the retrieved § 1910.29(b)(1)).
3. **If ≥ 4 ft and unprotected, select a compliant system** — guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, positioning). System criteria are in § 1910.29; personal fall protection equipment and use in § 1910.140.
4. **Check for a paragraph-specific rule that governs instead.** Subpart D's opening clause — "Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part" — means a surface-specific paragraph can change *how* protection is provided (and occasionally *whether* it is required), even where the 4 ft number is unchanged.
5. **Train before exposure.** § 1910.30 requires training of employees exposed to fall hazards, and § 1910.29(a)(2) requires the employer to provide and install all required fall protection systems **before** any employee begins work that necessitates them.

## Where the 4 ft answer is modified or displaced (scope qualifiers — the headline number does not change)

- **Low-slope roofs, § 1910.28(b)(13).** Protection is required based on **distance from the roof edge**, not a 4 ft height trigger: within **less than 6 ft (1.6 m)** of the edge, a guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest system is required; at **6 ft to less than 15 ft**, one of those systems is required but a **designated area** is permitted for work that is both infrequent and temporary; at **15 ft (4.6 m) or more**, the employer must provide protection or a designated area, and need not provide fall protection at all if the work is both infrequent and temporary, but must implement and enforce a work rule prohibiting employees from coming within 15 ft of the edge without fall protection.
- **Dangerous equipment, § 1910.28(b)(6).** No de minimis height: an employee **less than 4 ft** above dangerous equipment must be protected by a guardrail system or travel restraint system unless the equipment is covered or guarded to eliminate the hazard; at **4 ft or more**, guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest is required.
- **Infeasible / greater hazard.** Where the employer can demonstrate that a required system is infeasible or creates a greater hazard, Subpart D permits a written fall protection plan instead (see § 1910.28(b)(1) and the plan requirements of § 1910.29(k)). This is a documented, narrow exception — it is not a general license to work unprotected above 4 ft.
- **Fixed ladders, § 1910.28(b)(9).** A separate trigger at **more than 24 ft (7.3 m)** above a lower level governs the personal fall arrest / ladder safety system requirements for fixed ladders (with the phase-in schedule for existing ladders).
- **Scaffolds, § 1910.28(b)(12)(i).** Fall protection on scaffolds is governed by reference to **29 CFR part 1926, subpart L** (construction), not by the 4 ft general-industry figure.
- **Repair/service/assembly pits under 10 ft deep, § 1910.28(b)(8).** A defined alternative compliance path (limited access, floor markings or warning line at least 6 ft from the pit edge, "Caution—Open Pit" signage) rather than a height trigger.

## Two traps to avoid

1. **Do not use the construction number.** The construction industry standard, **29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1)**, triggers at **6 feet (1.8 m)**. The question is expressly general industry; 6 ft is wrong here. The only 6 ft values in the retrieved general-industry text are roof-edge *distances* under (b)(13) and pit *marking distances* under (b)(8) — different quantities that must not be read as a height threshold.
2. **Do not stop at the federal rule if a state plan applies.** OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and may adopt a stricter trigger or additional surface-specific requirements. Confirm the establishment's jurisdiction (federal OSHA vs. a State Plan state) before finalizing the number in a written program. This is a verification step, not a change to the federal answer: **4 ft**.

## Version / currency

The 4 ft trigger is the product of the 2016 Walking-Working Surfaces rule (published November 18, 2016; effective January 17, 2017), which revised 29 CFR 1910 Subpart D and replaced the prior § 1910.23 framework. The pre-2017 general-industry rule also used 4 ft for open-sided floors and platforms, so the figure is stable across the revision. The retrieved CFR text used here is the 2024 edition of 29 CFR volume 5 and the current eCFR text, both showing 4 ft (1.2 m).

## One-line answer for a written program

*"Where an employee is exposed to an unprotected side or edge of a walking-working surface that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level, the employer must provide fall protection — guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system — in accordance with 29 CFR 1910.28(b) and 1910.29, before work begins."*

question: M6
answer:
ANSWER

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and, in addition, reserve fuel sufficient to fly for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed. The 20-minute figure applies both day and night — there is no day/night split for rotorcraft.

Reserve fuel = 20 minutes at normal cruising speed (usable fuel), in addition to the fuel required to fly to the first point of intended landing considering wind and forecast weather.

1. REGULATORY BASIS

14 CFR 91.151 (Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions), paragraph (b):

  "(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

For contrast, paragraph (a) of the same section governs airplanes and does carry a time-of-day split (30 minutes day / 45 minutes night). Those airplane figures do not apply to helicopters. Rotorcraft paragraph (b) is a single, time-of-day-independent 20 minutes.

Part 135 (on-demand/charter and commuter helicopter operations) is identical. 14 CFR 135.209(b):

  "(b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

So whether the flight is a private Part 91 flight or a Part 135 helicopter operation, the VFR reserve is 20 minutes. The FAA's own fuel-planning guidance (FAA publication at faa.gov/media/32056, "FAR Part 135 Helicopter VFR Operations") states it explicitly: "During day or night the required reserve fuel is the amount that allows continued operation for 20 minutes."

2. SCOPE — WHICH RULE APPLIES

  - Part 91 private/personal helicopter VFR flight: 91.151(b) -> 20 minutes.
  - Part 135 helicopter VFR (air taxi/charter, commuter, HAA): 135.209(b) -> 20 minutes.
  - Gyroplanes: they are rotorcraft, so 91.151(b) -> 20 minutes.
  - Day vs. night: no difference. 20 minutes in both cases.
  - IFR flight: out of scope of this question; note only that IFR carries a different (larger, 45-minute) requirement under 91.167/135.223 and must not be conflated with the VFR answer.
  - Non-US operations: out of scope; this answer is the FAA/US rule only.

3. WHAT THE 20 MINUTES IS AND IS NOT

  - It is a minimum. "At least 20 minutes." It is a floor, not a target.
  - It is measured at normal cruising speed (91.151(b)) / normal cruising fuel consumption (135.209(b)) — not at best-range or maximum-range speed, and not at a reduced fuel-flow descent profile.
  - It is usable fuel. Unusable fuel (the quantity the tank/tip-tank outlets cannot deliver in all attitudes) does not count toward the reserve; add it on top when converting the time reserve into a total fuel load.
  - It is in addition to, not inclusive of, the fuel to the first point of intended landing, and that leg is computed considering wind and forecast weather conditions.
  - The 20 minutes does not include taxi fuel, climb allowance, approach/hover time at the destination, or any traffic-delay contingency. Those are separate increments under the preflight-action rule, 91.103 (and 135.213/135.77 for Part 135), which require the pilot to become familiar with all available information including fuel required and known delays.
  - It is not a separate tank or a physically segregated quantity; it is a computed quantity of fuel that must be aboard at brake/takeoff release.

4. CONVERTING THE 20-MINUTE RESERVE INTO A QUANTITY

Use the helicopter's own Rotorcraft Flight Manual/POH cruise fuel-flow figure at normal cruising speed. Reserve quantity:

  Reserve (gal) = 20/60 x hourly cruise fuel flow (gal/hr) = hourly cruise fuel flow / 3

Worked examples (arithmetic shown; burn rates are illustrative placeholders — substitute the specific RFM/POH value, since fuel flow varies with temperature, altitude, weight, and power setting):

  - 30 gal/hr cruise -> 30/3 = 10 gal reserve
  - 24 gal/hr cruise -> 24/3 = 8 gal reserve
  - 15 gal/hr cruise -> 15/3 = 5 gal reserve
  - 8.4 gal/hr cruise -> 8.4/3 = 2.8 gal reserve

Total fuel at start = (fuel to first point of intended landing, wind/forecast-adjusted) + reserve + taxi/climb/contingency allowances + unusable fuel.

If the operator prefers to work in pounds, convert gallons using the fuel density in the POH (Jet A/A-1 ~ 6.7 lb/gal; 100LL ~ 6.0 lb/gal); the 20-minute time value is unchanged.

5. PREFLIGHT PLANNING PROCEDURE

  Step 1. Compute time en route to the first point of intended landing using forecast winds and planned cruise power; convert to fuel using POH cruise fuel flow.
  Step 2. Add the reserve: 20 minutes at normal cruising speed (= one-third of the hourly cruise burn).
  Step 3. Add taxi/hover, climb, approach, and any known delay or contingency fuel per 91.103 preflight action.
  Step 4. Add unusable fuel per the RFM.
  Step 5. Compare the resulting total against usable capacity; verify the departure fuel load is at or below maximum gross weight with that fuel aboard.
  Step 6. Confirm at engine start that the actual usable fuel aboard equals or exceeds the Step 5 total. If not, reduce payload/route or add fuel before beginning the flight.

6. COMMON ERRORS THIS ANSWER GUARDS AGAINST

  - Applying the airplane 30/45-minute day/night figures to a helicopter. Wrong: rotorcraft get 20 minutes, day or night.
  - Applying the 45-minute IFR reserve to a VFR flight. Wrong: that is 91.167/135.223, IFR only.
  - Counting the 20 minutes as part of, rather than in addition to, the fuel to the first point of intended landing.
  - Computing the reserve at best-range or max-endurance speed instead of normal cruising speed.
  - Counting unusable fuel toward the reserve.
  - Treating 20 minutes as adequate operational planning. It is a legal minimum; weather, wind, diversion options, and the operator's own fuel policy normally warrant a larger margin.

question: M8
answer:
## Answer

**1. The deprecating RFC is RFC 8996.** Its abstract opens: "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346)." RFC 8996 is an Internet Best Current Practice — it updates RFC 7525 and is therefore part of **BCP 195** (its "Status of This Memo" reads: "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice").

**2. The status it gave the defining RFCs is Historic.** The same abstract sentence continues: "Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status." Section 1 of RFC 8996 states the same disposition explicitly: "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012. Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

So the two documents that defined the deprecated protocol versions, and their new status, are:

| Protocol version | Defining RFC | Original category | Status assigned by RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | RFC 2246 (Dierks & Allen) | Standards Track | **Historic** |
| TLS 1.1 | RFC 4346 (Dierks & Rescorla) | Standards Track | **Historic** |

The current RFC Editor info pages confirm the resulting state: RFC 2246 is listed as "Historic" and RFC 4346 is listed as "Historic".

## Precision points that matter when citing this

- **"Historic" is the status; "deprecated" is the action.** RFC 8996 *deprecates* the versions and *moves the documents to Historic*. Do not conflate the two terms when quoting.
- **Historic is not the same as Obsolete.** RFC 2246 was already obsoleted by RFC 4346, and RFC 4346 by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2); the RFC Editor pages record that separately ("This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 5246"). RFC 8996's contribution is the change of document *status* to Historic plus normative updates to the many RFCs that still referenced TLS 1.0/1.1 — not a new Obsoletes relationship. Saying RFC 8996 "obsoleted" TLS 1.0/1.1 is imprecise; saying it "deprecated them and moved the defining RFCs to Historic" is exact.
- **Scope of the same RFC.** RFC 8996 also deprecates DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) and moves it to Historic, but explicitly does *not* deprecate DTLS 1.2, and notes there is no DTLS 1.1. If the question is strictly about TLS, DTLS is context only.
- **Collateral status change.** RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites) was also moved to Historic by RFC 8996, because the only TLS versions for which those suites were defined are now Historic. RFC 8996 additionally updates many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1, including RFC 7525 (BCP 195) and RFC 6347.
- **Stated rationale** (RFC 8996, Section 1 and Security Considerations): mandatory-to-implement older cipher suites (e.g., TLS 1.0 requires TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA), absence of AEAD cipher suites before TLS 1.2, handshake integrity and peer authentication both resting on SHA-1, and increased attack surface / misconfiguration risk from supporting four protocol versions.

## One-line citation form

> RFC 8996 (BCP 195), "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1," formally deprecates TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) and moves both defining documents to Historic status.

## Not asserted here

The fetched passages do not contain RFC 8996's publication date field, so no date is stated as sourced. (The document is commonly cited as March 2021; verify against the RFC header before publishing a dated citation.)
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 1.0 on rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246 and 1.1 on rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4346. The first reads: "This document specifies Version 1.0 of the Transport Layer Security"

question: M10
answer:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for calendar year 2026 is $184,500.

Status: this is a final, announced determination by the Social Security Administration, not an estimate or projection. It applies to wages paid and self-employment income earned in calendar year 2026.

1. PRIMARY SOURCES (all SSA, all agree)
- SSA COLA Fact Sheet, "2026 SOCIAL SECURITY CHANGES" (ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2026.html): "Maximum Taxable Earnings — Social Security (OASDI only): 2025 $176,100; 2026 $184,500. Medicare (HI only): No Limit."
- SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, "Automatic Determinations in Recent Years" (ssa.gov/oact/COLA/autoAdj.html): 2026 row, Contribution and benefit base = $184,500 (2025 = $176,100; 2027 = $192,300).
- SSA Publication No. 42-007, EFW2 Tax Year 2026 specifications (ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf): "The Social Security Wage Base for tax year 2026 is $184,500"; Social Security wages/tips must not exceed $184,500 for TY2026, and Social Security tax withheld "should not exceed $11,439.00 for tax year 2026."
- SSA OACT, "Contribution and benefit bases, 1937-2027" (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html): 2026 = $184,500.

2. STATUTORY BASIS AND VERIFICATION OF THE NUMBER
Legal authority: Section 230 of the Social Security Act, as amended (automatic adjustment of the contribution and benefit base). The base is wage-indexed, not price-indexed, and the formula applies in a year only if a cost-of-living increase is effective for December of the preceding year; a COLA was effective for December 2025, so the formula applied to the 2026 determination.

Formula: Base(Y) = $60,600 × [AWI(Y-2) ÷ AWI(1992)], rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base.

Inputs for Y = 2026:
- 1994 base: $60,600
- AWI for 1992: $22,935.42
- AWI for 2024 (the Y-2 index used): $69,846.57

Computation:
  60,600 × 69,846.57 ÷ 22,935.42
  = 60,600 × 3.045358...
  = $184,548.7
  Rounded to nearest $300: 184,548.7 ÷ 300 = 615.16 → 615 × 300 = $184,500

Cross-check of the method against SSA's own published 2027 determination (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbbdet.html): $60,600 × 72,800.33 ÷ 22,935.42 = $192,353.14 → $192,300, which is the published 2027 base. This confirms the index vintages used above (Y-2 AWI) are correct, so the $184,500 result for 2026 is reproduced from the statute rather than merely copied.

3. TAX CONSEQUENCES OF THE BASE (for payroll/benefit use)
- Employee: 6.2% OASDI on earnings up to $184,500 → maximum employee OASDI tax for 2026 = $11,439.00 (matches SSA's EFW2 maximum withholding figure exactly: 184,500 × 0.062 = 11,439.00).
- Employer: matching 6.2%, another $11,439.00 per employee at or above the base.
- Self-employed: 12.4% OASDI on net self-employment earnings up to $184,500 → $22,878.00 (derived: 184,500 × 0.124), before the income-tax deduction for one-half of SE tax.
- Earnings above $184,500 in 2026 are not subject to OASDI tax and are not creditable for Social Security benefit computation purposes.
- The 6.2% rate is the OASDI portion only; the combined employee rate is 7.65% because Medicare's Hospital Insurance (HI) portion is 1.45% and has no earnings cap. HI is therefore not part of this answer.

4. ADJACENT 2026 FIGURES (do not confuse with the base)
- Medicare (HI) taxable maximum: none — no cap in 2026. (Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies to wages above $200,000 single / $250,000 married filing jointly; that threshold is statutory and not indexed.)
- Retirement earnings test exempt amounts, 2026: $24,480/yr ($2,040/mo) under full retirement age; $65,160/yr ($5,430/mo) in the year full retirement age is reached.
- Quarter of coverage, 2026: $1,890.
- For contrast only: the 2025 base was $176,100 and the already-determined 2027 base is $192,300. The question asks 2026, which is $184,500.

5. HOW TO CITE
"Social Security Administration, 2026 Social Security Changes (COLA Fact Sheet), Maximum Taxable Earnings — Social Security (OASDI only): $184,500; see also SSA OACT, Contribution and Benefit Bases, 1937-2027, and SSA Pub. No. 42-007 (EFW2, Tax Year 2026)."

6. SCOPE NOTE
This answer covers the federal OASDI taxable maximum for 2026 as announced by SSA. It does not address state disability or paid-leave wage bases, Railroad Retirement tier treatment, or nonresident alien/Totalization Agreement exceptions, each of which can modify payroll treatment but none of which changes the $184,500 OASDI base.

question: M12
answer:
ANSWER

For tax year 2026, an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan are limited to $24,500 — before any catch-up contribution. This is the IRC §402(g)(1) limit on the exclusion for elective deferrals, as adjusted for cost of living.

AUTHORITY (all IRS, all in agreement)

1. IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 COLA notice, published in IRB 2025-49 at page 761): "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3) ... is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
2. IRS COLA table, '401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing plans, etc.' — Elective deferrals: 2026 $24,500; 2025 $23,500; 2024 $23,000; 2023 $22,500.
3. IRS Publication 560, Limit on Elective Deferrals: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $23,500 for 2025 and increases to $24,500 for 2026."
4. IRS 'Retirement topics — 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits': "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."

STATUTORY FRAME

- Code section: IRC §402(g)(1); implementing/adjustment authority §402(g)(4)–(5) and §415(d).
- Ceiling structure: the operative limit is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation. For any employee earning at least $24,500 in compensation for the year, $24,500 is the binding number.
- Per-person, per-calendar-year: the limit is not per plan and not per employer. An employee deferring into two 401(k) plans (same controlled group, or unrelated employers) aggregates all elective deferrals against the single $24,500 figure.
- Deferral type: pre-tax (traditional) and designated Roth elective deferrals both count against the same $24,500. Designating a deferral as Roth does not create additional room.
- Compensation cap: compensation taken into account for plan purposes is limited to $360,000 for 2026 (§401(a)(17)); this does not change the $24,500 deferral limit.

WHAT THIS NUMBER IS NOT (common mis-applications)

- Not the catch-up-inclusive maximum. Catch-up contributions are excluded by the request. For reference only, the 2026 age-50+ catch-up limit is $8,000, and the SECURE 2.0 enhanced catch-up for participants attaining age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026 is $11,250; those sit on top of the $24,500, for a maximum of $32,500 or $35,750 respectively, if the plan permits.
- Not the SIMPLE 401(k) limit. If the plan is a SIMPLE 401(k) under §401(k)(11), the 2026 employee deferral limit is $17,000, not $24,500. Confirm plan type before communicating a number.
- Not the total-contribution limit. The §415(c) annual additions limit for 2026 is $72,000 (elective deferrals + employer match + nonelective + forfeitures, excluding catch-up).
- Not the 403(b)/457(b) figures by accident — they happen to be the same $24,500 for 2026, but the citation and plan type differ.

HR OPERATING PROCEDURE

1. Confirm plan type from the plan document / adoption agreement: standard 401(k) (including safe harbor) → $24,500; SIMPLE 401(k) → $17,000.
2. Confirm the plan document does not impose a lower limit; if it does, the lower limit governs payroll.
3. Set the payroll system's annual deferral cap to $24,500 for the plan year beginning 2026-01-01, with a separate catch-up bucket if the plan permits catch-up and the participant is eligible.
4. Apply the controlled-group aggregation rule at onboarding: ask whether the employee participates in another 401(k), 403(b), SARSEP, or 457(b) plan of the same employer/controlled group, and reduce the cap accordingly.
5. If deferrals exceed $24,500 in the aggregate, the excess is includible in the employee's gross income for the year; correct under the IRS EPCRS excess-deferral correction procedures and issue the appropriate Form 1099-R / W-2 reporting.
6. Re-verify against the annual IRS COLA notice each fall; the figure is subject to cost-of-living adjustment for later years.

CAVEATS

- Scope is US federal tax law only (assumed; no other jurisdiction specified). State tax conformity is generally to federal but should be confirmed where relevant.
- Plan-specific and payroll-specific facts (plan type, plan-document limits, other-plan participation) can lower the operative number; they cannot raise it above $24,500.
- Effective for the 2026 calendar/tax year; confirm the plan's limitation year aligns with the calendar year.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 11250 on irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-401k-and-profit-sharing-plan-contribution-limits and 5250 on irs.gov/retirement-plans/cola-increases-for-dollar-limitations-on-benefits-and-contributions. The first reads: "For 2026, this higher catch-up contribution limit is $11,250."

question: M2
answer:
CURRENT U.S. NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5
Answer as of 2026-11-16 (date the cited sources were retrieved). If a later EPA rulemaking has occurred, re-verify per the procedure in Section 5.

1. ANSWER

  Ask 1 — Primary annual PM2.5 standard: 9.0 µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter), annual arithmetic mean.
  Ask 2 — Primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard: 35 µg/m³, 24-hour average.

These are the health-based primary NAAQS for fine particulate matter established under Clean Air Act § 109 and codified at 40 CFR 50.20.

2. AUTHORITATIVE CITATION AND REGULATORY FORM

Source of the levels: 40 CFR 50.20, "National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5" (added by the EPA final rule "Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter," signed/published February 7, 2024; 89 FR 16202; effective May 2024). Codified text as it appears in the CFR 2025 edition (Title 40, vol. 2):

  § 50.20(a): "The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 ... by either: (1) A reference method based on appendix L ... or (2) An equivalent method ..."
  § 50.20(b): "The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m3."
  § 50.20(c): "The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3."

Form of the standards (needed to apply the numbers correctly; 40 CFR part 50, appendix N):

  Indicator | Averaging time | Primary level | Form
  PM2.5     | Annual         | 9.0 µg/m³     | Annual arithmetic mean, averaged over 3 years
  PM2.5     | 24-hour        | 35 µg/m³      | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 years

Both standards are met at a monitoring site when the 3-year averaged value is less than or equal to the level (≤ 9.0 µg/m³ annual; ≤ 35 µg/m³ 24-hour). A single year's value, or a 24-hour value other than the 98th percentile, is not the regulatory test.

3. WHY THE ANSWER IS 9.0 AND NOT 12.0 — THE § 50.18 / § 50.20 COEXISTENCE

This is the one point where a careful reader will see an apparent conflict, so it is addressed directly.

The current CFR contains TWO sections with the same title:

  • § 50.18 — carries the 2012-era primary PM2.5 standards: 12.0 µg/m³ annual arithmetic mean and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour (source: [78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]; still shown at 12.0 in the current eCFR text).
  • § 50.20 — carries the 2024-revised primary PM2.5 standards: 9.0 µg/m³ annual arithmetic mean and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour.

The February 7, 2024 final reconsideration revised the level of the primary annual standard from 12.0 to 9.0 µg/m³ and expressly retained the primary 24-hour standard at 35 µg/m³. EPA's own summary of the action states: "EPA is revising the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard from 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) to 9.0 µg/m3" and "EPA is retaining the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard at the level of 35 µg/m3." The agency's "New Standards" table lists: PM2.5 annual, Primary 9.0 µg/m³, form = annual arithmetic mean averaged over 3 years; PM2.5 24-hour, Primary and Secondary 35 µg/m³, form = 98th percentile averaged over 3 years.

EPA placed the revised standards in a new section (§ 50.20) rather than amending § 50.18 in place, and left § 50.18 in the CFR. Consequently, § 50.18 does not state the current health-based primary standard for going-forward NAAQS purposes; § 50.20 does. § 50.18 remains cross-referenced by pre-existing implementation provisions and by the rule's own transition/grandfathering language (for example, the implementation fact sheet states that permit applicants who received a final PSD permit before the effective date of the new standards need not make adjustments). Practical rule for users:

  - If the question is "what are the current primary PM2.5 NAAQS?" → 9.0 µg/m³ annual; 35 µg/m³ 24-hour (§ 50.20).
  - If the question is "what standard does my permitting/designation program cross-reference?" → check the specific program regulation. Older program text may still point to § 50.18 and therefore to 12.0 µg/m³ for the annual standard. That is an implementation-program question, not a question about the current NAAQS levels.

4. SCOPE AND EXCLUSIONS (stated so the answer is not over-read)

  - Primary (health-based) standards only, as asked. For context and to prevent confusion: the secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards are 15.0 µg/m³ annual arithmetic mean and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour (98th percentile); the 2024 action did not change the secondary annual standard or the 24-hour standards. These are NOT the values requested and must not be substituted for the primary levels.
  - PM10 standards (150 µg/m³, 24-hour, primary and secondary; not to be exceeded more than once per year on average over 3 years) were unchanged by the 2024 action and are outside this request.
  - These are federal NAAQS. State or local ambient standards, and area-specific attainment designations under the 2024 annual standard, are separate matters.

5. VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (how a reviewer confirms these two numbers)

  Step 1 — Primary source of record. Open 40 CFR 50.20 (eCFR: https://ecfr.gov/current/title-40/section-50.20; GovInfo CFR-2025-title40-vol2 PDF). Confirm the two numbers 9.0 (annual) and 35 (24-hour) and the two attainment sentences (≤ 9.0; ≤ 35).
  Step 2 — Do not stop at § 50.18. If the only page checked is 40 CFR 50.18, the answer will read 12.0 µg/m³, which is the superseded annual level. Confirm which section is the operative one per Section 3 above.
  Step 3 — Corroborate against the rulemaking record. EPA's final reconsideration page (https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/final-reconsideration-national-ambient-air-quality-standards-particulate-matter-pm) and the February 2024 overview fact sheet (pm-naaqs-overview.pdf) both state 9.0 µg/m³ primary annual and retention of the 35 µg/m³ 24-hour standard, with the form table reproduced in Section 2.
  Step 4 — Date check. Confirm no PM NAAQS rulemaking has been finalized after the retrieval date of these sources (2026-11-16). If a later final rule exists, the levels in this answer are superseded and must be replaced; the statutory review cycle makes periodic revision expected.

6. ONE-LINE RESTATEMENT

Current U.S. national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5: 9.0 µg/m³, annual arithmetic mean averaged over 3 years (40 CFR 50.20(a),(b)); and 35 µg/m³, 98th percentile 24-hour concentration averaged over 3 years (40 CFR 50.20(a),(c)).

question: M4
answer:
SAFETY ENGINEERING DETERMINATION — GENERAL INDUSTRY FALL PROTECTION TRIGGER HEIGHT FOR UNPROTECTED SIDES AND EDGES

1. ANSWER
4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level. At and above that height the employer must protect each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling.

Governing provision: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1) (OSHA Walking-Working Surfaces; general industry, 29 CFR Part 1910 Subpart D). Effective date of the current rule: January 17, 2017 (81 FR 82494); text unchanged in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 CFR editions examined.

2. SUBSTANCE OF THE REQUIREMENT
1910.28(b)(1) requires that, except as provided elsewhere in the section, each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level be protected from falling by one or more of:
 (i) guardrail systems;
 (ii) safety net systems; or
 (iii) personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

The catch-all paragraph, 1910.28(b)(15) 'Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed,' restates the same trigger in the same words — 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level — and is quoted identically in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 CFR text. Every other height-triggered paragraph in Subpart D (stairway landings, 1910.28(b)(11)(i); rope descent systems, 1910.28(b)(12)(ii); slaughtering facility platforms, 1910.28(b)(14)(i)) uses the same 4-foot (1.2 m) figure, which confirms 4 ft as the subpart's baseline.

Note on history: the pre-2017 general industry rule (former 1910.23(c)(1)) also used 4 feet for open-sided floors, platforms and runways. The 2017 rule reorganized and expanded the requirements but did not change the 4-foot trigger. A program written to the old 4-foot number remains numerically correct but must be re-cited and re-checked against the new system criteria in 1910.29 and the training duties in 1910.30.

3. HOW THE HEIGHT IS MEASURED
Vertical distance from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands (or works) to the lower level onto which the employee could fall. The trigger is met at exactly 4 ft — the rule reads '4 feet (1.2 m) or more.' There is no duration or frequency qualifier and no 'temporary and infrequent' exemption in 1910.28(b)(1): a 10-minute task at 4 ft or above requires protection. 'Unprotected side or edge' is defined in 1910.21(b) as any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system protecting the employee from falling to a lower level.

4. WHAT COUNTS AS PROTECTION AT OR ABOVE 4 FT
Guardrail system meeting 1910.29(b) — top rail 42 in ±3 in (107 cm ±8 cm) above the surface, with midrail/screen/mesh/equivalent intermediate member; safety net system per 1910.29(c); or a personal fall protection system (fall arrest, travel restraint, positioning) per 1910.29(d)-(f) and 1910.140. A warning line, floor marking, cone, sign or barricade tape alone does NOT satisfy 1910.28(b)(1) for an unprotected side or edge; warning lines are a component of the designated-area option only where the standard specifically allows it (e.g., low-slope roof work under 1910.28(b)(13) and 1910.29(d)).

5. EXCEPTIONS AND OTHER HEIGHT THRESHOLDS AN EMPLOYER MUST NOT CONFUSE WITH THE 4-FOOT ANSWER
- Infeasibility: where the employer can demonstrate that guardrails, nets or personal fall protection are infeasible or create a greater hazard, a written fall protection plan is required (1910.28(b)(2) with 1910.29(k)); the 4-foot trigger is not waived, it is satisfied by a different, documented means.
- Holes (1910.28(b)(3)): protection required for holes, including chutes, 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above lower levels.
- Dangerous equipment (1910.28(b)(6)): below 4 ft, guardrail system or travel restraint (unless the equipment is covered or guarded to eliminate the hazard); at 4 ft or more, guardrail, safety net, travel restraint or personal fall arrest. This is the one place where a height under 4 ft still compels protection.
- Openings (1910.28(b)(7)): where the inside bottom edge of the opening is less than 39 in (99 cm) above the walking-working surface and the outside bottom edge is 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level, guardrail, net, travel restraint or personal fall arrest is required.
- Repair/service/assembly pits (1910.28(b)(8)): conditional alternative using access limits within 6 ft (1.8 m) of the edge for trained employees, floor markings and/or a warning line at least 6 ft (1.8 m) from the edge, and 'Caution—Open Pit' signage.
- Fixed ladders (1910.28(b)(9)): personal fall arrest or ladder safety system required for ladders extending more than 24 ft (7.3 m) above a lower level; cages/wells no longer accepted.
- Stairway landings (1910.28(b)(11)(i)): 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level — guardrail or stair rail system.
- Rope descent systems (1910.28(b)(12)(ii)): 4 ft (1.2 m) or more — personal fall arrest system.
- Low-slope roofs (1910.28(b)(13)): keyed to distance from the roof edge, not to height above grade — full protection (guardrail, net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest) when work is performed less than 6 ft (1.6 m) from the edge, with the intermediate band up to 15 ft (4.6 m) and the 15-ft work-rule option; a designated area/warning line is permitted only in the circumstances the paragraph allows. A low roof (e.g., 10 ft) still triggers these duties.
- Scaffolds (1910.28(b)(12)(i)): fall protection per 29 CFR 1926 Subpart L, not the 4-foot figure.

6. FRAMEWORK DISTINCTIONS (do not cross-apply)
- Construction: 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) — 6 ft (1.8 m) above a lower level.
- Shipyard: 29 CFR 1915 Subpart M — 5 ft (1.5 m).
- Longshoring: 29 CFR 1917/1918 have their own triggers.
This determination is general industry only, as asked.

7. JURISDICTION CAVEAT
This is the federal OSHA answer. OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and in practice adopt the 4-foot general industry trigger, but a State Plan may add requirements (permits, plan documents, training records, stricter means) and, in a few states, different numbers in adjacent standards. The employer must confirm the current State Plan text for the site before finalizing. Federal OSHA does not cover state and local government employees in states without a State Plan, and public-sector, maritime, mining (MSHA) and aviation (FAA) workplaces may be governed by other regimes.

8. EMPLOYER VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (how to apply the 4-ft answer on site)
Step 1 — Walk the site and list every walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge (platforms, mezzanines, runways, docks, loading areas, roofs, pits, stairway landings).
Step 2 — For each, measure the vertical drop from the working surface to the lower level; record it. Flag everything at 4 ft (1.2 m) or more.
Step 3 — For each flagged surface, record the protection in place and verify it against 1910.29 (top rail height 42 in ±3 in; midrail; strength; net installation; anchorage and system capacity for personal fall protection per 1910.140).
Step 4 — Where no protection exists, select and install a compliant system before any employee begins work (1910.29(a)(2)); where the employer intends to rely on infeasibility, prepare the written fall protection plan required by 1910.28(b)(2)/1910.29(k) and document the basis.
Step 5 — Train affected employees per 1910.30 and retain the records; re-verify whenever the surface, task or equipment changes.
Step 6 — Separately screen for the special thresholds in section 5 (dangerous equipment, holes, openings, pits, fixed ladders, low-slope roofs) because those duties can apply at heights below 4 ft or use different geometry.

9. LIMITS OF THIS DETERMINATION
This answers the general-industry trigger height for an unprotected side or edge on a walking-working surface under federal OSHA. It does not determine the correct system for a specific surface, does not substitute for a site-specific hazard assessment, and does not address State Plan add-ons or non-OSHA regimes. Where the actual workplace involves a low-slope roof, fixed ladder, pit, scaffold or dangerous equipment, the applicable paragraph in section 5 governs over the baseline 4-foot figure.
