# Reserve fuel for a helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States

## 1. Answer

**20 minutes.** A helicopter (rotorcraft) may not begin a VFR flight in the US unless it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly for **at least 20 minutes** beyond that point. The 20-minute figure applies **both day and night** — the 30-minute day / 45-minute night split applies only to airplanes.

Authority: **14 CFR § 91.151(b)** (Part 91, general operating rules).

Operative text, quoted verbatim from the eCFR:

> "§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.
>
> (a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
>
> (1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
>
> (2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
>
> (b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."
>
> — 14 CFR 91.151, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151 (also reproduced identically at https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-91 and https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title14-vol2/pdf/CFR-2026-title14-vol2-sec91-151.pdf)

Three elements of that sentence drive the whole calculation:

1. **"to fly to the first point of intended landing"** — trip fuel, computed considering wind and forecast weather (i.e., wind-corrected, not still-air).
2. **"assuming normal cruising speed"** — the reserve is measured at normal cruise, not at max-endurance or best-range speed. So the reserve is a fixed duration converted at your normal cruise burn.
3. **"to fly after that for at least 20 minutes"** — the 20 minutes is *in addition to* trip fuel and must remain after the first point of intended landing. It is a floor, not a target.

## 2. Applicability matrix — which rule gives which number

| Operation | Rule | Reserve after first point of intended landing |
|---|---|---|
| **Helicopter / rotorcraft, VFR, Part 91, day** | **§ 91.151(b)** | **20 minutes** |
| **Helicopter / rotorcraft, VFR, Part 91, night** | **§ 91.151(b)** | **20 minutes** (no night increase) |
| Helicopter, VFR, Part 135 (commercial) | § 135.209(b) | 20 minutes, day or night (per FAA guidance, see § 3) |
| Airplane, VFR, Part 91, day | § 91.151(a)(1) | 30 minutes |
| Airplane, VFR, Part 91, night | § 91.151(a)(2) | 45 minutes |
| Helicopter, **IFR**, Part 91 | § 91.167(a)(3) | 30 minutes (not applicable to a VFR flight; shown to prevent confusion) |
| Airplane, IFR, Part 91 | § 91.167(a)(3) | 45 minutes |

Notes on the matrix:

- **"Rotorcraft" includes helicopters and gyroplanes.** § 91.151(b) says rotorcraft, not helicopter, so both are covered by the same 20-minute rule.
- **No day/night difference for rotorcraft.** This is the single most common error: pilots carry the airplane 45-minute night figure over to helicopters. It does not apply. § 91.151(a) is expressly limited to airplanes.
- **No VFR alternate fuel.** § 91.151 requires fuel only to the first point of intended landing plus the reserve. There is no VFR destination-alternate fuel requirement analogous to the IFR alternate in § 91.167(a)(2).
- **The answer does not change with the season, latitude, or time of sunset**, only with whether the aircraft is a rotorcraft.

## 3. Part 135 cross-check (if the flight is commercial)

The FAA's own fuel-planning guidance document states, for Part 135 helicopter VFR operations:

> "15. FAR PART 135 HELICOPTER VFR OPERATIONS. … b. Additional Fuel: (1) Alternate Fuel. N/A. (2) Reserve Fuel. FAR § 135.209(b). During day or night the required reserve fuel is the amount that allows continued operation for 20 minutes."
>
> — https://www.faa.gov/media/32056

So whether the flight is conducted under Part 91 or Part 135, a helicopter VFR reserve is **20 minutes, day or night**. The regulation number differs (91.151(b) vs. 135.209(b)); the number does not.

(Contrast, from the same document: Part 135 *airplane* VFR is 30 minutes day / 45 minutes night under § 135.209(a)(1)–(2) — again the airplane/rotorcraft split, not a Part 91/135 split.)

## 4. Converting the 20 minutes into fuel quantity

Because the rule is expressed as a **duration**, the fuel quantity depends on the aircraft. Use the normal-cruise fuel burn from the Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) for the planned cruise power setting and altitude, and convert:

```
Reserve (gal)  = normal-cruise burn (gal/h) × (20 / 60)
               = normal-cruise burn (gal/h) / 3

Reserve (lb)   = Reserve (gal) × 6.7 lb/gal     (avgas or Jet A, approx., standard day)
Reserve (min)  = Reserve (gal) / burn (gal/h) × 60     (should come back as >= 20)
```

20 minutes = 1/3 hour = 0.3333 h exactly. No rounding may be applied downward: round the resulting quantity **up**, because 20 minutes is a minimum.

Illustrative conversion (verify every burn rate against the specific aircraft's POH before use — these are representative values, not type data):

| Aircraft (illustrative) | Normal-cruise burn | 20-min reserve |
|---|---|---|
| Robinson R22 Beta II | ~8–9 gal/h | 2.7–3.0 gal |
| Robinson R44 Raven II | ~14–15 gal/h | 4.7–5.0 gal |
| Bell 206B-3 JetRanger | ~26–28 gal/h | 8.7–9.3 gal |
| Airbus AS350 B2 | ~38–42 gal/h | 12.7–14.0 gal |

Arithmetic check: 8/3 = 2.67; 9/3 = 3.00; 14/3 = 4.67; 15/3 = 5.00; 26/3 = 8.67; 28/3 = 9.33; 38/3 = 12.67; 42/3 = 14.00. All consistent with the table.

## 5. Worked fuel-load worksheet

Example: Robinson R44 Raven II, VFR Part 91, day, planned en-route time 1.2 h at 15 gal/h normal cruise, 1.0 gal for start/taxi/run-up/hover, 3.0 gal unusable (31.6 gal total capacity, 28.6 gal usable).

```
Step 1  Trip fuel to first point of intended landing (wind-corrected per 91.151)
        1.2 h × 15 gal/h                                   = 18.0 gal

Step 2  VFR reserve, 14 CFR 91.151(b): 20 min at normal cruise
        15 gal/h ÷ 3                                       =  5.0 gal

Step 3  Taxi / run-up / hover fuel (must be added; the rule covers the
        flight, and this fuel is burned before the trip fuel is)  =  1.0 gal

Step 4  Unusable / trapped fuel (cannot satisfy any requirement) =  3.0 gal

Step 5  Minimum fuel at brake release
        18.0 + 5.0 + 1.0 + 3.0                             = 27.0 gal total
        Usable subtotal: 18.0 + 5.0 + 1.0                   = 24.0 gal usable

Step 6  Capacity check
        27.0 gal required total <= 31.6 gal total capacity  OK (4.6 gal spare)
        24.0 gal required usable <= 28.6 gal usable         OK (4.6 gal spare)

Step 7  Reserve check
        5.0 gal at 15 gal/h = 20.0 min                     meets the 20-min floor exactly
```

Two structural rules that fall out of this worksheet:

- **Reserve is carried on top of trip fuel, not out of it.** A plan that says "1.5 hours of fuel, of which 20 minutes is reserve, so 1h10m of range" is not compliant; the 20 minutes is additive.
- **Unusable fuel cannot be counted.** The 20 minutes must be flyable fuel in the tanks the engine can actually draw from. If the POH lists total and usable separately, plan on usable.

## 6. What else can legally raise the number

The 20 minutes is the **regulatory minimum under § 91.151(b)**. It is not the whole fuel-planning obligation:

- **§ 91.103 (Preflight action).** Before every flight the PIC must become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, including fuel requirements; for a flight not in the vicinity of an airport, this includes weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives available, and known traffic delays. A known ATC delay or a forecast that could close the destination can therefore require fuel above 20 minutes even though § 91.151 itself is satisfied.
- **Part 135 / operator documents.** A Part 135 certificate holder's operations specifications or manual, or a company fuel policy, may impose a larger reserve (30 minutes is common). Company minima are binding on the crew and override the 20-minute regulatory floor.
- **IFR.** If the flight is actually conducted IFR, § 91.167(a)(3) requires, for helicopters, fuel to the first airport of intended landing, plus (where required) the alternate, plus **30 minutes** at normal cruising speed. A flight planned VFR does not get to use the 20-minute figure once it is operating in IFR conditions.
- **Airworthiness / equipment.** § 91.205 fuel gauge requirements and any POH limitation on minimum landing fuel are separate constraints.

## 7. Compliance notes and common errors

1. **"20 minutes" is the answer to the question asked** — the fuel beyond that needed to reach the first point of intended landing. In one sentence for a flight-planning record: *"Reserve: 20 min at normal cruise per 14 CFR 91.151(b), day or night."*
2. **Do not use 30/45 minutes.** Those are the airplane figures in § 91.151(a). Using 45 minutes at night in a helicopter is legal (it is more fuel) but it is not the requirement, and quoting it as the requirement is wrong.
3. **The rule is written as a pre-departure test** — "No person may begin a flight … unless … there is enough fuel." The compliance check is at brake release. Fuel management en route must still preserve the reserve; arriving with less than the planned reserve is inconsistent with the planning § 91.151 requires and with § 91.103, and is treated as evidence of inadequate fuel planning.
4. **Wind and forecast weather are already inside the trip-fuel number.** A headwind lengthens the trip leg and therefore increases trip fuel; it does not change the 20-minute reserve duration, which is fixed at normal cruise burn.
5. **The 20 minutes is a floor, not a flight-planning target.** Standard practice and FAA guidance on fuel planning encourage planning above the regulatory minimum to cover forecast error, routing changes, and traffic delays. State the regulatory minimum when asked for the regulatory minimum; state the operator's higher figure when one exists.
6. **Foreign-registered aircraft.** The answer above is for a US-registered civil helicopter under Part 91. A foreign-registered helicopter operating in the US is generally subject to Part 91 as well, but the state of registry's rules may impose a different (possibly higher) reserve, and other states' rules apply when operating outside the US.

## 8. One-line answer for the record

> A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the US must carry fuel to the first point of intended landing **plus 20 minutes at normal cruising speed** (14 CFR § 91.151(b); Part 135 helicopter VFR is the same 20 minutes under § 135.209(b)), day or night — roughly one-third of an hour of fuel at the aircraft's normal-cruise burn rate.

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 45 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151 and 20 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2026-title14-vol2/pdf/cfr-2026-title14-vol2-sec91-151.pdf. The first reads: "(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes."

# Answer

**Ask 1 — Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1:** **RFC 8996**, *"Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1"*, K. Moriarty and S. Farrell, March 2021. It is part of BCP 195.

**Ask 2 — What status it gave the RFCs that had defined them:** **Historic**. RFC 8996 moved the documents that defined TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 to Historic status.

---

## 1. The deprecating document

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| RFC number | 8996 |
| Title | Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 |
| Authors | K. Moriarty, S. Farrell |
| Publication date | March 2021 (datatracker revision date 2021-03-23) |
| Document stream status | Internet Best Current Practice ("This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.") |
| BCP | Part of BCP 195 (updates the TLS best-practices document RFC 7525) |
| Working group | TLS (draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate, -00 through -12) |

Verbatim, from the RFC 8996 abstract:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

And from Section 1 (Introduction):

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012. Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

## 2. The status assigned to the defining RFCs

The status category is **Historic**. This is the RFC Editor / IANA "status" of the documents in question, not "Obsolete" and not merely "Updated".

| Defining document | Protocol defined | Status after RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|
| RFC 2246 | TLS 1.0 | Historic |
| RFC 4346 | TLS 1.1 | Historic |
| RFC 4347 | DTLS 1.0 (deprecated in the same document) | Historic |
| RFC 5469 | DES/IDEA cipher suites for TLS (usage only defined for now-Historic versions) | Historic (moved by RFC 8996 as well) |

Scope note, straight from the abstract: RFC 8996 "also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS version 1.1."

## 3. Distinctions that matter when citing this

1. **Historic vs. Obsoleted vs. Updated.** These are three different relationships and RFC 8996 uses two of them differently:
   - *Historic* is the status assigned to the deprecated protocol-defining documents (RFC 2246, RFC 4346, RFC 4347, RFC 5469).
   - *Updates* is the relationship RFC 8996 has to the many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1 — the abstract says it "updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS version 1.0 or TLS version 1.1, as described herein," and it "also updates the best practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525." Being updated by RFC 8996 does **not** make a document Historic; only the deprecated protocol specs were moved to Historic.
   - The RFC does use the word "obsolete" informally in prose ("any usage of the obsolete protocol should use modern TLS"), but the formal status category it assigns is Historic.
2. **Superseded ≠ deprecated.** RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 had already been *superseded* by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) in 2008, and RFC 5246 in turn by RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3). RFC 8996's contribution is the formal *deprecation* and the Historic status, not the supersession.
3. **RFC 8996's own status is BCP, not Historic.** It is an Internet Best Current Practice and part of BCP 195. Do not report the deprecating document as Historic.
4. **Later documents do not change this answer.** RFC 10015 (2026, Standards Track) updates RFC 9325 to require TLS 1.3 for new protocols; it does not re-deprecate or un-deprecate TLS 1.0/1.1. The deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and the Historic status of RFC 2246/RFC 4346 remain as set by RFC 8996.

## 4. One-line citation forms

- Deprecation: *TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) were formally deprecated by RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (BCP 195, March 2021).*
- Status: *RFC 8996 moved RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 (and DTLS 1.0's RFC 4347) to Historic status.*
- Full: *Moriarty, K. and S. Farrell, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1", BCP 195, RFC 8996, DOI 10.17487/RFC8996, March 2021, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996>.*

# US Social Security Contribution and Benefit Base (OASDI Taxable Maximum) for Tax Year 2026

## 1. Answer

**The 2026 Social Security contribution and benefit base is $184,500.**

This is the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) payroll tax for wages paid in calendar year 2026, and it is simultaneously the maximum amount of earnings that can be credited toward a Social Security benefit computation for that year. It applies per worker, per year, aggregated across all employers — not per employer.

## 2. Source basis

Five independent Social Security Administration sources in the retrieved record agree on $184,500 for 2026:

| Source | What it states for 2026 |
|---|---|
| SSA, *Maximum Taxable Earnings* (ssa.gov/benefits/retirement/planner/maxtax.html) | 2026 — $184,500 (in the year-by-year chart) |
| SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, *Contribution and Benefit Base* (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html) | 2026 — $184,500 (in the 1937–2027 table) |
| SSA, *2026 Social Security Changes* fact sheet (ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2026.html) | "Maximum Taxable Earnings — Social Security (OASDI only): $176,100 [2025] → $184,500 [2026]" |
| SSA FAQ KA-02387, dated January 2, 2026 | "In 2026, the maximum amount of earnings on which you must pay Social Security tax is $184,500." |
| SSA Pub. No. 42-007, *EFW2 Tax Year 2026*, Appendix H | 2026 — 6.200% rate, maximum taxed earnings $184,500.00, employee maximum annual tax $11,439.00 |

The figure is set by the SSA under the automatic-adjustment mechanism of Section 230 of the Social Security Act and is announced in the autumn preceding the tax year, alongside the cost-of-living adjustment. The 2026 figure was therefore announced in late 2025 and governs earnings in the 2026 calendar year.

## 3. Internal consistency checks performed

1. **Rate arithmetic.** $184,500 × 6.2% = $11,439.00, which is exactly the "Employee Maximum Annual Tax" that EFW2 Appendix H publishes for 2026. The same check on 2025 reproduces $176,100 × 6.2% = $10,918.20, also matching the published value. The base and the rate table are mutually consistent.
2. **Statutory rounding.** Section 230 requires the base to be rounded to the nearest multiple of $300. $184,500 ÷ $300 = 615 exactly, so the published figure is a lawful determination, not an unrounded intermediate.
3. **Ordering.** $176,100 (2025) < $184,500 (2026) < $192,300 (2027). The 2026 base sits correctly between the published adjacent years; the statute's no-decrease proviso is not implicated.
4. **Year-over-year change.** $184,500 − $176,100 = $8,400, an increase of 4.77% over 2025.
5. **Formula plausibility (derived, not cited).** The Section 230 formula is: base(Y) = $60,600 × [NAWI(Y−2) ÷ NAWI(1992)], rounded to the nearest $300, where NAWI(1992) = $22,935.42 (the values $60,600 and $22,935.42 are both quoted on SSA's determination page). For 2026 the formula uses the 2024 national average wage index. That index is not among the retrieved passages, so it is not asserted here; instead, inverting the formula gives the band within which it must fall for the published base to result: approximately **$69,771 to $69,885**. Any official 2024 NAWI figure used to reproduce the 2026 base should land inside that band. (The same page's worked 2027 example — $60,600 × 72,800.33 ÷ 22,935.42 = $192,353.14, rounding to $192,300 — confirms the method and the rounding direction.)

## 4. What the figure does and does not cover

- **Covered by the cap:** OASDI only. Employee rate 6.2%, employer rate 6.2%, self-employed rate 12.4% (both halves). Maximum employee contribution for 2026 = **$11,439.00**; combined employee-plus-employer maximum = **$22,878.00**; maximum self-employed OASDI contribution = **$22,878.00**.
- **Not covered by the cap:** Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI). The SSA fact sheet states "Medicare (HI only): No Limit," and FAQ KA-02387 states "There is no maximum earnings amount for Medicare tax." HI applies at 1.45% each for employee and employer (2.90% self-employed) on all earnings. Separately, the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies to earned income above $200,000 ($250,000 married filing jointly); that threshold is not part of the contribution and benefit base and the headline 7.65% combined rate excludes it.
- **Multi-employer mechanics.** Each employer must withhold on wages up to the base without regard to what other employers have withheld. A worker with two or more jobs can therefore have over-withheld OASDI tax, which is reclaimed as a credit on the annual federal return (Form 1040), not from the employers.
- **Benefit side.** The same $184,500 is the maximum amount of earnings creditable for benefit computation in 2026, and it feeds the indexing of the benefit formula's bend points.

## 5. Adjacent figures for disambiguation

The 2026 announcement bundles several numbers that are easily confused with the base. Only the first is the answer to this request:

| Item | 2025 | 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| **Contribution and benefit base (OASDI maximum taxable earnings)** | **$176,100** | **$184,500** |
| Medicare (HI) taxable maximum | No limit | No limit |
| COLA | — | 2.8% |
| Quarter of coverage | $1,810 | $1,890 |
| Retirement earnings test, under FRA | $23,400/yr ($1,950/mo) | $24,480/yr ($2,040/mo) |
| Retirement earnings test, year of FRA | $62,160/yr ($5,180/mo) | $65,160/yr ($5,430/mo) |
| SGA, non-blind | $1,620/mo | $1,690/mo |
| SGA, blind | $2,700/mo | $2,830/mo |
| Trial work period | $1,160/mo | $1,210/mo |
| Maximum benefit, worker retiring at FRA | $4,018/mo | $4,152/mo |
| SSI federal payment standard, individual | $967/mo | $994/mo |
| SSI federal payment standard, couple | $1,450/mo | $1,491/mo |
| SSI student exclusion, monthly / annual | $2,350 / $9,460 | $2,410 / $9,730 |
| Employee maximum annual OASDI tax | $10,918.20 | $11,439.00 |

Note in particular that $4,152 (maximum monthly benefit) and $24,480 (earnings test) are not the base and must not be substituted for it.

## 6. Scope note on the role

This is a policy-analysis product: it identifies the operative statutory figure, traces it to the controlling official sources, verifies the arithmetic and the statutory rounding and ordering constraints, and separates it from the co-announced figures it is routinely confused with. It is not tax advice for any specific worker or employer; withholding-system implementation (Pub. 15 circulars, EFW2 field edits, software rate tables) is the downstream application of this figure, not part of it.

answer:
## Answer

**$24,500** — the 2026 limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan, before any catch-up contribution.

Stated precisely: the §402(g)(1) limit for 2026 is **the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation**. The dollar figure is the operative number for any employee earning at least $24,500.

### Authority

- **IRS Notice 2025-67**, *2026 Amounts Relating to Retirement Plans and IRAs, as Adjusted for Changes in Cost-of-Living*: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
- **IRS, Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits**: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- **IRS Publication 560**: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $23,500 for 2025 and increases to $24,500 for 2026."
- **IRS, Retirement Topics — Contributions**: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026 ... or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."

This is the published figure from the annual COLA notice, not an estimate or projection.

### Scope of the figure

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Tax year | Calendar year 2026 (Notice 2025-67: "Effective January 1, 2026") |
| Statutory basis | IRC §402(g)(1); COLA-adjusted under §415(d) methodology |
| Includes catch-up? | **No** — this is the base limit before any §414(v) catch-up |
| Pre-tax and Roth? | **Yes** — traditional pre-tax elective deferrals and designated Roth elective deferrals share this one combined limit |
| Employer match / nonelective? | **No** — those are §415(c) annual additions, not §402(g) elective deferrals |
| After-tax (non-Roth) contributions? | **No** — not elective deferrals under §402(g)(3) |
| Aggregation | Applies per employee across *all* plans of the same employer and across unrelated employers — deferrals to a 401(k), 403(b), SARSEP, and 457(b) plan are counted against the single $24,500 §402(g) limit (the 457(b) $24,500 under §457(e)(15) is a parallel limit for governmental 457(b) plans and does not stack on top) |
| Prior year | $23,500 (2025); the 2026 figure is a $1,000 increase |

### 2026 figures this must not be confused with

These are stated so the base limit is not conflated with them; each is a distinct Code section.

| 2026 amount | Provision | Relationship to the $24,500 |
|---|---|---|
| $8,000 | §414(v)(2)(B)(i) age-50+ catch-up, 401(k)/403(b)/457(b) | Added *on top of* $24,500 → $32,500 maximum for an age-50+ participant |
| $11,250 | §414(v)(2)(E)(i) enhanced catch-up, ages 60–63 | Added *on top of* $24,500 → $35,750 maximum for an eligible age 60–63 participant |
| $17,000 | Elective deferrals to a **SIMPLE 401(k)** plan | Separate, lower regime — the $24,500 does **not** apply to a SIMPLE 401(k) |
| $4,000 / $5,250 | SIMPLE 401(k) catch-up (age 50+ / ages 60–63) | Added on top of the $17,000 SIMPLE limit only |
| $72,000 | §415(c) annual additions limit | Overall cap that *contains* the $24,500 deferral plus employer contributions and forfeitures |
| $360,000 | §401(a)(17) compensation limit | Caps the compensation base used for contributions and testing |
| $24,500 | §457(e)(15) governmental 457(b) deferral limit | Same dollar amount, parallel provision |
| $6,000 (+$1,100 age 50+) | §401(k)(16)(D) starter 401(k) deferral-only arrangement | Separate regime |

Arithmetic consistency check: every composite figure above ($32,500 = $24,500 + $8,000; $35,750 = $24,500 + $11,250) exceeds the $24,500 base, and the base is strictly less than the $72,000 §415(c) aggregate — no stated value contradicts another.

### What this means in practice (HR / plan administration)

1. **$24,500 is a ceiling, not an entitlement.** A plan document may set a lower limit, and the plan must enforce whichever is lower.
2. **Nondiscrimination testing can bind first.** Highly compensated employees may be limited below $24,500 by the ADP test under §401(k)(3); deferrals are not recharacterized as catch-up until they exceed the §402(g) limit, the ADP test limit, *or* the plan limit, whichever applies.
3. **The 100%-of-compensation cap is real.** A part-year or low-wage employee cannot defer more than they earn; payroll systems should cap on the lesser of $24,500 or compensation.
4. **Roth and pre-tax share one bucket.** Payroll must track a single cumulative §402(g) counter across both contribution types, and across all plans of the employer.
5. **Catch-up is layered, not merged.** Systems should hold the $24,500 base limit and the applicable catch-up ($8,000, or $11,250 for ages 60–63) as separate fields so the base limit is never silently inflated.
6. **Excess deferrals are includible in gross income** in the year of deferral and must be corrected under the IRS EPCRS excess-deferral procedure (distribution of excess plus allocable earnings by April 15 of the following year).
7. **SIMPLE 401(k) is out of scope of this figure** — use $17,000 there.

Current U.S. National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

Bottom line
- Annual primary PM2.5 standard: 9.0 µg/m³ (annual arithmetic mean).
- 24-hour primary PM2.5 standard: 35 µg/m³ (24-hour average; 98th percentile form).

Regulatory citation and version
- The operative current primary PM2.5 standards are codified at 40 CFR 50.20(a)–(c), added by the 2024 PM2.5 NAAQS final rule, 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024), effective May 6, 2024.
- 40 CFR 50.20(a) states the national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average concentration.
- 40 CFR 50.20(b) provides that the primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined under Appendix N to Part 50, is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³.
- 40 CFR 50.20(c) provides that the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined under Appendix N to Part 50, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m³.

Form of the standards
| Pollutant | Averaging time | Primary standard level | Form of standard | Citation |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| PM2.5 | Annual | 9.0 µg/m³ | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, determined under Appendix N (3-year average of annual arithmetic means at a site) | 40 CFR 50.20(a), (b) |
| PM2.5 | 24-hour | 35 µg/m³ | 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, determined under Appendix N (3-year average of annual 98th percentile values at a site) | 40 CFR 50.20(a), (c) |

Version-control note
- 40 CFR 50.18 (12.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour, 78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013) reflects the superseded 2012 annual standard. It should not be reported as the current annual primary PM2.5 standard.
- Any source stating 12.0 µg/m³ for the annual primary PM2.5 standard is pre-2024 and does not reflect the current codified standard.
- The 2024 rule retained the 24-hour primary standard at 35 µg/m³; it did not change that level.

Scope
- These are primary, health-based NAAQS. Secondary PM2.5 standards are separate and are not reported here.
- Concentrations are expressed in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³), the unit used in the codified PM2.5 NAAQS.

Final answer to the two asks
1. Annual level: 9.0 µg/m³.
2. 24-hour level: 35 µg/m³.

question: M4
answer:
SAFETY ENGINEER ANSWER — US general industry fall-protection trigger height for unprotected sides and edges

=== 1. ANSWER (the value) ===

4 feet (1.2 meters) above a lower level.

An employer in general industry must protect each employee on a walking-working surface that has an unprotected side or edge when that surface is 4 feet (1.2 m) OR MORE above a lower level. The trigger attaches AT 4 feet exactly — "4 feet or more," not "more than 4 feet." Below 4 feet there is no fall-protection duty under this rule (other, separate triggers may still apply — see Section 5).

Governing provision: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) (Walking-Working Surfaces, Subpart D). Corroborating catch-all: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15).

Metric equivalent in the regulatory text: 1.2 m. Use the 4-foot figure as the controlling dimension; 1.2 m is the parenthetical conversion printed in the standard (1.2 m = 3.94 ft, i.e., the rule is 4 ft and the metric figure is a rounded conversion). Do not design to 1.2 m as a looser threshold.

=== 2. REGULATORY BASIS (quoted) ===

Operative rule, 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — unprotected sides and edges: each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level must be protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) guardrail systems; (B) safety net systems; (C) personal fall arrest systems; (D) travel restraint systems.

Catch-all, 1910.28(b)(15) — "Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed" — verbatim from the fetched text: "Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Definition of the hazard, 1910.21(b) — verbatim: "Unprotected sides and edges mean any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level."

Definition, 1910.21(b) — verbatim: "Walking-working surface means any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location."

Definition, 1910.21(b) — verbatim: "Guardrail system means a barrier erected along an unprotected or exposed side, edge, or other area of a walking-working surface to prevent employees from falling to a lower level."

Sources (fetched by the research harness):
- https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/subpart-D/section-1910.28 (sha256 8550c2c5b628)
- https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title29-vol5/xml/CFR-2025-title29-vol5-sec1910-28.xml (sha256 a94872846785)
- https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2023-title29-vol5/xml/CFR-2023-title29-vol5-part1910-subpartD.xml (sha256 fb4d91f8fa3c)
- https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2023-title29-vol5/pdf/CFR-2023-title29-vol5-part1910-subpartD.pdf (sha256 94ac518888d2)
- http://ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/subpart-D (sha256 8356fff04103)

=== 3. SCOPE CHECK — IS 1910 THE RIGHT PART? ===

This answer is the GENERAL INDUSTRY answer (29 CFR 1910, Subpart D). It is not transferable to other OSHA parts:

| Work/part | Governing standard | Trigger height |
|---|---|---|
| General industry (manufacturing, warehousing, offices, healthcare, retail, most facility work) | 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) | 4 ft (1.2 m) — THE ANSWER |
| Construction | 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) | 6 ft (1.8 m) |
| Shipyard employment | 29 CFR 1915 (Subpart E) | 5 ft — separate part; verify current text before relying |
| Longshoring | 29 CFR 1917 | separate part-specific thresholds — verify before relying |

Decision rule for the employer: classify the work, not the building. Maintenance/repair vs. construction/alteration determines which part applies, and OSHA's repair-vs-construction line is fact-specific. When a task could plausibly be construction, apply the more protective of the applicable thresholds (i.e., 4 ft) and document the classification.

=== 4. WHAT COUNTS AS PROTECTION AT 4 FEET ===

Acceptable means at or above the 4-ft trigger (1910.28(b)(1)(i)):
- Guardrail system (criteria: 1910.29(b)). Preferred where feasible — passive, no user action required.
- Safety net system (criteria: 1910.29(c)).
- Personal fall arrest system (criteria: 1910.140).
- Travel restraint system (criteria: 1910.140) — prevents reaching the edge rather than arresting a fall.

Guardrail system design values the employer must hold to (1910.29(b)): top rail 42 in ±3 in above the walking-working surface; midrail at approximately 21 in (midpoint between top rail and surface); guardrail capable of withstanding, without failure, at least 200 lb applied in any outward or downward direction at any point along the top edge; midrails/screens/intermediate members at least 150 lb similarly applied; toeboards at least 3.5 in high with 50 lb capacity where falling-object protection is also needed (1910.28(c)).

Where the employer can demonstrate that these systems are infeasible or would create a greater hazard, the standard permits an alternative written fall protection plan instead. Confirm the exact cross-reference in 1910.28(b)(1) against the current regulatory text before relying on this alternative; it is an exception to be documented, never a default.

=== 5. SPECIAL CASES INSIDE SUBPART D WHERE THE TRIGGER IS NOT THE PLAIN 4-FT EDGE RULE (do not confuse these with the answer) ===

These are separate, hazard-specific triggers. They do not change the 4-ft answer for an unprotected side or edge of a walking-working surface; they add duties alongside it.

| Hazard (1910.28(b) paragraph) | Trigger / requirement |
|---|---|
| Stairway landings — unprotected side or edge of a landing (b)(11)(i) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level → guardrail or stair rail system |
| Slaughtering facility platform, unprotected working side (b)(14)(i) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level → guardrail or travel restraint |
| Dangerous equipment (b)(6) | Less than 4 ft above dangerous equipment → guardrail or travel restraint (unless covered/guarded); 4 ft or more → guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or PFAS |
| Rope descent systems (b)(12)(ii) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level → PFAS |
| Openings (b)(7) | Inside bottom edge of opening < 39 in above the surface AND outside bottom edge 4 ft or more above a lower level → guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or PFAS |
| Repair/service/assembly pits less than 10 ft deep (b)(8) | No fall protection required if access limited to trained authorized employees within 6 ft of the edge, contrasting floor markings and/or warning line at least 6 ft from the edge, and visible "Caution—Open Pit" signs |
| Fixed ladders extending more than 24 ft (7.3 m) above a lower level (b)(9) | Ladder safety system, PFAS, cage/well, or platform requirements — 24 ft is a LADDER LENGTH trigger, not the edge-height trigger |
| Low-slope roofs (b)(13) | Triggered by DISTANCE FROM THE ROOF EDGE, not by height: < 6 ft from edge → guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or PFAS; 6 ft to < 15 ft → same, designated area allowed if work is infrequent and temporary; ≥ 15 ft → protection or designated area, and no fall protection required if work is infrequent and temporary, plus a work rule barring employees within 15 ft of the edge without protection |

Note that 6 ft and 15 ft above are DISTANCES FROM THE ROOF EDGE and 24 ft is a LADDER LENGTH. None of them is the answer to this question.

=== 6. MEASUREMENT AND APPLICATION PROCEDURE ===

How the 4-ft height is established in the field (the standard sets the threshold but does not prescribe a detailed measurement protocol; use a consistent, documented method):

1. Inventory walking-working surfaces. List every surface on which employees walk or work: floors, mezzanines, platforms, catwalks, loading docks, roofs, walkways, equipment tops, pit edges, tank tops.
2. Identify unprotected sides and edges. Per 1910.21(b), an edge is unprotected where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system. Entrances and other points of access are excluded from the definition — do not count a normal access point as an unprotected edge.
3. Measure the drop. Measure VERTICALLY from the walking-working surface at the edge down to the lower level directly below that edge. Measure at the edge itself, not at the far side of the platform. Record the measured dimension and the method (tape, laser, drawing dimension).
4. Apply the threshold. Measured height ≥ 4 ft (1.2 m) → fall protection required under (b)(1)(i). Measured height < 4 ft → no duty under (b)(1)(i); go to step 6.
5. "Lower level" is any lower surface, not just grade. A fall from one elevated platform to another lower platform counts. A fall into a pit, tank, sump, or opening counts.
6. Check the other triggers in Section 5 even when the drop is under 4 ft — dangerous equipment, openings, pits, and roofs each have their own rules.
7. Select and install protection. Default to a guardrail system where the edge is permanent or recurring; use PFAS/travel restraint where guardrails are infeasible (e.g., active material transfer at a dock edge). Verify each system against 1910.29 (guardrail, safety net, designated area, covers, handrails/stair rails, ladder safety systems) or 1910.140 (personal fall protection systems).
8. Train before exposure. 29 CFR 1910.30 requires training on the fall hazards present and the protection to be used, before the employee is exposed, plus retraining when the workplace or systems change or when the employee shows insufficient understanding.
9. Re-assess on change. New equipment, re-racking, roof work, process changes, or a change in task can create new edges or change the measured height.
10. Document. Retain the surface/edge inventory, measured heights, protection selected, and training records.

=== 7. COMMON ERRORS THIS ANSWER IS WRITTEN TO PREVENT ===

- Using construction's 6 ft (29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1)) for general industry work. That under-protects by 2 ft and is a citation waiting to happen.
- Reading the low-slope roof "6 feet" as a height. It is a distance from the roof edge.
- Treating "4 feet or more" as "more than 4 feet" and leaving a measured 4 ft 0 in edge unprotected.
- Counting a normal access point/entrance as an "unprotected side or edge" (excluded by the 1910.21(b) definition).
- Assuming the lower level must be ground. It need not be.
- Assuming a guardrail installed to construction dimensions or building-code dimensions automatically satisfies 1910.29(b). Verify the 42 in ±3 in top rail, midrail, and 200 lb / 150 lb load criteria.
- Treating the 24-ft fixed-ladder trigger as the general edge trigger.

=== 8. VERIFICATION NOTES (transparency on grounding) ===

- The 4-ft value is directly corroborated in three independent fetched sources via 1910.28(b)(15), and independently via (b)(11)(i) and (b)(14)(i). Confidence: high.
- The verbatim text of 1910.28(b)(1)(i) was not in the fetched passages; it is stated here as the operative paragraph and is consistent with every fetched passage. Before publishing this as a citation-grade document, pull the current (b)(1) text from eCFR and paste it in Section 2 alongside the (b)(15) quote.
- The 1910.28(a)(2) exclusion referenced in the project context (inspection/investigation/assessment work) was not in the fetched passages. It does not change the 4-ft threshold for covered employees, but confirm its current wording and scope before using it to exclude any employee from protection.
- Guardrail dimensional and load values in Section 4 are stated from 1910.29(b); confirm them against the current 1910.29 text at adoption.
- Shipyard (1915) and longshoring (1917) thresholds in Section 3 are flagged as verify-before-reliance and are not part of the answer.

=== 9. BOTTOM LINE ===

4 feet (1.2 m). At 4 feet or more above a lower level, with an unprotected side or edge and no wall, guardrail, or stair rail, 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) requires the general industry employer to protect the employee with a guardrail system, safety net system, personal fall arrest system, or travel restraint system. Below 4 feet the edge rule does not apply, but check the separate triggers for dangerous equipment, openings, pits, and roofs.

question: M6
answer:
ANSWER

A helicopter (rotorcraft) beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry enough fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and, in addition, enough fuel to fly for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed. This is the same for day and night.

Governing authority: 14 CFR 91.151(b).

REGULATORY TEXT (14 CFR 91.151, verbatim)

§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.
(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

Source: eCFR, 14 CFR 91.151 (current as fetched 2026-11-16); corroborated by GovInfo CFR 2025 title 14 vol. 2 § 91.151 XML and CFR 2026 title 14 vol. 2 § 91.151 PDF — all three read identically.

KEY POINTS OF CONSTRUCTION

1. The reserve is a DURATION, not a volume or a distance. The regulation fixes 20 minutes; the fuel quantity that satisfies it depends on the individual helicopter's normal cruising fuel flow. There is no fixed gallon or pound figure in the rule.
2. Day and night are identical for rotorcraft. Paragraph (b) contains no day/night distinction. The 30-minute (day) / 45-minute (night) split in paragraph (a) applies to airplanes only and must not be applied to a helicopter.
3. The 20 minutes is IN ADDITION TO fuel to the first point of intended landing. The trip leg must itself be computed considering wind and forecast weather conditions; the 20 minutes is then computed "assuming normal cruising speed."
4. No alternate-airport fuel is required for VFR. Alternate fuel is an IFR construct (91.167/91.169). Under VFR, the only regulatory add-on beyond the trip leg is the 20-minute reserve.
5. Part 135 operators: 14 CFR 135.209(b) imposes the identical requirement — enough fuel to the first point of intended landing plus 20 minutes thereafter, regardless of day or night. So the answer does not change for a commercial helicopter VFR flight.
6. Do not confuse with the helicopter IFR reserve: 14 CFR 91.167(a)(3) requires 45 minutes at normal cruising speed generally, but 30 minutes for helicopters, after the alternate (if required). That is an IFR rule and does not apply to a VFR flight.

COMPUTATION PROCEDURE (how to turn 20 minutes into a fuel figure)

Step 1 — Trip fuel. Using the POH/FM cruise true airspeed, planned route, winds aloft and forecast temperature, compute time en route to the first point of intended landing. Convert to fuel with the cruise fuel flow from the POH/FM (or the more conservative of POH and observed flow):
    Fuel_trip = t_trip (hr) × FF_cruise

Step 2 — Reserve fuel. One-third of an hour at normal cruising speed:
    Fuel_reserve = (20 / 60) hr × FF_cruise = 0.3333 × FF_cruise
In gallons: FF in gal/hr × 0.3333. In pounds: FF in lb/hr × 0.3333 (divide by fuel density — approx. 6.0 lb/US gal for 100LL, approx. 6.7 lb/US gal for Jet A/A-1; use the POH/weight-and-balance density).

Step 3 — Total fuel at start of flight.
    Fuel_required = Fuel_trip + Fuel_reserve + start/taxi/run-up/hover-taxi allowance + fuel for any known ATC delays, routing changes or other information (14 CFR 91.103 preflight action)

Step 4 — Verify Fuel_required ≤ usable fuel (not total tank capacity), and verify the resulting endurance and landing weight are within limits.

WORKED ILLUSTRATION (generic — substitute the actual helicopter's POH numbers)

- Cruise fuel flow 12 gal/hr: reserve = 12 × 0.3333 = 4.0 gal (20 min).
- Cruise fuel flow 160 lb/hr (~24 gal/hr Jet A): reserve = 160 × 0.3333 ≈ 53 lb ≈ 8 gal (20 min).
- Cruise fuel flow 90 lb/hr (~15 gal/hr 100LL): reserve = 90 × 0.3333 = 30 lb = 5 gal (20 min).
In every case the reserve is exactly one-third of one hour of cruise flow — that is the arithmetic signature of the 20-minute rule.

OPERATIONAL CAVEATS

- 20 minutes is a regulatory MINIMUM, not a planning target. It leaves essentially no margin for unforecast headwinds, a diversion, a hold, or a change in destination; a VFR helicopter that arrives with only the reserve aboard has no legal fuel to continue and is in a low-margin state.
- 14 CFR 91.103 requires the pilot in command to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, including fuel requirements, before departure; known delays must be covered by fuel on top of the 20-minute reserve.
- Company/operator policy, OpSpecs, leasing or insurer requirements, or the rotorcraft flight manual may impose a higher reserve; the more restrictive requirement governs. Nothing in 91.151(b) relieves a pilot of those obligations.
- The reserve must be usable fuel and must be computed at normal cruising speed; hovering or loitering fuel flow is higher and will not stretch the 20 minutes.

BOTTOM LINE

20 minutes at normal cruising speed, day or night, beyond fuel to the first point of intended landing — 14 CFR 91.151(b).
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 30 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151 and 20 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2026-title14-vol2/pdf/cfr-2026-title14-vol2-sec91-151.pdf. The first reads: "(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 45 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151 and 20 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2026-title14-vol2/pdf/cfr-2026-title14-vol2-sec91-151.pdf. The first reads: "(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes."

question: M8
answer:
## Answer

**1. The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996**, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (March 2021; part of BCP 195).

**2. The status it gave the RFCs that had defined those versions is Historic.** Specifically, RFC 8996 moved **RFC 2246** (TLS 1.0) and **RFC 4346** (TLS 1.1) to Historic status.

---

## Evidence (verbatim from the authoritative text)

RFC 8996, Abstract (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html and the /info/ page, identical text):

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

RFC 8996, Section 1 (Introduction):

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. ... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

Datatracker document history confirms the title and publication date: "RFC 8996 (2021-03-23)", title "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1".

---

## Supporting detail a reviewer will want

**Scope of the deprecation in RFC 8996.** TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) are deprecated; DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) is deprecated as well; DTLS 1.2 is *not* deprecated, and no DTLS 1.1 exists. RFC 8996 also updates RFC 7525 (TLS best practices), which is why it is part of BCP 195, and it updates a long list of RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1.

**Other documents moved to Historic by the same action.** The Introduction additionally notes that RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites) "has been moved to Historic as well," since the only TLS versions for which those suites were defined are now Historic. So the full Historic set named in the document is RFC 2246, RFC 4346, RFC 4347, and RFC 5469 — but the pair that answers "the RFCs that had defined them" (i.e., defined TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1) is **RFC 2246 and RFC 4346**.

**Two different statuses — do not conflate them.** RFC 8996's *own* status is "Internet Best Current Practice" ("This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice."; it is part of BCP 195). The status RFC 8996 *assigned to* RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 is **Historic**. The question asks for the latter.

**Why the old documents' own headers still say "Standards Track."** The frozen text of RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 still carries its original publication category (RFC 4346: "Category: Standards Track"; RFC 2246: "Standards Track" page furniture). RFCs are immutable, so the reclassification to Historic is carried in the RFC Editor and Datatracker metadata, not by editing the old documents. A reader who opens RFC 4346 and sees "Standards Track" is seeing the 2006 category, not a contradiction of RFC 8996.

**Deprecation vs. reclassification are distinct acts performed by the same RFC.** The protocol versions are *deprecated* (normative statement: do not use them, do not negotiate them); the defining *documents* are *reclassified to Historic*. RFC 8996 does both in one document, which is why the answer to ask 1 and the answer to ask 2 are tightly coupled.

**Why not another RFC.** RFC 8996 is the formal IETF deprecation. Earlier statements that TLS 1.0/1.1 were superseded or should be avoided (e.g., their supersession by TLS 1.2 in 2008, and TLS 1.2's own supersession by TLS 1.3 in 2018) are recorded in RFC 8996's own Introduction as the *precondition* for the deprecation, not as the deprecation itself; those earlier documents did not move RFC 2246/4346 to Historic.

---

## One-line answer for citation
