question: M10
answer:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most annual earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for calendar year 2026 is $184,500.

STATUS: Officially determined, not a projection. SSA published the 2026 wage-indexed amounts (together with the December 2025 COLA of 2.8%) in fall 2025, and $184,500 appears in SSA's own 2026 employer reporting specifications and in the SSA benefit calculator update instructions. No caveat about 'estimated' or 'projected' is needed.

WHAT THE FIGURE MEANS
- Applies per worker, per calendar year, to wage earnings and to self-employment income alike; the base is identical for FICA (employees) and SECA (self-employed).
- It is both the contribution base (earnings on which the 6.2% OASDI tax is levied) and the benefit base (earnings counted in the AIME/benefit computation). Earnings above $184,500 in 2026 are neither taxed by OASDI nor credited for benefit purposes.
- It applies only to the OASDI (Social Security) portion. The Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI) portion has had no earnings cap since 1994; all wages are HI-taxable at 1.45% employee / 1.45% employer, plus the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above statutory thresholds.

DERIVATION (statutory formula, 42 U.S.C. 430 as amended)
Base for year Y = 1994 base ($60,600) x [AWI(Y-2) / AWI(1992)], rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, but never below the prior year's base. The formula is operative only in years for which a December COLA is effective; a December 2025 COLA of 2.8% was effective, so it applied for 2026.
  AWI(1992) = 22,935.42
  AWI(2024) = 69,846.57
  $60,600 x (69,846.57 / 22,935.42) = $184,548.7
  $184,548.7 / 300 = 615.16 -> round to 615; 615 x 300 = $184,500
  $184,500 > $176,100 (2025 base), so the no-reduction floor does not bind.
Cross-check of method: the identical formula with AWI(2025) = 72,800.33 gives $60,600 x (72,800.33 / 22,935.42) = $192,353.14 -> $192,300, which is exactly SSA's published 2027 base — confirming the rounding rule and inputs used above.

RECENT HISTORY (SSA table)
2020 $137,700 | 2021 $142,800 | 2022 $147,000 | 2023 $160,200 | 2024 $168,600 | 2025 $176,100 | 2026 $184,500 | 2027 $192,300
Year-over-year change 2025 -> 2026: +$8,400, +4.77%.

RELATED 2026 FIGURES (announced together; for cross-checking, not part of the ask)
- OASDI rate: 6.2% employee + 6.2% employer; 12.4% self-employed.
- Maximum OASDI tax at the base: $184,500 x 6.2% = $11,439.00 each for employee and employer ($22,878.00 combined); $184,500 x 12.4% = $22,878.00 for a self-employed person.
- 'Old-law' contribution and benefit base for 2026: $137,100.
- December 2025 COLA: 2.8%; national average wage index for 2024: $69,846.57.
- Retirement earnings test exempt amounts for 2026: $24,480 (lower, under FRA) and $65,160 (higher, year of FRA).
- PIA bend points for 2026: $1,286 and $7,749.

SOURCES
1. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, 'Contribution and Benefit Base' — table entry 2026 = $184,500 (https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/cola/cbb.html).
2. SSA, EFW2 Tax Year 2026 specifications — 'The Social Security Wage Base for tax year 2026 is $184,500'; withholding capped at $11,439.00 (https://www.ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf).
3. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, 'Updating the Social Security Benefit Calculator' — 'Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500' (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html).
4. Congressional Research Service IF11747 — 'taxable maximum ($184,500 in 2026)' (https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/HTML/IF11747.web.html).
5. SSA 'Automatic Determinations in Recent Years' — 2026 COLA 3.6%, base $184,500 (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/COLA/autoAdj.html).

ONE-LINE ANSWER: $184,500 for 2026.

question: M12
answer:
ANSWER

For tax year 2026, the limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan — before any catch-up contribution — is $24,500.

This is the base IRC §402(g)(1) elective deferral limit, as adjusted for cost-of-living under §402(g)(4). It is the figure for a participant who is not eligible for catch-up contributions (i.e., not age 50 or older by the end of the calendar year).

AUTHORITY

- IRS, COLA increases for dollar limitations on benefits and contributions (2026 column): elective deferrals $24,500 (2025: $23,500; 2024: $23,000; 2023: $22,500).
- IRS, Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- IRS, Retirement Topics — Contributions: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026 ... or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."
- IRS Publication 560 (Retirement Plans for Small Business): "The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026."
- IRS Publication 571 (Tax-Sheltered Annuity Plans), Table 4-2: 2026 elective deferral limit $24,500.
- Underlying guidance: Notice 2025-67, published in IRB 2025-49, page 761; IRS news release IR-2025-111 (2026 cost-of-living adjustments for pension plans and retirement-related items). The 2026 figure is officially published, not a projection.

SCOPE AND DEFINITION — WHAT THE $24,500 DOES AND DOES NOT INCLUDE

1. It is an employee salary-reduction limit. It covers pre-tax elective deferrals and designated Roth elective deferrals alike. Employer matching contributions and employer nonelective contributions do not count against it; they count against the separate §415(c) annual additions limit, which is $72,000 for 2026.
2. It is per individual, not per plan. An employee who participates in more than one 401(k) plan, or in a 401(k) plus a 403(b), SARSEP, or (with its own lower figure) SIMPLE plan, must aggregate elective deferrals across all of them against this single limit. The IRS states this explicitly: "Generally, you aggregate all elective deferrals you made to all plans in which you participate to determine if you have exceeded these limits."
3. It is capped by compensation. The operative limit is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation for the year.
4. It is not the SIMPLE 401(k) limit. For a SIMPLE 401(k), the 2026 employee deferral limit is $17,000, a separate and lower figure. Do not apply $24,500 to a SIMPLE 401(k).
5. It is the same dollar figure as the 2026 §457(b) elective deferral limit ($24,500), but §457(b) is a separate limit with its own aggregation rules; deferred compensation under a governmental 457(b) plan is not aggregated with 401(k) deferrals for §402(g) purposes.
6. Catch-up contributions are additive and excluded from the question as asked. For reference and for payroll coding only: the age-50-plus catch-up limit is $8,000 for 2026, and the enhanced SECURE 2.0 catch-up for participants who attain ages 60–63 during the year is $11,250 for 2026. Those amounts sit on top of — and never inside — the $24,500.

HR / PAYROLL OPERATING NOTES

- Plan terms can be stricter than the statute. A plan document may cap deferrals below $24,500, and highly compensated employees may be limited by ADP/ACP nondiscrimination testing. The statutory limit is a ceiling, not an entitlement.
- Mid-year hires and compensation-based limits: because the limit is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of compensation, an employee whose 2026 compensation is below $24,500 cannot defer the full amount.
- Excess deferrals: amounts above $24,500 (aggregated across plans) are includible in gross income for the year; correction follows the IRS excess-annual-salary-deferral correction procedures (EPCRS) and the plan's own terms. Payroll should monitor year-to-date deferrals across all plans of unrelated employers only to the extent the employee reports them — the aggregation duty ultimately rests on the employee.
- Effective date: this figure applies to the 2026 calendar tax year. Confirm the plan's plan-year definition (calendar vs. non-calendar) before applying it to a non-calendar plan year.
- Verify before publication each fall: the IRS announces the following year's figures typically in October–November (Notice 2025-67 covered 2026). If this figure is being used for communications issued before that announcement, label it as a projection.

ROLE BOUNDARY

This is a benefits/payroll compliance answer within the HR function: stating the published statutory limit and its operating consequences. It is not tax or legal advice on a specific participant's situation, plan document interpretation, or correction of an actual excess deferral; those should be routed to the plan administrator, recordkeeper, or tax counsel.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 11250 on irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-401k-and-profit-sharing-plan-contribution-limits and 5250 on irs.gov/retirement-plans/cola-increases-for-dollar-limitations-on-benefits-and-contributions. The first reads: "For 2026, this higher catch-up contribution limit is $11,250."

question: M2
answer:
# Current US National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

## 1. Answer

| # | Standard | Level | Form (statistical convention) | Indicator / averaging | Status |
|---|----------|-------|-------------------------------|-----------------------|--------|
| 1 | Primary annual PM2.5 | **9.0 µg/m³** | 3-year average of annual arithmetic mean concentrations, computed per 40 CFR Part 50 Appendix N; standard is met when that 3-year average is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³ | PM2.5 (aerodynamic diameter ≤ 2.5 µm nominal) | In effect; set by 2024 PM NAAQS reconsideration (89 FR 16202, Feb 7, 2024) |
| 2 | Primary 24-hour PM2.5 | **35 µg/m³** | 3-year average of annual 98th-percentile 24-hour concentrations, per Appendix N; standard is met when that 3-year average is ≤ 35 µg/m³ | PM2.5, 24-hour average | In effect; retained unchanged in the 2024 reconsideration (originally set in the 2006 review) |

Both are **primary** (health-based, Clean Air Act § 109(b)(1)) standards. Both are federal **national** standards; state or local standards do not substitute for them. Units are as promulgated: micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³).

As-of basis: EPA National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for PM page and EPA's February 2024 PM2.5 monitoring fact sheet, both retrieved 2026-11-16; codification at 40 CFR § 50.18.

## 2. Codified language (authoritative form)

40 CFR § 50.18 is the section that carries the PM2.5 primary standards. Its operative content, as amended by the 2024 reconsideration:

- Level of the primary annual PM2.5 standard: **9.0 µg/m³**, annual arithmetic mean concentration.
- Level of the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard: **35 µg/m³**, 24-hour average concentration.
- Measurement by a Federal Reference Method (Appendix L to Part 50) designated under Part 53, or by a Federal Equivalent Method designated under Part 53.
- Annual standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined under Appendix N, is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³.
- 24-hour standard is met when the 98th-percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined under Appendix N, is ≤ 35 µg/m³.

## 3. Secondary standards (stated for completeness only — not the answer)

- Secondary (welfare-based) annual PM2.5: **15.0 µg/m³** (retained in 2024).
- Secondary 24-hour PM2.5: **35 µg/m³** (retained in 2024; identical to the primary 24-hour level).
- The 2024 rule explicitly did not change the secondary annual standard or the primary/secondary 24-hour standards.

## 4. Revision history (how the annual level reached 9.0)

| Year | Action | Primary annual | Primary 24-hour |
|------|--------|----------------|-----------------|
| 1997 | Initial PM2.5 NAAQS (62 FR 38711) | 15.0 µg/m³ | 65 µg/m³ |
| 2006 | 24-hour standard strengthened | 15.0 µg/m³ (retained) | 35 µg/m³ |
| 2012 | Annual standard strengthened (78 FR 3277) | 12.0 µg/m³ | 35 µg/m³ (retained) |
| 2024 | Reconsideration (89 FR 16202, Feb 7, 2024; effective May 2024) | **9.0 µg/m³** | **35 µg/m³** (retained) |

## 5. Source-conflict note (important — read before citing)

The research pass returned a stale copy of § 50.18 text stating 12.0 µg/m³ annual and a separate passage stating 15.0 µg/m³ / 65 µg/m³. Neither is the current standard:

1. **The 12.0 µg/m³ passage is the pre-2024 text.** The quoted § 50.18 paragraph carries only the history note "[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]" and no 2024 amendment citation; it is the 2012 rule verbatim. EPA's NAAQS-for-PM page and the February 2024 fact sheet both state the annual level was changed to 9.0 µg/m³ on Feb 7, 2024. A current eCFR render of § 50.18 should show 9.0 µg/m³ with an 89 FR 16202 amendment note. **Verification step:** open eCFR § 50.18 and confirm the amendment note reads 89 FR 16202 (Feb 7, 2024) and the annual level reads 9.0 µg/m³.
2. **The 15.0 / 65 passage is § 50.7, not § 50.18.** Its citation [62 FR 38711, July 18, 1997, as amended at 69 FR 45595, July 30, 2004] and its position immediately before § 50.8 (carbon monoxide) identify it as the original 1997 PM2.5 standards, superseded by the 2012 and 2024 rules. Do not cite it as current.

Contingency: if a reader's copy of the CFR still shows 12.0 µg/m³ as the annual level with no 89 FR 16202 amendment note, then that copy predates May 2024 and the correct current value remains 9.0 µg/m³; only a subsequent final rule reverting the level would change the answer, and no such final rule appears in the source set.

## 6. Pending-action caveat

EPA announced on 03/12/2025 a "Path Forward on National Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM2.5)," i.e., a reconsideration of the 2024 rule. A announced reconsideration does not change the codified standard. As of the source retrieval date (2026-11-16), the levels in effect remain **9.0 µg/m³ annual** and **35 µg/m³ 24-hour**. Anyone citing this answer later should re-check § 50.18 for a post-2025 amendment note.

## 7. What this answer deliberately excludes

- **Attainment/nonattainment designations** — these are area-specific determinations from monitored data using the Appendix N forms, not part of the standard's level.
- **Air Quality Index breakpoints** — revised in 2024 but a communications tool, not a NAAQS level.
- **PM10 standards** — 150 µg/m³ 24-hour primary/secondary, different pollutant.
- **Monitoring network design requirements** (Part 58) — implementation, not level.

## 8. One-line citation form

> U.S. EPA, National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5 (40 CFR § 50.18): 9.0 µg/m³ annual arithmetic mean (3-year average of annual means) and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average (3-year average of 98th percentile), as revised at 89 FR 16202 (Feb. 7, 2024).

question: M4
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — GENERAL-INDUSTRY FALL-PROTECTION TRIGGER HEIGHT

1. ANSWER

4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level.

A US general-industry employer must protect each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level from falling. The regulatory metric equivalent is 1.2 m (exact conversion of 4 ft = 1.2192 m; the regulation rounds to 1.2 m). The threshold is inclusive — "4 feet (1.2 m) or more" — so protection is required at exactly 4 ft, not only above it. Below 4 ft, the general duty to provide fall protection for unprotected sides and edges does not attach (the dangerous-equipment provision in §1910.28(b)(6)(i) is a separate, stricter rule and is noted in the exception table below).

2. GOVERNING AUTHORITY

29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D (Walking-Working Surfaces), §1910.28 "Duty to have fall protection." The general rule is §1910.28(b)(1)(i): except as provided elsewhere in the section, each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level must be protected by one or more of: (A) guardrail systems; (B) safety net systems; or (C) personal fall protection systems (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems).

The same 4-foot figure is corroborated throughout the section in the current regulatory text:
- §1910.28(b)(15) (walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed): "the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."
- §1910.28(b)(6)(ii) (dangerous equipment): 4 feet (1.2 m) or more.
- §1910.28(b)(7) (openings): outside bottom edge of the opening 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.
- §1910.28(b)(11)(i) (stairway landings): 4 feet (1.2 m) or more.
- §1910.28(b)(12)(ii) (rope descent systems): 4 feet (1.2 m) or more.
- §1910.28(b)(14)(i) (slaughtering facility platforms): 4 feet (1.2 m) or more.

Because the catch-all paragraph (b)(15) independently imposes the 4-foot trigger on any walking-working surface not addressed by a more specific paragraph, the 4-foot answer holds even if the reader's copy of the section does not reproduce paragraph (b)(1)(i) verbatim.

3. DEFINITIONS THAT CONTROL APPLICABILITY (29 CFR 1910.21(b))

- Walking-working surface: any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
- Unprotected sides and edges: any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.

Both definitions must be satisfied before the 4-foot duty attaches. A side or edge that is closed by a wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system is not an "unprotected" side or edge, and the 4-foot trigger is not engaged by that edge.

4. HEIGHT-THRESHOLD TABLE (all height triggers in the general-industry rule are 4 ft / 1.2 m; the other numbers below are geometry or distance criteria, not height triggers — do not conflate them)

| Condition | Criterion | Character of criterion | Paragraph |
|---|---|---|---|
| Walking-working surface, unprotected side or edge (general rule) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level | HEIGHT TRIGGER | §1910.28(b)(1)(i) |
| Walking-working surface not otherwise addressed (catch-all) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more | HEIGHT TRIGGER | §1910.28(b)(15) |
| Employee above dangerous equipment | Under 4 ft: guardrail or travel restraint required unless equipment covered/guarded; 4 ft or more: guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest | HEIGHT TRIGGER (stricter below 4 ft) | §1910.28(b)(6) |
| Opening in a walking-working surface | Inside bottom edge of opening less than 39 in (99 cm) above the surface AND outside bottom edge 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level | 39 in = OPENING GEOMETRY; 4 ft = HEIGHT TRIGGER | §1910.28(b)(7) |
| Stairway landing with unprotected side or edge | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more | HEIGHT TRIGGER (guardrail or stair rail system) | §1910.28(b)(11)(i) |
| Rope descent system | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more | HEIGHT TRIGGER (personal fall arrest system) | §1910.28(b)(12)(ii) |
| Slaughtering facility platform, unprotected working side | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more | HEIGHT TRIGGER (guardrail or travel restraint) | §1910.28(b)(14)(i) |
| Low-slope roof work | Less than 6 ft (1.6 m) from roof edge: full protection. At least 6 ft but less than 15 ft (4.6 m) from edge: full protection, or designated area if work is infrequent and temporary. 15 ft (4.6 m) or more from edge: protection or designated area; no fall protection required if work is both infrequent and temporary, plus an enforced work rule barring employees within 15 ft of the edge without protection | DISTANCE FROM EDGE — not a height trigger | §1910.28(b)(13) |
| Employee on a scaffold | Fall protection per 29 CFR Part 1926, Subpart L | Cross-reference to construction scaffold rule (applies in general industry to scaffolds) | §1910.28(b)(12)(i) |

Key reading note for auditors: in the general-industry rule, height above a lower level is never the variable — 4 ft (1.2 m) is the uniform height trigger. The only distance-based provisions are the low-slope-roof provisions in (b)(13), which turn on horizontal distance from the roof edge, and they do not raise or lower the 4-foot height trigger for other surfaces.

5. SCOPE, EXCLUSIONS, AND THE MOST COMMON ERROR

- Construction work is governed by 29 CFR Part 1926, not §1910.28. The request excludes construction, so the Part 1926 threshold is not the answer here and must not be substituted. Note the one bridge: §1910.28(b)(12)(i) sends scaffold fall protection in general industry to Part 1926 Subpart L.
- The frequently cited 6-foot figure belongs to the construction standard, not to general industry. A program document that states 6 ft as the general-industry trigger is non-compliant on its face: it would leave employees unprotected at 4 ft 0 in through 5 ft 11 in.
- The 39-inch figure in §1910.28(b)(7) is an opening-geometry dimension, not a fall-height trigger. It must not be presented as a height threshold.
- State-plan states: OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as the federal standard; a State Plan may adopt a stricter trigger, so verify the applicable State Plan before finalizing a site-specific program.

6. COMPLIANCE VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (field/desk audit, 6 steps)

Step 1 — Confirm jurisdiction and standard set: general industry under Part 1910 Subpart D (or the applicable State Plan). Confirm the task is not construction, maritime, or agriculture, each of which has its own part.
Step 2 — Identify each walking-working surface and measure its height above the lower level, using a consistent datum (top of the working surface to the surface an employee would land on). Record to the nearest inch. Any measurement of 48 in (1.2 m) or greater engages the duty.
Step 3 — For each surface at or above 48 in, determine whether each side or edge is "unprotected" per §1910.21(b) — i.e., no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system. Document each unprotected side or edge on a plan or photograph.
Step 4 — Verify a compliant means of protection is present for each unprotected side or edge: guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system, each meeting §1910.29 criteria. Where a fall protection system is used, verify the system and its components meet §1910.29 and that employees are trained per §1910.30.
Step 5 — Test the exceptions: does the surface fall under a more specific paragraph — dangerous equipment (b)(6), openings (b)(7), stairways (b)(11), scaffolds/rope descent (b)(12), low-slope roofs (b)(13), slaughtering platforms (b)(14)? If yes, apply that paragraph, noting that none of them relaxes the 4-foot trigger except the roof provisions, which substitute a distance test. Where the employer relies on infeasibility, verify the written fall protection plan and documentation required by §1910.28(b)(1) and §1910.29.
Step 6 — Record the determination: surface ID, measured height, protected/unprotected status, applicable paragraph, selected protection method, inspection date, and inspector. Re-audit whenever a surface, edge condition, or task changes.

7. DISPOSITION

The single controlling value for this request is 4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level, per 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i), reinforced by §1910.28(b)(15) and the parallel 4-foot thresholds in §1910.28(b)(6), (b)(7), (b)(11)(i), (b)(12)(ii), and (b)(14)(i). No ask in this request is blocked; the answer is fully supported by the current regulatory text.

question: M6
answer:
ANSWER

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry fuel sufficient to reach the first point of intended landing and then, assuming normal cruising speed, fly for at least 20 more minutes. Reserve = 20 minutes of flight at normal cruising speed.

GOVERNING REGULATION

14 CFR 91.151(b) (Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions), verbatim: "No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

KEY PROPERTIES OF THE REQUIREMENT

1. Expressed as time, not volume. The rule is a duration at normal cruising speed. There is no gallon or pound figure in the regulation; the volumetric equivalent depends on the individual helicopter's cruise fuel burn (see worksheet below).
2. No day/night split for rotorcraft. 91.151(b) sets a single 20-minute figure that applies day and night. The 30-minute (day) / 45-minute (night) numbers in 91.151(a) are the airplane rules and do not apply to helicopters.
3. No alternate-airport requirement. 91.151 contains no alternate-destination provision for rotorcraft VFR. Do not import the airplane night case; the only figures in 91.151 are (a)(1) 30 min airplane day, (a)(2) 45 min airplane night, and (b) 20 min rotorcraft.
4. "Considering wind and forecast weather conditions" is part of the rule. The 20 minutes is measured after the fuel needed to reach the first landing point *as planned with forecast winds*; a headwind on the outbound leg lengthens that leg and therefore increases total fuel required, but it does not change the 20-minute reserve figure itself.
5. Part 135 is the same number. 14 CFR 135.209(b), verbatim: "No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes." A commercial operator flying a helicopter VFR therefore also plans on 20 minutes, not the 30/45-minute airplane figures in 135.209(a).

Therefore: whether the flight is Part 91 or Part 135, day or night, the regulatory minimum reserve beyond the first point of intended landing is 20 minutes at normal cruising speed.

CALCULATION WORKSHEET (converting the 20 minutes to usable fuel)

Step 1. Establish normal cruising speed and the corresponding cruise fuel burn (Q, in gal/hr or lb/hr) from the helicopter's operating handbook for the planned cruise configuration and altitude.
Step 2. Reserve volume = Q x (20 / 60) = Q x 0.3333.

Worked examples (illustrative burn rates only):
- Q = 10 gal/hr -> reserve = 10 x 0.3333 = 3.33 gal.
- Q = 16 gal/hr -> reserve = 16 x 0.3333 = 5.33 gal.
- Q = 25 gal/hr -> reserve = 25 x 0.3333 = 8.33 gal.

Step 3. Total minimum fuel at start = fuel to first point of intended landing (computed with forecast wind) + reserve from Step 2. Compare against usable fuel; the reserve must be *usable* fuel, and the total must not exceed usable capacity minus any fuel that is unuseable in the tanks.

Step 4. Express the plan in hours on the VFR flight plan, consistent with 91.153(a)(7) ("The amount of fuel on board (in hours)").

SCOPE NOTES AND VARIANTS

- IFR: out of scope here. If the flight is conducted IFR, 14 CFR 91.167 applies instead (45 minutes beyond the destination/alternate, with different structure). The 20-minute figure above is VFR only.
- Operator/OEM/insurance policy: the 20 minutes is the FAA minimum. Many operators, OEM performance planners, and insurers impose larger margins (commonly 30 minutes or a fixed reserve plus contingency), and prudent helicopter planning adds margin for hover/approach fuel, weather deviation, and the fact that a helicopter diverted at low altitude burns fuel at a much higher rate than cruise. Those are policy or airmanship additions layered on top of, not replacements for, the 20-minute legal minimum.
- If the operation is neither Part 91 nor Part 135 (e.g., public aircraft, military, or a foreign operator under its own state's rules), the 20-minute figure does not automatically govern; the applicable national rule must be checked.

BOTTOM LINE

20 minutes of flight at normal cruising speed, beyond fuel to reach the first point of intended landing, day or night, under both 14 CFR 91.151(b) and 14 CFR 135.209(b).
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 30 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-i/subchapter-g/part-135/subpart-d/section-135.209 and 20 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title14-vol2/pdf/cfr-2025-title14-vol2-sec91-151.pdf. The first reads: "(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 45 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-i/subchapter-g/part-135/subpart-d/section-135.209 and 20 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title14-vol2/pdf/cfr-2025-title14-vol2-sec91-151.pdf. The first reads: "(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes."

question: M8
answer:
# Deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 — Direct Answer

## Answer 1 — The deprecating RFC

**RFC 8996**, *"Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1"*, by K. Moriarty and S. Farrell, published **March 2021** (DOI 10.17487/RFC8996). It is part of **BCP 195** (it updates the TLS best-practice document RFC 7525) and was produced by the IETF TLS working group from `draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12`.

Primary evidence, from the RFC's own Abstract:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

Corroborating metadata from the RFC Editor record (`rfc8996.json`):

```
doc_id:     RFC8996
title:      Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
authors:    K. Moriarty; S. Farrell
pub_date:   March 2021
pub_status: BEST CURRENT PRACTICE
status:     BEST CURRENT PRACTICE
doi:        10.17487/RFC8996
obsoletes:  RFC5469, RFC7507
updates:    RFC3261, RFC3329, RFC3436, ... , RFC7525, RFC7562, RFC7568, RFC8261, RFC8422
```

## Answer 2 — The status assigned to the defining RFCs

RFC 8996 assigned **Historic** status to the RFCs that defined the two deprecated protocol versions:

| Protocol version | Defining RFC | Status assigned by RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | **RFC 2246** | **Historic** |
| TLS 1.1 | **RFC 4346** | **Historic** |

Primary evidence, Section 1 (Introduction) of RFC 8996:

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012. Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. **Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status.**"

### Terminology precision (important, and commonly gotten wrong)

- **RFC 8996 is not itself Historic.** Its "Status of This Memo" reads: *"This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice."* It is a **BCP** document. Only the *targets* of the deprecation become Historic.
- The verb used for RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 is **"moved to Historic"**, not "obsoleted". The RFC Editor's relation list for RFC 8996 contains `obsoletes: RFC5469, RFC7507` and does **not** list RFC 2246 or RFC 4346 as obsoleted — their change is a *status* change, not an obsoletion by RFC 8996.
- "Superseded by TLS 1.2 / TLS 1.3" (a technical statement about protocol versions) is distinct from the RFC-Editor status keyword **Historic**. RFC 8996 uses both ideas; the status it *assigned* is Historic.

## Additional documents covered (context; does not change Answers 1–2)

RFC 8996 applies the same treatment beyond the two TLS base specs:

| Document | What RFC 8996 did |
|---|---|
| **RFC 4347** (DTLS 1.0) | Deprecated; moved to **Historic** (DTLS 1.2, RFC 6347, is *not* deprecated; no DTLS 1.1 exists) |
| **RFC 5469** (DES/IDEA cipher suites for TLS) | Moved to **Historic** — "since the only versions of TLS for which their usage is defined are now Historic, [RFC5469] has been moved to Historic as well" |
| **RFC 7507** (TLS Fallback SCSV) | **Obsoleted** — "the functionality from [RFC7507] has been superseded" by the TLS 1.3 ServerHello.Random sentinel mechanism |
| **RFC 6347** (DTLS 1.2) | **Updated** — its allowance for negotiating DTLS 1.0 is now forbidden |
| ~80 other RFCs (RFC 3261, 3329, 3436, 3501, 3552, 4513, 5246-adjacent profiles, 7525, 8422, etc.) | **Updated** to require TLS 1.2 or later where they normatively referenced TLS 1.0/1.1 |

Documents already Historic before RFC 8996 (e.g., RFC 6460, RFC 4744, RFC 4743) are listed only to reiterate that obsolete-protocol usage should move to modern TLS; RFC 8996 marks them updated without changing their status.

## Verification procedure (how to re-check this answer independently)

1. Fetch `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html`.
2. Read the **Abstract** — confirms the deprecation of TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) and the move to Historic (Answer 1).
3. Read **Section 1 (Introduction)** — second paragraph ends "...have been moved to Historic status" (Answer 2).
4. Read **Status of This Memo** — confirms RFC 8996's own status is Best Current Practice, guarding against the common error of calling RFC 8996 Historic.
5. Cross-check `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.json` for the `obsoletes` / `updates` / `pub_status` fields to confirm the Historic-vs-Obsoleted distinction.
6. Confirm current status of RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 on `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246/` and `.../rfc4346/`, which show **Historic**.

## Scope and currency notes

- **Scope of "the RFCs that defined them"**: interpreted as the base protocol specifications — RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1). Cipher-suite and extension RFCs are not "the RFCs that defined" TLS 1.0/1.1 and are treated only in the context table above.
- **As-of date**: status as stated in RFC 8996 (March 2021). No later RFC in the sources consulted reverses the Historic status of RFC 2246 or RFC 4346; the errata page for RFC 8996 contains only inline editorial errata to its own text. The RFC Editor's current info pages continue to show both as Historic.
- Both asks are fully answerable from the primary RFC text; nothing is blocked.

question: M10
answer:
# US Social Security Contribution and Benefit Base for 2026

## Answer

**$184,500**

The contribution and benefit base (also called the taxable maximum or the OASDI wage base) for tax year 2026 is **$184,500**. Earnings above that amount are not subject to the 6.2% Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax; the Medicare (HI) portion has no earnings cap and continues on all wages.

## Primary-source corroboration

Five separate Social Security Administration pages, all fetched 2026-11-16, state the same figure:

| Source | What it says |
|---|---|
| SSA COLA Fact Sheet, "2026 Social Security Changes" (ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2026.html) | Table "Maximum Taxable Earnings — Social Security (OASDI only)": 2025 = $176,100; **2026 = $184,500**; Medicare (HI only) = No Limit |
| SSA, "Maximum Taxable Earnings" chart (ssa.gov/benefits/retirement/planner/maxtax.html) | Year-by-year table: 2025 $176,100; **2026 $184,500** |
| SSA FAQ KA-02387 (ssa.gov/faqs/en/questions/KA-02387.html) | "In 2026, the maximum amount of earnings on which you must pay Social Security tax is **$184,500**. … There is no maximum earnings amount for Medicare tax." |
| SSA Publication EN-05-10024 (ssa.gov/pubs/EN-05-10024.pdf) | "You pay Social Security taxes based on your earnings, up to a certain amount. In 2026 that amount is **$184,500**." |
| SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Contribution and Benefit Base table (ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html) | 2024 $168,600; 2025 $176,100; **2026 $184,500**; 2027 $192,300 |

## Derived figures (for payroll setup), all computed from the $184,500 base

- Employee OASDI: 6.2% × $184,500 = **$11,439.00** maximum withheld for 2026.
- Employer OASDI: 6.2% × $184,500 = **$11,439.00** maximum per employee for 2026.
- Combined OASDI per employee: **$22,878.00**.
- Self-employed OASDI: 12.4% × $184,500 = **$22,878.00** (same base applies to self-employment income under SECA).
- Total FICA rate 7.65% (6.2% OASDI + 1.45% HI) applies only up to $184,500; above that, only the 1.45% HI rate (plus the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above $200,000 single / $250,000 MFJ) applies.

Arithmetic check: 184,500 × 0.062 = 11,439.00; 184,500 × 0.124 = 22,878.00; 11,439 × 2 = 22,878. Consistent.

## Year-over-year context

- 2025 base: $176,100
- 2026 base: $184,500
- Increase: $8,400, or **+4.77%** (8,400 / 176,100 = 0.04770)

The base is indexed to the national average wage index, not to the COLA. The 2.8% COLA for 2026 and the 4.77% wage-base increase are therefore different numbers from different series; the divergence is expected and is not evidence of an error.

## Common confusions to avoid

1. **$192,300 is the 2027 base, not 2026.** The SSA actuarial page publishes 2027 alongside 2026. The 2027 determination uses the 1994 base of $60,600 × (2025 average wage index 72,800.33 / 1992 average wage index 22,935.42) = $192,353.14, rounded to the nearest $300 = $192,300. Do not use this for 2026.
2. **Medicare has no cap.** The 1.45% HI tax (2.9% self-employed) applies to all earnings; only the 6.2% OASDI portion stops at $184,500.
3. **Not the earnings-per-credit amount.** For 2026, one Social Security credit is earned per $1,890 of earnings (max 4 credits); that is a separate 2026 parameter.
4. **Not the benefit bend points.** The contribution and benefit base is the tax cap; the benefit formula bend points are distinct published figures.

## Provenance note

The figure is the SSA's own published 2026 determination, confirmed on both the COLA fact sheet and the Chief Actuary's statutory table. The statutory method (base for year Y = 1994 base of $60,600 × national average wage index for Y−2 ÷ 1992 index, rounded to the nearest $300, never reduced below the prior year's base) is the mechanism that produced it; the published number is authoritative and should be used directly rather than recomputed.

question: M12
answer:
ANSWER

For tax year 2026, the limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan — before any catch-up contribution — is $24,500.

This is the IRC §402(g)(1) limit on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in §402(g)(3). It is effective January 1, 2026.

AUTHORITY

1. IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 cost-of-living adjustments), which states: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
2. IRS, Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
3. IRS, Retirement Topics — Contributions: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."

WHAT THE $24,500 COVERS

- Pre-tax elective deferrals and designated Roth elective contributions combined. The §402(g) limit is a single limit applied to the employee's total elective deferrals; a participant cannot defer $24,500 pre-tax and a further $24,500 as Roth. The IRS definition is explicit that elective deferrals are amounts contributed at the employee's election which, "except to the extent they are designated Roth contributions, are excludable from the employee's gross income."
- The limit applies per individual, not per plan. An employee with more than one employer or more than one plan in 2026 still has one $24,500 limit in total; the IRS page states: "Generally, you aggregate all elective deferrals you made to all plans in which you participate to determine if you have exceeded these limits."
- The statutory backstop is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation.
- A plan's own terms, or nondiscrimination testing (ADP) applicable to highly compensated employees, may impose a lower limit on a given employee. $24,500 is a ceiling, not an entitlement.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED (do not add these to the figure above)

- Age 50+ catch-up under §414(v)(2)(B)(i): $8,000 for 2026 (increased from $7,500).
- Enhanced "super catch-up" under §414(v)(2)(E)(i) for participants attaining age 60, 61, 62 or 63 in 2026: $11,250 (unchanged).
- For reference only, and not part of the requested figure: base limit plus age 50+ catch-up = $32,500; base limit plus age 60–63 catch-up = $35,750.

DO NOT CONFUSE WITH THESE 2026 FIGURES

- SIMPLE 401(k) elective deferrals: $17,000 (a SIMPLE 401(k) is a different plan type; the standard 401(k) figure does not apply to it).
- §415(c) total annual additions (employee deferrals + employer contributions + forfeitures): $72,000.
- §401(a)(17) compensation limit used for contributions and testing: $360,000.
- §457(e)(15) deferred compensation limit for state/local government and tax-exempt employers: $24,500 (same dollar amount, different Code section and different plan type).
- IRA and 403(b) limits are separate regimes.

PRACTICAL APPLICATION NOTES FOR PAYROLL / PLAN ADMINISTRATION

1. Configure the 2026 deferral election cap at $24,500 per employee across all plans of the employer, counting pre-tax and Roth deferrals in the same bucket. Do not reset the cap per plan.
2. If the employee participates in another employer's plan, obtain the employee's certification of year-to-date deferrals elsewhere; excess deferrals are the employee's responsibility to monitor and correct.
3. Excess deferrals (amounts over $24,500 across all plans) are includible in the employee's gross income. To avoid double taxation, the employee must notify the plan administrator before April 15, 2027 to have the excess, adjusted for earnings, distributed; the April 15 date is not tied to the return due date, and the corrective distribution is not subject to the 10% early distribution tax.
4. Catch-up eligibility and amounts are administered separately and must not be netted against the $24,500 base limit.
5. Beginning in 2026, catch-up contributions must be made on a Roth basis for participants whose prior-year wages with the plan sponsor exceeded $150,000 (the 2025 threshold used to test 2026 catch-ups, per Notice 2025-67). This affects catch-up administration only, not the $24,500 base limit.

question: M4
answer:
SAFETY ENGINEER ANSWER — GENERAL-INDUSTRY FALL-PROTECTION DUTY HEIGHT (US, FEDERAL OSHA)

1. ANSWER

4 feet (1.2 m). In general industry, a US employer must protect each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level from falling. Below 4 feet there is no general duty-to-protect trigger (but see Section 6 — several provisions trigger at lower heights or independently of height).

2. CONTROLLING TEXT AND CITATION

Primary: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1) — Walking-working surfaces, general requirements. Substance of the rule: "The employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Catch-all confirmation: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) — "Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed. Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems..."

Verbatim confirmation from the fetched regulatory text (eCFR current, 29 CFR 1910.28, and the GovInfo CFR volumes for 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025 — all four annual editions carry the same 4-foot figure):
- "...ing-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."
- "(15) Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed. Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or..."

Citation-format note: subparagraph lettering inside (b)(1) has been rendered both as (b)(1)(i)–(iii) (current eCFR) and as (b)(1)(i)(A)–(C) (2017-era publications). The number that matters — 4 feet (1.2 m) — is identical in every edition examined. Cite as 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1) (general) and 1910.28(b)(15) (catch-all).

Related definitions and criteria an employer needs to actually comply:
- 29 CFR 1910.21 — definitions (walking-working surface; lower level; unprotected side or edge).
- 29 CFR 1910.29 — criteria and practices for guardrail systems, safety net systems, personal fall protection systems (e.g., guardrail top rail 42 in ±3 in; design/performance loads).
- 29 CFR 1910.30 — training requirements for employees exposed to fall hazards.

3. SCOPE AND ASSUMPTIONS (state these whenever the figure is quoted)

- Jurisdiction: federal OSHA, 29 CFR Part 1910, general industry. If the workplace is in a State Plan state, the state's standard governs and may differ; verify before relying on 4 feet (see Section 8).
- Edition/date: current, post-effective-date rules (the walking-working surfaces rule was revised effective January 17, 2017, and the 4-foot general threshold is carried unchanged in the 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025 CFR volumes). Pre-2017 general-industry rules did not state a single clean vertical duty height for all walking-working surfaces; do not mix pre- and post-2017 text.
- Industry: general industry only. Construction (29 CFR 1926 Subpart M) is 6 feet; shipyard employment (29 CFR 1915) and longshoring/marine terminals (29 CFR 1917/1918) have their own triggers. Do not import the 6-foot construction figure into general industry.
- The 4 feet is measured from the walking-working surface the employee is on down to the lower level. It is a height, not a horizontal distance.

4. WHAT "PROTECT" MEANS (employer's option)

The employer selects one or more of: guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems), each meeting 1910.29 criteria, with employee training under 1910.30. Where the employer can demonstrate that a required system is infeasible or creates a greater hazard, OSHA's framework permits a documented fall protection plan in lieu of those systems (cross-reference in 1910.28 to 1910.29(k)); the plan must be site-specific, written, and enforced. Treat this as a narrow, documented exception, not a routine alternative.

5. WHY 4 FEET IS THE RIGHT SINGLE NUMBER FOR THIS ASK

The question asks for the height at which the duty attaches for "a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge" — that is the (b)(1) general rule, and (b)(15) sweeps in any surface not separately addressed. All of the section-specific provisions either restate 4 feet (stairway landings, rope descent systems, slaughtering facility platforms, openings with a 4-foot outside drop) or impose a stricter/different trigger (dangerous equipment below 4 feet; low-slope roof work measured horizontally from the edge). None of them raises the general trigger above 4 feet.

6. ADJACENT RULES THAT OVERRIDE OR PRECEDE THE 4-FOOT HEADLINE (do not omit these when advising)

- Dangerous equipment — 1910.28(b)(6): employees LESS THAN 4 feet (1.2 m) above dangerous equipment must still be protected from falling into or onto it by a guardrail system or travel restraint system, unless the equipment is covered or guarded to eliminate the hazard; at 4 feet or more, guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest is required. This is the main reason "under 4 feet, nothing required" is wrong.
- Openings — 1910.28(b)(7): where the inside bottom edge of an opening is less than 39 inches (99 cm) above the walking-working surface and the outside bottom edge is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level, protection (guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest) is required. Holes are addressed in 1910.28(b)(3) and must be covered or guarded.
- Stairway landings — 1910.28(b)(11)(i): unprotected side or edge of a stairway landing 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level requires a guardrail or stair rail system; flights with at least 3 treads and at least 4 risers require stair rail systems and handrails.
- Rope descent systems — 1910.28(b)(12)(ii): personal fall arrest system required at 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.
- Slaughtering facility platforms — 1910.28(b)(14): unprotected working side 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level requires guardrail or travel restraint (with a documented infeasibility route).
- Low-slope roofs — 1910.28(b)(13): the trigger here is HORIZONTAL DISTANCE from the roof edge, not height: less than 6 feet (1.6 m) from the edge — guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest; 6 feet (1.6 m) to less than 15 feet (4.6 m) — same systems, with a designated area permitted for work that is both infrequent and temporary; 15 feet (4.6 m) or more — the employer must either protect employees or implement and enforce a work rule prohibiting employees from going within 15 feet (4.6 m) of the roof edge without fall protection. Do not report these as heights.
- Hoist areas, dockboards, runways and similar walkways, ladders, repair/service/assembly pits, and scaffolds are addressed in their own paragraphs of 1910.28(b); scaffolds are protected per 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart L (1910.28(b)(12)(i)).

7. NUMERIC CONSISTENCY CHECK (internal verification of every figure stated above)

| Figure | Meaning | Consistent with the 4 ft (1.2 m) answer? |
|---|---|---|
| 4 ft / 1.2 m | General duty height, 1910.28(b)(1) and (b)(15) | This is the answer |
| 48 in | 4 ft expressed in inches | Yes — same quantity |
| 42 in ±3 in | Guardrail top-rail height under 1910.29 | Yes — hardware dimension above the trigger height, no conflict |
| 39 in (99 cm) | Inside bottom edge of opening, 1910.28(b)(7) | Yes — separate geometric condition, paired with a 4 ft outside drop |
| <4 ft and >=4 ft | Dangerous equipment bands, 1910.28(b)(6) | Yes — stricter sub-4 ft duty, not a competing general threshold |
| 6 ft / 15 ft | Horizontal distances from low-slope roof edge, 1910.28(b)(13) | Yes — horizontal, explicitly not heights |
| 3 treads / 4 risers | Stairway rail trigger, 1910.28(b)(11)(ii) | Yes — counts, not heights |
| 6 ft | Construction threshold, 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M | Yes — contrast only; out of scope for general industry |
| ~7.5 ft | Some State Plan general-industry thresholds (e.g., Cal/OSHA) | Yes — flagged as a jurisdiction variance to verify, not applied to the federal answer |

No value in this deliverable exceeds or contradicts a threshold the deliverable itself sets.

8. VERIFICATION STEPS BEFORE RELYING ON THE FIGURE

1) Confirm jurisdiction: federal OSHA or a State Plan. If a State Plan, read the state's walking-working surfaces standard; do not assume 4 feet. (California, for example, uses a different general-industry trigger for many operations.)
2) Confirm the work is general industry, not construction, shipyard, or longshoring/marine terminal.
3) Confirm the CFR edition in use is post-January 17, 2017.
4) Walk the surface and measure from the walking-working surface to the lower level; treat 4 feet (1.2 m) as the trigger and anything at or above it as requiring protection.
5) Separately screen for the Section 6 provisions — especially dangerous equipment below 4 feet and low-slope roof edge distances — because those duties can attach even where the general 4-foot trigger is not met.
6) Confirm the selected means of protection meets 1910.29 and that exposed employees are trained under 1910.30.

9. ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR CITATION IN A DOCUMENT

"Under federal OSHA general-industry rules, fall protection is required where an employee is on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level — 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1); see also 1910.28(b)(15). (Construction is 6 feet; State Plan requirements may differ.)"

question: M6
answer:
# VFR Reserve Fuel Requirement — Helicopter, United States

## 1. Answer

**20 minutes.** A helicopter may not begin a VFR flight in the US unless it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing **and then fly for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed** (Part 91) / **at normal cruising fuel consumption** (Part 135).

The regulation states the reserve as a **period of flight time**, not a fixed quantity of fuel. The gallon figure is therefore aircraft-specific: it is **one-third of the helicopter's normal-cruise hourly fuel burn** (20 min ÷ 60 min = 1/3).

## 2. Regulatory basis (verbatim)

**14 CFR § 91.151(b)** — *Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions* (general operating rules):

> "(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

**14 CFR § 135.209(b)** — *VFR: Fuel supply* (commercial operators):

> "(b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

FAA guidance (the agency's own fuel-planning handbook excerpt) confirms the same figure for both regimes:

> "15. FAR PART 135 HELICOPTER VFR OPERATIONS. … (2) Reserve Fuel. FAR § 135.209(b). During day or night the required reserve fuel is the amount that allows continued operation for 20 minutes."

## 3. Part 91 vs. Part 135 — the answer does not change

| Regime | Citation | Reserve after first point of intended landing | Day/night split? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Part 91 (general/private) | 91.151(b) | **20 minutes**, normal cruising speed | **No** |
| Part 135 (commercial) | 135.209(b) | **20 minutes**, normal cruising fuel consumption | **No** |

Because both regimes yield 20 minutes, the Part 91 / Part 135 ambiguity does not affect the answer. It only affects the wording of the performance basis ("normal cruising speed" vs. "normal cruising fuel consumption" — operationally the same calculation).

## 4. The three traps this question sets

1. **Do not use the airplane numbers.** 91.151(a)/135.209(a) give airplanes 30 minutes day and 45 minutes night. Those paragraphs do not apply to rotorcraft. There is **no day/night difference for helicopters** — 20 minutes applies day and night, VFR.
2. **Do not use the IFR number.** Helicopter IFR reserve is 30 minutes (91.167(a)(3); 135.223(a)(3)), plus alternate fuel where required. That is a different rule for a different flight condition and is not the VFR answer.
3. **Do not answer in gallons as if it were a constant.** 20 minutes is the legal requirement; the gallon value varies by type and by power setting.

## 5. Converting the 20-minute reserve into fuel quantity

**Formula (usable fuel):**

```
Reserve (gal)   = (20 / 60) x cruise fuel burn (gal/hr) = cruise burn / 3
Reserve (lb)    = (20 / 60) x cruise fuel flow (lb/hr)  = cruise flow / 3
Reserve (nm)    = cruise TAS (kt) x (20 / 60)           = TAS / 3   [still-air equivalent]
```

Use the **normal cruise** burn from the Rotorcraft Flight Manual / POH at the planned cruise power setting — not hover burn, not max-continuous, and not best-endurance. Then verify the total required fuel (trip + reserve) does not exceed **usable** fuel; unusable fuel does not count toward the requirement.

**Worked examples (representative figures — substitute the actual RFM/POH numbers for the specific aircraft):**

| Type (illustrative) | Cruise burn (gal/hr) | Reserve = burn ÷ 3 (gal) | At cruise TAS | Still-air equivalent (nm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Robinson R22 Beta II | 8.5 | 2.8 | 95 kt | 31.7 |
| Robinson R44 Raven II | 14 | 4.7 | 110 kt | 36.7 |
| Robinson R66 | 23 | 7.7 | 120 kt | 40.0 |
| Bell 206B-3 JetRanger | 45 | 15.0 | 115 kt | 38.3 |
| Airbus H125 (AS350 B3) | 75 | 25.0 | 130 kt | 43.3 |

Every row is arithmetic on the same rule: gallons = burn/3, nautical miles = TAS/3. Change the burn and the gallon reserve changes; the 20 minutes does not.

**Worked example, full calculation (R44, 120 nm trip, 110 kt cruise, 14 gal/hr, 30.6 gal usable):**

- Trip fuel = 120 nm ÷ 110 kt = 1.09 hr × 14 gal/hr = **15.3 gal**
- Reserve = 14 ÷ 3 = **4.7 gal** (20 min)
- Total required = **20.0 gal** vs. 30.6 gal usable → legal, with 10.6 gal (≈45 min) of discretionary margin on top of the regulatory minimum.

## 6. What "enough fuel to begin the flight" actually requires

To legally start the flight, all of the following must be true simultaneously:

1. **Trip + 20 minutes** of usable fuel is on board at brake release (not at some later point).
2. The calculation **considers wind and forecast weather conditions** — a headwind on the trip leg increases trip fuel and therefore the total.
3. The reserve is flown at **normal cruising speed/fuel consumption** — do not plan the reserve at a reduced burn rate to shrink the gallons.
4. **Usable fuel only.** Sump/tank unusable quantity is excluded.
5. **§ 91.103 preflight action** is satisfied: weather, fuel requirements, alternatives, and any known ATC delays are known before departure. (For Part 135, the FAA's guidance notes the same: any known delays or other information affecting the flight must be considered.)
6. **No alternate airport is required** for VFR — unlike the IFR rule, there is no "fly to the alternate" increment in 91.151(b)/135.209(b). If you plan one anyway, its fuel comes out of your discretionary margin, not out of the 20-minute minimum.
7. If a **VFR flight plan** is filed, fuel on board is stated **in hours** (§ 91.153(a)(7)) — that entry must be at least trip time + 0:20.

## 7. Common errors to avoid when applying this

- Using 30/45 minutes (airplane rule) for a helicopter.
- Using 30 minutes (helicopter IFR rule) for a VFR flight.
- Treating 20 minutes as a distance instead of a time — the distance equivalent falls out only after applying the aircraft's cruise speed.
- Planning the reserve at a lower-than-normal cruise burn to reduce the required gallons.
- Counting unusable fuel, or counting fuel that the gauges cannot substantiate.
- Omitting the wind/forecast adjustment to the trip leg, which effectively eats into the reserve.
- Assuming a company ops-spec, state, or operator standard: those may **add** to 20 minutes, never subtract from it. The 20 minutes is the floor.

## 8. Scope and currency note

- Applies to **rotorcraft (helicopters) operating under VFR in the United States** under Part 91 or Part 135. Gyroplanes fall under the same rotorcraft paragraph.
- Figures are taken from 14 CFR 91.151, 135.209, and FAA fuel-planning guidance as retrieved from eCFR/govinfo on 2026-11-16; re-verify against the current eCFR before operational use.
- Performance numbers in §5 are illustrative only and must be replaced with the specific aircraft's RFM/POH values.

**Bottom line: 20 minutes of fuel at normal cruise, on top of fuel to the first point of intended landing — day or night, Part 91 or Part 135.**

question: M8
answer:
## Answers

**1. The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1: RFC 8996**, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (K. Moriarty, S. Farrell), published March 2021, Internet Best Current Practice, part of BCP 195. DOI 10.17487/RFC8996.

**2. The status it gave the RFCs that defined them: Historic.** RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) were both moved to Historic status.

### Verbatim grounding

RFC 8996, Abstract (identical text in the HTML, the RFC Editor info page, the XML, and the inline-errata rendering):

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

RFC 8996, Section 1 (Introduction):

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. ... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

Status of This Memo:

> "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice."

RFC Editor metadata record (rfc8996.json) corroborates: `doc_id: RFC8996`, `title: Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1`, `pub_date: March 2021`, `pub_status: BEST CURRENT PRACTICE`, `status: BEST CURRENT PRACTICE`, `source: Transport Layer Security`, `stream`: IETF, `part of BCP 195`.

## Two distinctions worth recording alongside the citation

**(a) Protocol deprecation vs. document status.** These are two separate acts in RFC 8996 and should not be conflated in a changelog or compliance note. The *protocol versions* TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are formally deprecated ("MUST NOT" be used, per the normative text); the *documents* RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 are reclassified to Historic in the RFC Editor index. A reader asking "is TLS 1.0 deprecated?" and a reader asking "what does the index say about RFC 2246?" are asking different questions with different answers — deprecated protocol, Historic document.

**(b) RFC 8996 is itself a BCP, not a Standards Track document.** It is part of BCP 195 (which it also updates, since RFC 7525 is BCP 195). It does not define a protocol version; it changes the status of other documents and updates many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1.

## Full set of status changes RFC 8996 makes (for completeness)

| Document | What it was | What RFC 8996 did |
|---|---|---|
| RFC 2246 | TLS 1.0, Proposed Standard | Moved to **Historic** |
| RFC 4346 | TLS 1.1, Proposed Standard | Moved to **Historic** |
| RFC 4347 | DTLS 1.0 | Moved to **Historic** |
| RFC 5469 | DES/IDEA cipher suites for TLS | Moved to **Historic** |
| RFC 7507 | TLS Fallback SCSV | **Obsoleted** (superseded by TLS 1.3's ServerHello.Random sentinel mechanism) |
| RFC 7525 | BCP 195 (TLS best practices) | **Updated** |
| ~80 other RFCs | Various | **Updated** (normative TLS 1.0/1.1 references raised to TLS 1.2+) |

DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347) was **not** deprecated; RFC 8996 updates RFC 6347 only to forbid negotiating DTLS 1.0. There is no DTLS 1.1.

## Correction to a stated assumption

The project context asserts that RFC 8996 moved "RFC 5077, RFC 5246, and RFC 8446" to Historic alongside RFC 2246 and RFC 4346. **That is not supported by the source and should not be repeated.** Specifically:

- **RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2)** and **RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3)** are not marked Historic by RFC 8996. RFC 5246 was obsoleted by RFC 8446; RFC 8996 references both but changes neither's status. The `obsoletes` field of the RFC 8996 metadata record lists exactly two documents: RFC5469 and RFC7507.
- **RFC 5077** (TLS Session Resumption without Server-Side State) is not among the documents RFC 8996 moves to Historic, and is not in its `updates` list.

Only RFC 2246, RFC 4346, RFC 4347, and RFC 5469 are moved to Historic by RFC 8996.

## Citation form for downstream use

> Moriarty, K. and S. Farrell, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1", BCP 195, RFC 8996, DOI 10.17487/RFC8996, March 2021, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/>.

Single-sentence form for a changelog or audit note: *TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) were formally deprecated by RFC 8996 (BCP 195, March 2021), which moved both defining documents to Historic status.*

## Verification note

All five fetched renderings of RFC 8996 (HTML, info page, XML, inline-errata HTML, Datatracker history) agree on the abstract sentence and the Historic status assignment; the inline-errata page carries the same abstract text, so no erratum alters the answer. Datatracker history confirms the document was published as RFC 8996 on 2021-03-23 from draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12.

question: M10
answer:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for tax year 2026 is:

  $184,500

This is the officially determined, announced figure for calendar year 2026 — not a projection. It was announced by the Social Security Administration in the fall of 2025 as part of the annual automatic-adjustment release accompanying the 2.8% COLA for 2026.

SOURCE AND VERIFICATION

The figure is confirmed identically by three independent SSA pages:

1. SSA 2026 COLA Fact Sheet (ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2026.html) — 'Maximum Taxable Earnings: Social Security (OASDI only): 2025 $176,100 | 2026 $184,500; Medicare (HI only): No Limit.'
2. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Contribution and Benefit Base history table (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html) — lists 2025 = $176,100, 2026 = $184,500, 2027 = $192,300.
3. SSA Detailed Benefit Calculator update page (ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html) — 'Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500.'
4. SSA Fast Facts & Figures 2026 — 'Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026: OASDI 184,500; HI No limit.'

Statutory basis: under the Social Security Act the base is set by formula — the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for year (Y-2) to that for 1992, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base. $184,500 is an exact multiple of $300 (615 x $300), consistent with the statutory rounding rule.

WHAT THE FIGURE MEANS IN PRACTICE (2026)

- Employee OASDI withholding: 6.2% on earnings up to $184,500; maximum employee OASDI tax = 0.062 x $184,500 = $11,439.00 for the year.
- Employer OASDI: matching 6.2%, maximum $11,439.00 per employee for the year.
- Self-employed: 12.4% OASDI on net self-employment earnings up to $184,500; maximum OASDI self-employment tax = 0.124 x $184,500 = $22,878.00. (Half of total SE tax, including the Medicare portion, is deductible for income tax purposes.)
- Earnings above $184,500 in 2026 are not subject to OASDI tax, but they ARE subject to Medicare (HI) tax at 1.45% (2.9% combined) with no cap, plus the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on earned income above $200,000 single / $250,000 married filing jointly. These are separate from the answer and are a common source of confusion.
- The same $184,500 limit applies for crediting earnings in the benefit computation (maximum taxable earnings counted toward a worker's record for 2026).

DISAMBIGUATION — VALUES THAT ARE NOT THE ANSWER

- $192,300 is the base for 2027, not 2026. It appears prominently on the Actuary's contribution-and-benefit-base page and in the 2027 determination; it must not be reported as the 2026 figure.
- $137,100 is the 'old-law' contribution and benefit base for 2026, used only in certain benefit-computation contexts — not the payroll tax cap.
- $176,100 is the 2025 base.
- Medicare (HI) has no earnings cap in 2026; any statement of a 'Medicare wage base' would be wrong.

APPLICABILITY NOTES

- Calendar year 2026 (Jan 1 – Dec 31, 2026), US federal OASDI under FICA/FSECA. State programs, railroad retirement Tier I (which uses the same Social Security base), and private plans are outside scope; household-employee and tip-income rules affect reporting thresholds, not the base itself.
- This is informational and computational in nature; payroll-system configuration for 2026 withholding caps should key on $184,500 and should be re-verified against the SSA COLA fact sheet at implementation time.

# 2026 401(k) elective deferral limit (before catch-up)

## Answer

**$24,500** — the maximum an employee may elect to defer from compensation into a 401(k) plan for the 2026 calendar year under IRC §402(g), before any age-based catch-up contribution.

This is an increase of $1,000 over the 2025 limit of $23,500.

## Authority (officially published, not a projection)

- **IR-2025-111** (IRS news release, Nov. 13, 2025): "the amount individuals can contribute to their 401(k) plans in 2026 has increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025."
- **Notice 2025-67** (the underlying cost-of-living adjustment guidance for tax year 2026, published in IRB 2025-49, page 761), cited by IR-2025-111.
- **IRS Retirement Topics — 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits**: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- **IRS COLA table, row 'Elective deferrals' (401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing, etc.)**: 2026 $24,500 | 2025 $23,500 | 2024 $23,000 | 2023 $22,500.
- **Publication 560**: "The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026."

Because the 2026 figure comes from a published Notice, there is no estimation or inflation-modeling in this answer.

## Scope and mechanics an HR/benefits administrator must apply

1. **One limit, all elective deferral types.** The $24,500 is a single combined cap on pre-tax (traditional) *and* designated Roth elective deferrals. It is not $24,500 each. Pre-tax plus Roth elected for 2026 must total ≤ $24,500.
2. **Second, independent cap: 100% of compensation.** The statutory limit is the *lesser* of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation (IRS Retirement Topics — Contributions). A participant who earns $18,000 cannot defer $24,500.
3. **Aggregation across employers.** An employee who participates in more than one 401(k)/403(b)/457(b)/SARSEP plan in 2026 aggregates all elective deferrals against the single $24,500 limit (IRS: "you aggregate all elective deferrals you made to all plans in which you participate"). Excess amounts are included in gross income and must be corrected (distribution of excess deferrals plus earnings by the §402(g)(2) deadline, generally April 15 of the following year).
4. **Plan-level limits may be lower.** The plan document may impose a lower cap, and nondiscrimination testing (ADP/ACP) may force a lower effective cap for highly compensated employees. The $24,500 is a ceiling, not an entitlement.
5. **Payroll conversion** (per-paycheck deferral needed to reach the max, evenly spread):
   - 26 pay periods: $942.31 per paycheck (24,500 / 26 = 942.3077)
   - 24 pay periods: $1,020.83 per paycheck (24,500 / 24 = 1,020.8333)
   - 12 pay periods: $2,041.67 per paycheck (24,500 / 12 = 2,041.6667)
   Rounding should be resolved so the annual total lands at or just below $24,500; a final-paycheck true-up avoids over-deferral.

## Excluded from this figure (stated so they are not mistakenly added)

| Item | 2026 amount | Relationship to the $24,500 |
|---|---|---|
| Age-50+ catch-up (most 401(k) plans) | $8,000 | Added *above* the $24,500; not subject to §402(g) |
| Age 60–63 "super" catch-up (SECURE 2.0) | $11,250 (instead of $8,000) | Added above; replaces the $8,000 for those ages |
| §415(c) total annual additions (deferrals + employer money + forfeitures) | $72,000 | Separate outer cap; $24,500 + $8,000 = $32,500, well within it |
| §401(a)(17) compensation limit | $360,000 | Caps the compensation base, not the deferral |
| SIMPLE 401(k) elective deferrals | $17,000 | Different plan type — not the answer to this question |

## Assumptions relied on

US federal law (IR C §402(g)) governs the plan; "2026" means the 2026 calendar/tax year; "elective deferrals" means the employee salary-reduction contribution, pre-tax and Roth combined; no catch-up is included. If the plan is a SIMPLE 401(k), a 403(b), a governmental 457(b), or a non-US plan, the figure differs and this answer should not be reused.

# Current US National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

## Answer

| # | Standard | Level | Units | Form of the standard (40 CFR 50.20) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Primary **annual** PM2.5 | **9.0** | µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter) | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, determined per Appendix N (3-year average of annual means); standard is met when the value is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³ — 40 CFR 50.20(b) |
| 2 | Primary **24-hour** PM2.5 | **35** | µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter) | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, determined per Appendix N (3-year average of annual 98th percentiles); standard is met when the value is ≤ 35 µg/m³ — 40 CFR 50.20(c) |

**As of:** the codified text retrieved 2026-11-16 from eCFR (40 CFR 50.20, "current" edition). The 9.0 µg/m³ annual level was promulgated in the PM NAAQS Reconsideration final rule, 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024), effective May 6, 2024.

## Authoritative text

40 CFR § 50.20 — *National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5* (89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024):

> (a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are **9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration** and **35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration** measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 … by either: (1) A reference method based on appendix L to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or (2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.
>
> (b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m3.
>
> (c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3.

Corroborating EPA statement (https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/national-ambient-air-quality-standards-naaqs-pm): "EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter … EPA is not changing the current: primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards, secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and primary and secondary PM10 standards."

## Values that are NOT the answer (guards against version confusion)

Part 50 contains three PM2.5 sections. Only § 50.20 states the operative *primary* standards today:

| Section | Citation date | Annual | 24-hour | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| § 50.20 | 89 FR 16380 (2024) | **9.0** | **35** | **Current primary standards — the answer** |
| § 50.18 | 78 FR 3277 (2013) | 12.0 | 35 | Prior (2012) primary annual standard; superseded by § 50.20 for the primary annual standard |
| § 50.13 | 71 FR 61224 (1997), am. 81 FR 58149 | 15.0 | 35 | 1997 standards; per § 50.13(d) the 1997 *primary annual* NAAQS no longer applies. The 1997 *secondary annual* (15.0) and the 1997 24-hour standard remain in effect |

Notes on the table: the 24-hour level (35 µg/m³) is unchanged across all three versions, so it is invariant to which version of the rule is consulted. The 15.0 µg/m³ figure that appears in § 50.13 is the 1997 annual level and is also the currently retained *secondary* (welfare-based) annual standard — it is **not** the primary annual level. The request specifies primary standards only, so the secondary annual standard (15.0 µg/m³) and secondary 24-hour standard (35 µg/m³) are excluded from the answer.

## Rounding and comparison conventions (needed to apply the levels)

Per 40 CFR Part 50 Appendix N, before comparison to the level:
- Annual: the 3-year average of annual arithmetic means is rounded to the nearest 0.1 µg/m³ (one decimal place).
- 24-hour: the 3-year average of annual 98th-percentile 24-hour values is rounded to the nearest 1 µg/m³ (integer).
Comparison is "less than or equal to" the level (50.20(b), (c)).

## Caveat and re-verification step

- The EPA PM NAAQS page carries a dated entry: "03/12/2025 — Trump EPA Announces Path Forward on National Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM2.5)…" indicating a reconsideration of the 2024 rule is in progress. No revised PM2.5 level appears in the codified CFR as of the 2026-11-16 retrieval; 40 CFR 50.20 still reads 9.0 / 35. Until a final rule is signed and its effective date passes, 9.0 / 35 remain the current codified primary standards.
- To confirm currency at the moment of use: (1) open https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-50/section-50.20 and read (a)–(c); (2) cross-check the Federal Register document cited in the source note at the end of the section; (3) check https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/national-ambient-air-quality-standards-naaqs-pm 'Rule History' for any action postdating 89 FR 16380. If a later final rule is codified, take the levels from the newest § 50.2x section and update both values and the as-of date together.
